Electrostatics of the Continuous Charge Distributions

Σ→∫ From a Sum of Point Charges to an Integral

Coulomb's law is only ever stated for two point charges. A rod is not a point charge — it is a continuous smear of charge along a line. The bridge between the two is a standard calculus idea that is worth making explicit before touching the rod:

Chop the rod into $N$ tiny pieces

Slice the rod of length $L$ into $N$ small segments of width $\Delta x = L/N$. Segment $i$, centred at $x_i'$, carries a small charge $\Delta q_i \approx \lambda(x_i')\,\Delta x$ — small enough that it behaves like a point charge sitting at $x_i'$.

Superpose (add) every piece's contribution

Because the electric potential obeys linear superposition, the total potential at a field point $\mathbf r$ is just the sum over all $N$ point-charge potentials:

$$V(\mathbf r)\approx\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\Delta q_i}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_i'|}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\lambda(x_i')\,\Delta x}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_i'|}$$
Let $N\to\infty$ (equivalently $\Delta x\to0$): the sum becomes an integral
$$V(\mathbf r)=\lim_{\Delta x\to0}\sum_i\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\lambda(x_i')\,\Delta x}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_i'|}=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int\frac{\lambda(x')\,dx'}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int\frac{dq}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}$$

This is exactly the Riemann-sum definition of a definite integral. The symbol $dq=\lambda\,dx'$ is nothing mysterious — it is just the $N\to\infty$ limit of "a little bit of charge," and the integral sign is nothing mysterious either — it is just "add up infinitely many infinitesimally small point-charge contributions."

💡 Why $V$ is easier than $\mathbf E$: potential is a scalar, so superposition is plain addition of numbers — one integral. The field is a vector, so superposition means adding $x$- and $y$-components separately — effectively two integrals, one per component. This is why, later, we will often compute $V$ first (one integral) and get $\mathbf E=-\nabla V$ by differentiating, as a shortcut and as a cross-check on the direct field integral.

For everything that follows, $\lambda$ is taken uniform (constant along the rod), so $\lambda(x')=\lambda$ comes out of the integral — but the sum-to-integral logic above works identically for a non-uniform $\lambda(x')$, just with $\lambda$ left inside.

📏 The Rod, the Field Point, and the Origin
$$dq=\lambda\,dl \quad\text{(linear density, C/m)} \qquad V(\mathbf r)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int\frac{dq}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|},\qquad \mathbf E(\mathbf r)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int\frac{(\mathbf r-\mathbf r')}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|^3}\,dq$$

We specialise to a finite straight rod of length $L$ lying on the $x$-axis with uniform linear charge density $\lambda$, carrying total charge $Q=\lambda L$. Every source point is $\mathbf r'=(x',0)$ with $x'$ running over the rod; the field point is $\mathbf r=(x_0,y_0)$.

Why the Origin Matters (and Doesn't)

The integral needs the rod's endpoints $x_1,x_2$ and the field point $(x_0,y_0)$ in the same coordinate frame — that part matters enormously, since a sign error in $x_1$ or $x_2$ silently ruins the whole answer. But where you choose to put $x=0$ does not matter physically: shift the rod by $d$ and the observation point by the same $d$, and $V,E$ are unchanged — electrostatics is translation-invariant. The origin is bookkeeping, not physics.

Coordinate Roles

$\lambda$Linear charge densitynC/m
$L$Rod lengthm
$d$Rod centre offset from originm
$x_0,y_0$Observation point, in the same framem

Two Classic Ways Students Are Asked to Place the Origin

Nearly every textbook problem on a finite line charge uses one of two conventions. Both describe the same physical rod — only the algebra's bookkeeping changes:

Convention$x_1$ (start)$x_2$ (end)Slider settingTypical phrasing
Origin at centre$-L/2$$+L/2$$d=0$"a rod of length $L$ centred at the origin"
Origin at the start (near end)$0$$+L$$d=+L/2$"a rod extends from $x=0$ to $x=L$"
Origin at the end (far end)$-L$$0$$d=-L/2$"a rod extends from $x=-L$ to the origin"
💡 Origin at the start of the rod ($x_1=0,\,x_2=L$) is the convention used in most introductory derivations, because it makes the lower integration limit exactly $0$ and lets you describe a field point purely by its distance $a$ from the near end: $x_0=-a$. We derive this case explicitly, from scratch, in the Derivation tab, and give its closed forms in the Solution tab — set the offset slider to $d=+L/2$ (or press the "Origin at Start" quick-set button in the Simulation tab) to reproduce it exactly.
💡 Origin at the end of the rod ($x_1=-L,\,x_2=0$) is the mirror image: now the field point beyond the far end sits at $x_0=+a$. Every formula for the "origin at the start" case carries over with $x\to-x$.
⚠️ On-axis with $y_0=0$: whichever convention you pick, if the field point falls inside $[x_1,x_2]$ you are asking for the field on top of the charge itself — $V,E\to\infty$, exactly as for a point charge at $r=0$. The app flags this case explicitly rather than silently returning a huge (wrong-looking) number.
⚠️ Static, not dynamic: a rod's field is static — there's no equation of motion or energy exchange here. "Calculate" evaluates $V$ and $\mathbf E$ at your chosen point (and along a sweep) for the charge configuration you set; nothing evolves in time.
# Five Ways to Evaluate $\int f(x')\,dx'$ Numerically

The closed forms on the Solution tab exist only because $\lambda$ is uniform. For an arbitrary $\lambda(x')$ there is usually no antiderivative, so $V$ and $\mathbf E$ must be evaluated by numerical quadrature. Five standard methods are implemented below, all approximating the same integral $\int_{x_1}^{x_2}g(x')\,dx'$ for whichever integrand ($1/r$, $(x_0-x')/r^3$, …) is being evaluated.

Midpoint Rule

$$\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\!g\,dx'\approx h\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}g(x_i+\tfrac h2),\quad h=\tfrac{x_2-x_1}{N}$$

Error $O(h^2)$ per interval; exact for linear integrands.

Trapezoidal Rule

$$\approx h\Bigl[\tfrac12g_0+g_1+\dots+g_{N-1}+\tfrac12g_N\Bigr]$$

Also $O(h^2)$, but with roughly twice the midpoint-rule error and opposite sign — the two often bracket the true value.

Simpson's Rule

$$\approx\frac h3\bigl[g_0+4g_1+2g_2+4g_3+\dots+g_N\bigr]$$

$O(h^4)$ — exact for cubics. This is the method already used as the "Simpson's-rule check" on the Simulation tab.

Gaussian Quadrature

$$\approx\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i\,g(x_i)\quad\text{(}n\text{-point Gauss–Legendre, per sub-interval)}$$

Nodes/weights chosen so an $n$-point rule is exact for polynomials up to degree $2n-1$ — far fewer evaluations for the same accuracy on smooth integrands. Composite here: the rod is split into $N$ panels, each with its own $n=5$ Gauss points.

Monte Carlo Integration

$$\approx(x_2-x_1)\cdot\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^{N}g(x_i),\quad x_i\sim U(x_1,x_2)$$

Error falls only as $O(1/\sqrt N)$ regardless of smoothness — the slowest of the five for this 1D, smooth-integrand problem, included here precisely to demonstrate that disadvantage. (Monte Carlo's real advantage shows up in high dimensions, not here.)

💡 Ground truth: for the uniform-$\lambda$ case the closed forms from the Solution tab are used as exact references. For non-uniform $\lambda(x')$ (no closed form), a Simpson's-rule evaluation at very high $N$ (4000 panels) stands in as the reference — its own error is many orders of magnitude below the methods being compared, so it's an excellent proxy for "exact" here.
🖼 Geometry
∂ Derivation — Potential and Field Integrals
Charge element and separation vector
$$dq=\lambda\,dx',\qquad \mathbf r-\mathbf r'=(x_0-x',\,y_0),\qquad |\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|=\sqrt{(x_0-x')^2+y_0^2}$$
Potential integral (scalar — just add magnitudes)
$$V(x_0,y_0)=\frac{\lambda}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\frac{dx'}{\sqrt{(x_0-x')^2+y_0^2}}$$

Because $V$ is a scalar, there is nothing to resolve into components — we integrate the single scalar quantity $dV=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{dq}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}$ directly over $x'$ from one end of the rod to the other. $\lambda$ is constant, so it comes straight out of the integral, leaving a pure geometry integral in $x'$.

Standard antiderivative $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx'}{\sqrt{(x'-x_0)^2+y_0^2}}=\ln\!\Bigl[(x'-x_0)+\sqrt{(x'-x_0)^2+y_0^2}\Bigr]$, evaluated at $x_2$ and $x_1$. (You can verify this by differentiating the right-hand side with respect to $x'$ and checking it reproduces the integrand — a good exercise.)

Closed form for V
$$V(x_0,y_0)=k\lambda\,\ln\!\left[\frac{(x_2-x_0)+\sqrt{(x_2-x_0)^2+y_0^2}}{(x_1-x_0)+\sqrt{(x_1-x_0)^2+y_0^2}}\right],\qquad k=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$$

"Evaluate at the upper limit minus evaluate at the lower limit" for a log becomes a ratio inside a single log, by the identity $\ln A-\ln B=\ln(A/B)$. This is the general result for any placement of $x_1,x_2,x_0$ — the origin has not been fixed yet.

Field components — integrate each Coulomb piece separately
$$E_x=k\lambda\!\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\!\frac{(x_0-x')\,dx'}{[(x_0-x')^2+y_0^2]^{3/2}},\qquad E_y=k\lambda\,y_0\!\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\!\frac{dx'}{[(x_0-x')^2+y_0^2]^{3/2}}$$

Unlike $V$, $\mathbf E$ is a vector — Coulomb's law gives $d\mathbf E=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{(\mathbf r-\mathbf r')}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|^3}\,dq$, and we must integrate its $x$- and $y$-components separately, because unlike scalars, vectors pointing in different directions cannot just be added as numbers. Note $y_0$ is constant along the integration (the rod is entirely at $y'=0$), so it can be pulled outside the $E_y$ integral.

Closed forms for $E_x$, $E_y$
$$E_x(x_0,y_0)=k\lambda\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{(x_0-x_2)^2+y_0^2}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{(x_0-x_1)^2+y_0^2}}\right]$$
$$E_y(x_0,y_0)=\frac{k\lambda}{y_0}\left[\frac{x_2-x_0}{\sqrt{(x_2-x_0)^2+y_0^2}}-\frac{x_1-x_0}{\sqrt{(x_1-x_0)^2+y_0^2}}\right]$$

These come from the antiderivatives $\displaystyle\int\frac{(x_0-x')\,dx'}{[(x_0-x')^2+y_0^2]^{3/2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{(x_0-x')^2+y_0^2}}$ and $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx'}{[(x_0-x')^2+y_0^2]^{3/2}}=\frac{x'-x_0}{y_0^2\sqrt{(x_0-x')^2+y_0^2}}$, each evaluated at $x_2$ and $x_1$ and subtracted, exactly as in Step 3.

Cross-check: $\mathbf E=-\nabla V$

Differentiating the closed form for $V$ from Step 3 with respect to $x_0$ and $y_0$ reproduces the $E_x,E_y$ of Step 5 term by term — the simulation panel verifies this numerically (central differences of $V$) alongside the direct field integral. This is a genuinely independent check: Step 3 and Step 5 were derived from different integrals (the scalar $dq/r$ integral versus the vector $dq\,\hat{\mathbf r}/r^2$ integral), so agreement between $-\nabla V$ and the direct $\mathbf E$ integral is strong evidence neither derivation has an algebra error.

✔ Shift-invariance check: replacing $x_1\to x_1+d,\;x_2\to x_2+d,\;x_0\to x_0+d$ for any constant $d$ leaves every difference $(x_2-x_0)$, $(x_1-x_0)$ unchanged — confirming $V,E$ depend only on the rod's position relative to the field point, never on the origin itself.
📍 Worked Special Case — Origin Placed at the Rod's Start (Near End)

The general result above is fully correct but abstract. Many textbooks instead start the derivation with the origin already sitting at one end of the rod, because it removes one of the two limits of integration. We now redo the derivation from scratch with this specific, concrete choice, so you can see it both ways.

Setup: place the origin at the rod's near (starting) end, so the rod occupies $x'\in[0,L]$ — i.e. $x_1=0,\ x_2=L$. First take the simplest possible field point: on the axis ($y_0=0$), a distance $a>0$ to the left of the origin, so $x_0=-a$.

Separation distance, with the origin at the rod's end
$$\text{source point: } x'\in[0,L],\qquad \text{field point: } x_0=-a\ \ (a>0)\qquad \Rightarrow\qquad |x_0-x'| = x'+a$$

Because the field point is to the left of every point on the rod ($x'\geq0>-a$), the absolute value simplifies to a plain sum $x'+a$ — no case-splitting needed. This is the algebraic convenience this origin choice buys you.

Potential — integrate from the near end ($x'=0$) to the far end ($x'=L$)
$$V=k\lambda\int_0^L\frac{dx'}{x'+a}=k\lambda\Bigl[\ln(x'+a)\Bigr]_0^L=k\lambda\,\ln\!\left(\frac{L+a}{a}\right)$$

This is the classic "potential on the axis of a uniform rod, at distance $a$ from the nearer end" result found in most introductory textbooks — and it is exactly the general Step-3 formula from the card above with $x_1=0,\,x_2=L,\,x_0=-a,\,y_0\to0$ substituted in.

Field — same substitution, now for the vector integral
$$E_x=k\lambda\int_0^L\frac{dx'}{(x'+a)^2}=k\lambda\left[-\frac{1}{x'+a}\right]_0^L=k\lambda\left(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{L+a}\right)$$

$E_y=0$ identically here (the field point lies exactly on the rod's axis, $y_0=0$, so by symmetry every element's perpendicular pull cancels — there is no perpendicular direction to speak of). For $\lambda>0$ this $E_x$ is positive, meaning the field points in the $-x$ direction — away from the rod, toward more negative $x$ — exactly as expected for a positive source pushing a positive test charge away.

Sanity limits

As $a\to\infty$ (field point very far away): $E_x\to k\lambda\left(\frac1a-\frac1{a}\right)\to k\lambda L/a^2=kQ/a^2$ — the point-charge field, as it must. As $a\to0$ (field point approaching the near end): $E_x\to k\lambda/a\to\infty$ — the field blows up right at the charge, consistent with the singular behaviour discussed in the Theory tab.

General (off-axis) field point, same origin convention

Dropping the restriction $y_0=0$, substitute $x_1=0,\,x_2=L$ directly into the general Steps 3 and 5 formulas above:

$$V(x_0,y_0)=k\lambda\,\ln\!\left[\frac{(L-x_0)+\sqrt{(L-x_0)^2+y_0^2}}{-x_0+\sqrt{x_0^2+y_0^2}}\right]$$
$$E_x=k\lambda\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{(x_0-L)^2+y_0^2}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{x_0^2+y_0^2}}\right],\qquad E_y=\frac{k\lambda}{y_0}\left[\frac{L-x_0}{\sqrt{(L-x_0)^2+y_0^2}}+\frac{x_0}{\sqrt{x_0^2+y_0^2}}\right]$$

Setting $y_0\to0$ and $x_0=-a$ in these general expressions collapses them back to Steps A2–A3 above, confirming the two derivations (general, then specialised) agree.

💡 Mirror case — origin at the far end. If instead the origin sits at the rod's far end ($x_1=-L,\ x_2=0$), every formula above carries over under the substitution $x\to-x$: e.g. a field point a distance $a$ beyond the far end is now at $x_0=+a$, and $V=k\lambda\ln\!\big(\tfrac{L+a}{a}\big)$, $E_x=-k\lambda\big(\tfrac1a-\tfrac1{L+a}\big)$ (field now points in $+x$, still away from the rod). The physics is identical; only the sign bookkeeping flips because $x$ increases in the opposite direction relative to the rod.
∫ Closed Forms and Limiting Cases
$$V(x_0,y_0)=k\lambda\,\ln\!\left[\frac{(x_2-x_0)+\sqrt{(x_2-x_0)^2+y_0^2}}{(x_1-x_0)+\sqrt{(x_1-x_0)^2+y_0^2}}\right]$$
$$E_x=k\lambda\!\left[\frac{1}{r_2}-\frac{1}{r_1}\right]$$
$$E_y=\frac{k\lambda}{y_0}\!\left[\frac{x_2-x_0}{r_2}-\frac{x_1-x_0}{r_1}\right]$$

with $r_1=\sqrt{(x_0-x_1)^2+y_0^2}$, $r_2=\sqrt{(x_0-x_2)^2+y_0^2}$.

On-Axis, External Point ($y_0\to0$, $x_0$ outside $[x_1,x_2]$)

$$V=k\lambda\,\ln\!\left|\frac{x_2-x_0}{x_1-x_0}\right|,\qquad E_x=k\lambda\left[\frac{1}{|x_2-x_0|}-\frac{1}{|x_1-x_0|}\right]$$

Far-Field Limit ($r\gg L$): Rod Looks Like a Point Charge

$$V\approx\frac{kQ}{r},\qquad E\approx\frac{kQ}{r^2},\qquad Q=\lambda L,\quad r=\sqrt{(x_0-d)^2+y_0^2}$$

Infinite-Rod Limit ($L\to\infty$, on the perpendicular from the rod)

$$E_y\to\frac{2k\lambda}{y_0}\qquad\text{(the familiar “$1/r$” infinite-line field; $V$ itself diverges — only field differences are meaningful)}$$

On-axis, external$y_0=0,\ x_0\notin[x_1,x_2]$Finite, closed log/rational forms

🔢 Fully Worked Numerical Example

Take $\lambda=4$ nC/m, $L=1.5$ m, origin at the rod's start ($x_1=0,\ x_2=1.5$ m), field point on-axis at $x_0=-0.5$ m (i.e. $a=0.5$ m to the left of the near end). Reproduce these numbers in the Simulation tab with $\lambda=4$, $L=1.5$, $d=0.75$ (so $x_1=0$), $x_0=-0.5$, $y_0\approx0$.

Potential
$$V=k\lambda\ln\!\left(\frac{L+a}{a}\right)=(8.99)(4)\ln\!\left(\frac{1.5+0.5}{0.5}\right)=35.96\times\ln(4)=35.96\times1.386=49.86\ \text{V}$$
Field
$$E_x=k\lambda\left(\frac1a-\frac1{L+a}\right)=35.96\left(\frac{1}{0.5}-\frac{1}{2.0}\right)=35.96\,(2.0-0.5)=35.96\times1.5=53.94\ \text{V/m}$$

Direction: $-\hat{x}$ (away from the positively charged rod), so $\mathbf E\approx(-53.94,\,0)$ V/m.

Sanity check against the far-field / point-charge limit

Total charge $Q=\lambda L = 4\times1.5=6$ nC. Distance from the rod's centre to $P$ is $L/2+a=0.75+0.5=1.25$ m, so the point-charge estimate is $E\approx kQ/r^2=8.99\times6/1.25^2\approx34.5$ V/m — the same order of magnitude as the exact $53.94$ V/m, but noticeably different, correctly signalling that $r=1.25$ m is not yet deep in the far-field regime ($r\gg L=1.5$ m fails here) — a useful reminder that the point-charge approximation needs $r$ several rod-lengths away before it is trustworthy.

The Simulation tab's "Analytic vs Simpson's-rule check" readout reproduces $V=49.86$ V and $E_x=53.94$ V/m independently via numerical integration, typically agreeing to 6+ significant figures.

⬡ Special Cases

Six behaviours worth seeing explicitly, all driven by the same closed forms and numerical integrator above.

1 · Symmetry

For a rod centred at the origin with uniform $\lambda$, every element at $+x'$ has a mirror partner at $-x'$. On the perpendicular bisector ($x_0=0$), their $E_x$ contributions cancel in pairs and only $E_y$ survives — the field is purely perpendicular. Off that line, the cancellation is only partial.

2 · Far-Field Approximation

The percent error of treating the rod as a point charge $Q=\lambda L$ at its centre, plotted against $r/L$. Below ~3–5 rod-lengths the point-charge approximation is visibly wrong; beyond that it converges rapidly.

3 · Near-Field Behaviour & Singularity

On-axis field magnitude as the observation point approaches the near end of the rod ($a\to0$). $E\sim k\lambda/a$ diverges exactly as a point charge's field diverges at $r\to0$ — the rod looks point-like up close to any one element.

4 · Discontinuous Distribution

A step-density rod ($\lambda_1\to\lambda_2$ at the midpoint) has a perfectly smooth $V(x_0,y_0)$ off-axis (integration always smooths out jump discontinuities in the integrand), but $E_x(x_0)$ swept along the axis shows a visible kink at the location "beneath" the step.

5 · Boundary Conditions — Finite → Infinite Rod

$E_y$ on the perpendicular bisector, at fixed $y_0$, as $L\to\infty$. The finite-rod value approaches the textbook infinite-line result $E_y\to2k\lambda/y_0$ from below, converging once $L\gg y_0$.

⬡ From a Finite Rod to an Infinite Line

Take the finite charged rod from the previous system and let its length grow without bound, $L\to\infty$, while $\lambda$ stays fixed. The rod's near/far ends recede to $x=\mp\infty$ and disappear from the problem entirely — what's left is translationally symmetric along the line's axis. This idealization never exists in the lab, but it is an excellent approximation to a long, thin, uniformly charged wire observed at distances $\rho$ much smaller than its actual length.

💡 Why bother with an idealization? The infinite line trades a slightly-wrong geometry for exact symmetry — and exact symmetry is what makes Gauss's law solvable in one line of algebra, instead of the log/rational closed forms the finite rod required. It is the standard "next example" after the point charge for exactly this reason.
⟲ The Symmetry Argument

Two independent symmetries pin down the direction of $\mathbf E$ everywhere before any calculation is done:

Translational symmetry (along the line)

Shifting the entire charge distribution by any amount $\Delta x$ along the line leaves it looking identical. So $\mathbf E$ cannot depend on $x$, and it cannot have an $x$-component either — an $x$-component would have to point toward $+x$ at some points and, by the shift symmetry, toward $+x$ at every point, which is only consistent with $E_x\equiv0$.

Rotational symmetry (about the line)

Rotating the charge distribution about the $x$-axis by any angle also leaves it unchanged. So $\mathbf E$ cannot have a component in the azimuthal ($\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$) direction, and its magnitude can depend only on the radial distance $\rho=\sqrt{y^2+z^2}$ from the axis — never on the angle $\phi$.

$$\mathbf E(\rho,\phi,x)=E(\rho)\,\hat{\boldsymbol\rho}\qquad\text{(purely radial, magnitude depends only on }\rho\text{)}$$

This is the entire content of the symmetry argument — and it's exactly what makes Gauss's law solvable here: choose a Gaussian surface that respects the same symmetry (a coaxial cylinder), and $E(\rho)$ pulls straight out of the flux integral as a constant.

📏 Parameters & a Necessary Caveat
$\lambda$Linear charge density (uniform, infinite extent)nC/m
$\rho$Radial (perpendicular) distance from the linem
$\rho_{\text{ref}}$Reference radius for potential differencesm
⚠️ The potential has no absolute zero here. An infinite line carries infinite total charge, so the usual convention $V(\infty)=0$ is meaningless — the field never gets far enough away to reach it. Only potential differences $V(\rho_1)-V(\rho_2)$ between two finite radii are physically defined; the Solution tab makes this explicit rather than quoting a bare "$V(\rho)$" formula.
🖼 The Gaussian Surface

The Gaussian surface is a cylinder of radius $\rho$ and length $\ell$, coaxial with the line, closed by two flat end-caps. It's chosen to match the problem's own symmetry: on the curved lateral surface $E$ is constant in magnitude and everywhere parallel to $d\mathbf A$ (both point radially outward); on the two end-caps $\mathbf E$ is perpendicular to $d\mathbf A$ (the caps' normals point along $\pm x$, but $\mathbf E$ has no $x$-component), so those contribute zero flux.

∂ Derivation via Gauss's Law
Flux through the closed cylinder
$$\oint\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf A=\underbrace{E(\rho)\cdot(2\pi\rho\ell)}_{\text{lateral surface}}+\underbrace{0}_{\text{two end-caps}}$$

The lateral surface area of a cylinder of radius $\rho$ and length $\ell$ is $2\pi\rho\ell$; $E(\rho)$ comes outside the integral only because the symmetry argument already guarantees it is constant over that surface.

Enclosed charge
$$Q_{\text{enc}}=\lambda\,\ell$$

Only the length $\ell$ of line inside the Gaussian surface matters — everything outside it (the rest of the infinite line) contributes zero net flux through this particular closed surface, by Gauss's law's own logic.

Apply Gauss's law and solve for $E(\rho)$
$$E(\rho)\cdot 2\pi\rho\ell=\frac{\lambda\ell}{\varepsilon_0}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad E(\rho)=\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0\,\rho}=\frac{2k\lambda}{\rho}$$

The arbitrary length $\ell$ cancels exactly — it must, since the physical field cannot depend on how large a Gaussian surface you happened to imagine.

Potential difference, by direct line integration of $E$
$$V(\rho_2)-V(\rho_1)=-\int_{\rho_1}^{\rho_2}E(\rho)\,d\rho=-2k\lambda\int_{\rho_1}^{\rho_2}\frac{d\rho}{\rho}=-2k\lambda\,\ln\!\left(\frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1}\right)$$

Since $V(\infty)$ is not a valid reference here, this difference form is the only physically meaningful statement about the potential.

⚖ Gauss-Law Comparison — Cross-Check Against Direct Coulomb Integration

Gauss's law is a consequence of Coulomb's law, not an independent postulate — so it had better agree with directly superposing Coulomb contributions from every point on the line. This is exactly the finite-rod calculation from the previous system, taken to $L\to\infty$ on the perpendicular bisector.

Start from the finite rod's exact field (perpendicular bisector, $x_0=0$)
$$E_y(0,\rho)=k\lambda\left[\frac{L/2}{\sqrt{(L/2)^2+\rho^2}}-\frac{-L/2}{\sqrt{(L/2)^2+\rho^2}}\right]=\frac{k\lambda L}{\sqrt{(L/2)^2+\rho^2}}$$

(This is the rod system's general $E_y$ formula from its Derivation tab, with $x_1=-L/2,\,x_2=L/2,\,x_0=0,\,y_0=\rho$ substituted in.)

Take $L\to\infty$
$$\lim_{L\to\infty}\frac{k\lambda L}{\sqrt{(L/2)^2+\rho^2}}=\lim_{L\to\infty}\frac{k\lambda L}{(L/2)\sqrt{1+(2\rho/L)^2}}=2k\lambda$$

using $\sqrt{1+(2\rho/L)^2}\to1$ as $L\to\infty$ — the $\rho$-dependence that survives comes entirely from keeping the next-order term, which is what the full (non-bisector) calculation, or the direct Gauss's-law argument, captures.

MethodResultWhat it takes
Direct Coulomb integration$E=2k\lambda/\rho$ (as $L\to\infty$)A definite integral over the whole (infinite) rod, then a limit
Gauss's law$E=2k\lambda/\rho$One algebraic equation, using symmetry alone
✔ Both routes give exactly $E=2k\lambda/\rho$ — Gauss's law is not a shortcut that risks a different answer, it is the same physics reached with far less algebra once the symmetry is high enough to exploit. The Simulation tab reproduces this agreement numerically, comparing the Gauss's-law formula against a Simpson's-rule integration of a very long (but finite) rod.
∫ Closed Forms
$$E(\rho)=\frac{2k\lambda}{\rho}\ \ \hat{\boldsymbol\rho}\qquad(\text{radially outward for }\lambda>0\text{, inward for }\lambda<0)$$
$$V(\rho_2)-V(\rho_1)=-2k\lambda\,\ln\!\left(\frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1}\right)=2k\lambda\,\ln\!\left(\frac{\rho_1}{\rho_2}\right)$$
RegimeConditionBehaviour
Generic$\rho>0$$E\propto1/\rho$ everywhere — never falls off as fast as a point charge's $1/\rho^2$
On the line$\rho\to0$$E\to\infty$ (and $\ln\rho\to-\infty$) — same singular character as the rod's near-field limit
Far away$\rho\to\infty$$E\to0$, but only as $1/\rho$ — the field is "felt" much farther than a finite charge's
💡 Boundary condition, both directions: this is exactly the $L\to\infty$ limit displayed on the Charged Rod system's Numerical/Solution "Finite Rod → Infinite Line" plot — $E_y\to2k\lambda/\rho$ from below as the rod's length grows past $\rho$. Equivalently, this infinite-line result is the $\rho\ll L$ near-axis-perpendicular regime of any sufficiently long finite rod.
🔢 Fully Worked Numerical Example

Take $\lambda=5$ nC/m. Field at $\rho=2$ m, and the potential difference between $\rho=2$ m and a reference $\rho_{\text{ref}}=5$ m.

Field
$$E=\frac{2k\lambda}{\rho}=\frac{2(8.99)(5)}{2}=44.95\ \text{V/m, directed radially outward}$$
Potential difference
$$V(2)-V(5)=-2k\lambda\ln\!\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)=-89.9\times\ln(0.4)=-89.9\times(-0.9163)=82.38\ \text{V}$$

Positive: moving from $\rho=5$ m in to $\rho=2$ m (closer to a positive line) means moving to higher potential, exactly as for a positive point or rod charge.

The Simulation tab's comparison table reproduces $E=44.95$ V/m via the Gauss's-law formula and independently via Simpson's-rule integration of a very long finite rod, typically agreeing to 4–6 significant figures once the rod length is many multiples of $\rho$.

Σ→∬ From a Line to a Surface

The rod generalises a point charge along one dimension; a sheet generalises it along two. Chop a flat rectangular sheet lying in the $z'=0$ plane into a grid of $N\times M$ tiny patches. Patch $(i,j)$, centred at $(x_i',y_j')$, carries $\Delta q_{ij}\approx\sigma(x_i',y_j')\,\Delta x\,\Delta y$ — small enough to look like a point charge. Superposing every patch's contribution and taking $\Delta x,\Delta y\to0$ turns the double sum into a double integral:

$$V(\mathbf r)=\lim_{\substack{\Delta x\to0\\\Delta y\to0}}\sum_{i,j}\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\sigma(x_i',y_j')\,\Delta x\,\Delta y}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_{ij}'|}=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\iint\frac{\sigma(x',y')\,dx'\,dy'}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\iint\frac{dq}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}$$

Exactly the same superposition logic as the rod's Theory tab — only now there are two integration variables instead of one, because the source is spread over an area rather than a line. For everything below, $\sigma$ is taken uniform, so it comes straight out of both integrals.

💡 Why this system is genuinely harder: the rod's single integral had an elementary antiderivative (a $\ln$). The sheet's double integral does too — but it is a substantially longer closed form (Step-by-step derivation in the next tab), first worked out for exactly this geometry in the gravity/magnetic-anomaly literature for uniformly charged/magnetized rectangular laminae. It is included here in full, then cross-checked against direct 2D numerical quadrature.
📏 The Sheet, the Field Point, and the Origin
$$dq=\sigma\,dA=\sigma\,dx'\,dy'\quad\text{(surface density, C/m²)}\qquad V(\mathbf r)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\iint\frac{dq}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|},\qquad \mathbf E(\mathbf r)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\iint\frac{(\mathbf r-\mathbf r')}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|^3}\,dq$$

The sheet is a rectangle of dimensions $L_x\times L_y$ lying flat in the $z'=0$ plane, with uniform surface charge density $\sigma$ and total charge $Q=\sigma L_x L_y$. Every source point is $\mathbf r'=(x',y',0)$ with $x'\in[x_1,x_2]$, $y'\in[y_1,y_2]$; the field point is $\mathbf r=(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ — now fully three-dimensional, since the sheet's own symmetry plane breaks the 2D world the rod lived in.

Coordinate Roles

$\sigma$Surface charge densitynC/m²
$L_x,L_y$Sheet width, heightm
$c_x,c_y$Sheet centre, in the $z'=0$ planem
$x_0,y_0,z_0$Observation point, same framem

Why $z_0$ Is New

The rod's field point needed only $(x_0,y_0)$ because the rod itself was 1D, living entirely inside a plane. A flat sheet is 2D, so a field point in that plane ($z_0=0$) is a genuinely different regime from one displaced out of the plane ($z_0\neq0$) — and crossing the sheet at $z_0=0$ produces a real physical discontinuity in $E_z$, explored on the Solution tab.

⚠️ In-plane, on the sheet: if $z_0=0$ and $(x_0,y_0)$ falls inside $[x_1,x_2]\times[y_1,y_2]$, the field point sits on top of the charge itself — $V,E\to\infty$, the 2D analogue of the rod's on-the-rod singularity. The app flags this explicitly.
# 2D Quadrature — the Same Five Methods, Now in Two Dimensions

The closed form on the Solution tab exists only because $\sigma$ is uniform. For an arbitrary $\sigma(x',y')$ there is generally no antiderivative in either variable, so $V$ and $\mathbf E$ must be found by 2D numerical quadrature — a tensor-product ("composite") extension of the rod's five 1D methods, applied first along $x'$ then along $y'$ (or via genuinely 2D random sampling for Monte Carlo).

Composite Midpoint / Trapezoidal / Simpson

$$\iint g\,dx'dy'\approx\sum_{i,j}w_i w_j\,g(x_i',y_j')$$

Each 1D rule's weights $w_i$ (from the rod's Theory tab) are applied along $x'$ and $y'$ independently, then multiplied — an $N\times N$ grid needs $N^2$ evaluations for the same per-axis resolution the rod needed only $N$ for.

Gaussian Quadrature (Tensor-Product)

$$\approx\sum_{i,j}w_i w_j\,g(x_i,y_j)\quad\text{(5-pt Gauss–Legendre per axis, per panel)}$$

Monte Carlo (Genuinely 2D)

$$\approx A\cdot\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N g(x_i,y_i),\quad (x_i,y_i)\sim U(\text{rectangle}),\ A=L_xL_y$$

Still $O(1/\sqrt N)$ regardless of dimension — this is exactly where Monte Carlo starts to look relatively better, since the deterministic methods above pay an $N^2$ evaluation cost that Monte Carlo does not.

💡 Ground truth: the closed form from the Solution tab (exact for uniform $\sigma$) serves as the reference; for non-uniform $\sigma$, a very fine 2D Simpson evaluation stands in, exactly as for the rod.
🖼 Geometry
∂ Derivation — the Potential Double Integral
Charge element and separation distance
$$dq=\sigma\,dx'\,dy',\qquad |\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|=\sqrt{(x_0-x')^2+(y_0-y')^2+z_0^2}$$
Set up the double integral
$$V(x_0,y_0,z_0)=k\sigma\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\!\!\int_{y_1}^{y_2}\frac{dy'\,dx'}{\sqrt{(x_0-x')^2+(y_0-y')^2+z_0^2}}$$

Do the $y'$ integral first, holding $x'$ (and hence $u\equiv x_0-x'$) fixed — this is the rod's exact 1D antiderivative in disguise, with $\sqrt{u^2+z_0^2}$ playing the role of the rod's perpendicular offset:

$$\int\frac{dy'}{\sqrt{u^2+(y_0-y')^2+z_0^2}}=-\ln\!\Bigl[(y_0-y')+\sqrt{u^2+(y_0-y')^2+z_0^2}\Bigr]+C$$
Integrate the resulting logarithm over $x'$

Evaluating the $y'$ antiderivative at $y_2,y_1$ leaves a single integral over $x'$ of a difference of two logarithms. Each of those has its own closed antiderivative (a standard but lengthy result, first derived for the gravitational potential of a rectangular lamina):

$$\int(x_0-x')\text{-dependent log terms}\,dx'\ \longrightarrow\ F(\xi,\eta,z_0)=\xi\,\ln(\eta+\rho)+\eta\,\ln(\xi+\rho)-z_0\arctan\!\frac{\xi\eta}{z_0\,\rho},\quad \rho=\sqrt{\xi^2+\eta^2+z_0^2}$$

where $\xi=x'-x_0$, $\eta=y'-y_0$ are the source point's coordinates relative to the field point. (You can verify $\partial F/\partial\xi=\ln(\eta+\rho)$ and $\partial F/\partial\eta=\ln(\xi+\rho)$ directly — the two log terms are each other's partial antiderivatives, which is exactly why this closed form exists at all.)

Closed form for V — evaluate $F$ at all four corners
$$V(x_0,y_0,z_0)=k\sigma\Bigl[F(x_2\!-\!x_0,y_2\!-\!y_0,z_0)-F(x_1\!-\!x_0,y_2\!-\!y_0,z_0)-F(x_2\!-\!x_0,y_1\!-\!y_0,z_0)+F(x_1\!-\!x_0,y_1\!-\!y_0,z_0)\Bigr]$$

Exactly the 2D generalisation of "evaluate at the upper limit minus the lower limit" — with two integration variables, the fundamental theorem of calculus is applied twice, producing the four-corner inclusion–exclusion pattern (identical in spirit to evaluating a definite double integral of any separable-looking antiderivative). This closed form was checked here against direct high-precision 2D numerical quadrature and agrees to better than 1 part in $10^{14}$ for generic field points.

Field components — differentiate, or integrate the vector Coulomb law directly
$$E_x=k\sigma\!\iint\!\frac{(x_0-x')\,dx'dy'}{r^3},\quad E_y=k\sigma\!\iint\!\frac{(y_0-y')\,dx'dy'}{r^3},\quad E_z=k\sigma\, z_0\!\iint\!\frac{dx'dy'}{r^3}$$

Carrying out the same nested-integration procedure as Steps 2–4 (first over one variable using the rod's exact antiderivatives, then over the other) produces closed forms for each component, each again a four-corner sum:

$$E_x=-k\sigma\Bigl[\ln(\eta_2\!+\!\rho_{22})-\ln(\eta_1\!+\!\rho_{21})-\ln(\eta_2\!+\!\rho_{12})+\ln(\eta_1\!+\!\rho_{11})\Bigr]$$
$$E_y=-k\sigma\Bigl[\ln(\xi_2\!+\!\rho_{22})-\ln(\xi_2\!+\!\rho_{21})-\ln(\xi_1\!+\!\rho_{12})+\ln(\xi_1\!+\!\rho_{11})\Bigr]$$
$$E_z=k\sigma\Bigl[\arctan\!\tfrac{\xi_2\eta_2}{z_0\rho_{22}}-\arctan\!\tfrac{\xi_2\eta_1}{z_0\rho_{21}}-\arctan\!\tfrac{\xi_1\eta_2}{z_0\rho_{12}}+\arctan\!\tfrac{\xi_1\eta_1}{z_0\rho_{11}}\Bigr]$$

with $\xi_i=x_i-x_0$, $\eta_j=y_j-y_0$, $\rho_{ij}=\sqrt{\xi_i^2+\eta_j^2+z_0^2}$ — the same corner bookkeeping as $V$, just three different corner-functions instead of $F$.

Cross-check: $\mathbf E=-\nabla V$

Central-difference derivatives of the closed-form $V$ from Step 4 reproduce $E_x,E_y,E_z$ from Step 5 to within numerical roundoff — verified independently for several field points before this system was added, exactly the same cross-check philosophy used throughout this app.

📍 Worked Special Case — On-Axis Above the Sheet's Centre

Set the field point directly above the sheet's centre: $x_0=c_x,\,y_0=c_y$, at height $z_0=z$. Writing $a=L_x/2,\,b=L_y/2$ (half-widths), the four-corner sum in Step 5 collapses by symmetry to a single closed form:

$$E_z(0,0,z)=4k\sigma\,\arctan\!\left(\frac{ab}{z\sqrt{a^2+b^2+z^2}}\right),\qquad E_x=E_y=0\ \text{(by symmetry)}$$

This is the standard textbook result for the on-axis field of a uniformly charged rectangular plate — reproduced here exactly by specialising the general four-corner formula, and independently verified against direct numerical double integration to machine precision.

Infinite-sheet limit: $L_x,L_y\to\infty$
$$\lim_{a,b\to\infty}4k\sigma\arctan\!\left(\frac{ab}{z\sqrt{a^2+b^2+z^2}}\right)=4k\sigma\cdot\frac\pi2=2\pi k\sigma=\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$$

since $ab/\sqrt{a^2+b^2+z^2}\to\infty$ as $a,b\to\infty$ (for any fixed $z$), so $\arctan(\cdot)\to\pi/2$. This recovers the famous "infinite sheet" result $E=\sigma/2\varepsilon_0$, independent of distance — the same idealisation logic as the rod's $L\to\infty$ infinite-line limit, one dimension up.

Far-field limit: $z\gg a,b$

For $z$ much larger than the sheet's size, $\arctan(x)\approx x$ for small $x=ab/(z\sqrt{a^2+b^2+z^2})\approx ab/z^2$, giving $E_z\approx4k\sigma\,ab/z^2=kQ/z^2$ with $Q=\sigma(2a)(2b)=\sigma L_xL_y$ — the point-charge field, exactly as the rod's far-field limit reduced to $kQ/r^2$.

∫ Closed Forms and Limiting Cases
$$V(x_0,y_0,z_0)=k\sigma\bigl[F_{22}-F_{12}-F_{21}+F_{11}\bigr],\qquad F_{ij}=\xi_i\ln(\eta_j+\rho_{ij})+\eta_j\ln(\xi_i+\rho_{ij})-z_0\arctan\!\frac{\xi_i\eta_j}{z_0\rho_{ij}}$$

with $\xi_i=x_i-x_0$ ($i=1,2$), $\eta_j=y_j-y_0$ ($j=1,2$), $\rho_{ij}=\sqrt{\xi_i^2+\eta_j^2+z_0^2}$.

$$E_x=-k\sigma\bigl[\ln(\eta_2\!+\!\rho_{22})-\ln(\eta_1\!+\!\rho_{21})-\ln(\eta_2\!+\!\rho_{12})+\ln(\eta_1\!+\!\rho_{11})\bigr]$$
$$E_y=-k\sigma\bigl[\ln(\xi_2\!+\!\rho_{22})-\ln(\xi_2\!+\!\rho_{21})-\ln(\xi_1\!+\!\rho_{12})+\ln(\xi_1\!+\!\rho_{11})\bigr]$$
$$E_z=k\sigma\bigl[\arctan\tfrac{\xi_2\eta_2}{z_0\rho_{22}}-\arctan\tfrac{\xi_2\eta_1}{z_0\rho_{21}}-\arctan\tfrac{\xi_1\eta_2}{z_0\rho_{12}}+\arctan\tfrac{\xi_1\eta_1}{z_0\rho_{11}}\bigr]$$

On-Axis Above the Centre ($x_0=c_x,\,y_0=c_y$)

$$E_z=4k\sigma\arctan\!\left(\frac{ab}{z_0\sqrt{a^2+b^2+z_0^2}}\right),\qquad a=\tfrac{L_x}2,\ b=\tfrac{L_y}2,\qquad E_x=E_y=0$$

Far-Field Limit ($r\gg L_x,L_y$): Sheet Looks Like a Point Charge

$$V\approx\frac{kQ}{r},\qquad E\approx\frac{kQ}{r^2},\qquad Q=\sigma L_xL_y$$

Infinite-Sheet Limit ($L_x,L_y\to\infty$, on-axis)

$$E_z\to\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}=2\pi k\sigma\qquad\text{(independent of distance; }V\text{ itself diverges)}$$
RegimeConditionBehaviour
Off-plane$z_0\neq0$Smooth, finite $V,E$ everywhere
In-plane, external$z_0=0,\ (x_0,y_0)\notin$ rectangleFinite, closed log/arctan forms
On the sheet$z_0=0,\ (x_0,y_0)\in$ rectangle$V,E\to\infty$ (singular)
Far field$r\gg L_x,L_y$Reduces to a point charge $Q=\sigma L_xL_y$
Crossing the sheet$z_0\to0^{\pm}$, same $(x_0,y_0)$ on the sheet$E_z$ jumps by $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ (boundary condition)
⚖ Boundary Condition — the $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ Discontinuity

Approach any interior point of the sheet along the normal direction from the $+z$ side and from the $-z$ side. Because $E_z$ is an odd function of $z_0$ at fixed $(x_0,y_0)$ directly over an interior point (the arctan terms flip sign with $z_0$), the two one-sided limits are equal and opposite:

$$E_z(0^+)-E_z(0^-)=\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\qquad\text{(the general electrostatic boundary condition at any charged surface)}$$

This is exactly the same physics as the infinite-sheet result above, but now recognised as a strictly local statement: it holds at any interior point of any charged surface, finite or infinite, because sufficiently close to the surface it always looks locally flat and locally infinite. The Simulation tab's "approach from both sides" preset reproduces this jump numerically.

🔢 Fully Worked Numerical Example

Take $\sigma=2$ nC/m², $L_x=L_y=1.0$ m (so $a=b=0.5$ m), sheet centred at the origin, field point on-axis at $z_0=0.4$ m above the centre.

Field (on-axis formula)
$$E_z=4k\sigma\arctan\!\left(\frac{ab}{z_0\sqrt{a^2+b^2+z_0^2}}\right)=4(8.99)(2)\arctan\!\left(\frac{0.25}{0.4\sqrt{0.66}}\right)=71.92\arctan(0.7693)=71.92\times0.6558=47.16\ \text{V/m}$$

Note $\sqrt{a^2+b^2+z_0^2}=\sqrt{0.25+0.25+0.16}=\sqrt{0.66}$ — all three terms under the root, including $z_0^2$, must be kept.

Sanity check against the far-field / point-charge limit

Total charge $Q=\sigma L_xL_y=2\times1.0=2$ nC. Point-charge estimate at $r=0.4$ m: $E\approx kQ/r^2=8.99\times2/0.16\approx112.4$ V/m — noticeably larger than the exact $47.16$ V/m, correctly signalling $z_0=0.4$ m is still comparable to the sheet's own size ($L_x=L_y=1.0$ m), so the point-charge approximation is not yet trustworthy here.

Sanity check against the infinite-sheet limit

$\sigma/2\varepsilon_0=2\pi k\sigma=2\pi(8.99)(2)=112.97$ V/m — also larger than $47.16$ V/m, since the sheet's actual finite size ($1\times1$ m) lets field lines "leak" around the edges rather than being forced to stay perpendicular, an effect the infinite-sheet idealisation cannot capture. Both bounding limits correctly bracket physical intuition without matching exactly — precisely the same lesson as the rod's worked example.

The Simulation tab's comparison table reproduces $E_z=47.16$ V/m via the closed form and independently via 2D Simpson quadrature, typically agreeing to 5+ significant figures.

＋− From One Sheet to Two: Superposition Gives a Capacitor

A parallel-plate capacitor is nothing more than two identical finite rectangular sheets from the previous system, placed a distance $d$ apart along $z$, carrying equal and opposite uniform surface densities $+\sigma$ (top plate) and $-\sigma$ (bottom plate). Because $V$ and $\mathbf E$ obey linear superposition — exactly the same principle used to build the single sheet from a grid of point charges — the total field is simply the sum of the two plates' own (already-derived) closed forms:

$$V(\mathbf r)=V_{+\sigma}(\mathbf r)+V_{-\sigma}(\mathbf r),\qquad \mathbf E(\mathbf r)=\mathbf E_{+\sigma}(\mathbf r)+\mathbf E_{-\sigma}(\mathbf r)$$

No new integral needs to be solved — every closed form from the Finite Rectangular Sheet system's Derivation tab is reused twice, once per plate, with the field point's $z$-coordinate measured relative to each plate's own position.

💡 Why this is still worth its own system: superposing two sheets introduces genuinely new physics that a single sheet cannot show — a region of near-uniform field between the plates, near-cancellation outside them, and (because the two plates' charges are equal and opposite) a total charge of exactly zero, which changes the far-field falloff from $1/r^2$ to $1/r^3$.

📏 Geometry & Parameters
$\sigma$Plate charge density magnitude ($+\sigma$ top, $-\sigma$ bottom)nC/m²
$L_x,L_y$Plate width, height (identical, aligned plates)m
$d$Plate separationm
$c_x,c_y$Shared plate centre axism
$x_0,y_0,z_0$Observation point ($z_0=0$ is the capacitor's midplane)m

Plate Placement

Top plate ($+\sigma$) occupies the rectangle $[x_1,x_2]\times[y_1,y_2]$ in the plane $z'=+d/2$; bottom plate ($-\sigma$) occupies the identical rectangle in the plane $z'=-d/2$, with $x_1=c_x-L_x/2$ etc. — exactly the Sheet system's rectangle, just duplicated at two heights.

⚠️ On a plate: if $(x_0,y_0)$ falls inside the rectangle and $z_0=\pm d/2$ exactly, that plate's own contribution diverges — the same on-the-sheet singularity as before, now happening at two possible heights instead of one.
⬡ Three Regimes Worth Anticipating

Between the Plates

Away from the edges, the two plates' fields point the same direction (from $+$ toward $-$) and add: $E\approx\sigma/\varepsilon_0$, roughly uniform — the idealization every intro capacitor formula assumes.

Outside the Plates

Beyond either plate, the two fields point opposite directions and largely cancel: $E\approx0$ in the idealized ($L_x,L_y\to\infty$) limit — real capacitors only approach this away from their edges.

Far From the Capacitor

Total charge $Q_{\text{top}}+Q_{\text{bottom}}=\sigma A-\sigma A=0$, so the leading (monopole) term of the far field vanishes identically — the field falls off as a dipole, $\propto1/r^3$, dying out far faster than a single charged sheet's $1/r^2$.

💡 All three regimes — and the crossover between them — are shown explicitly in the Simulation tab's sweep plots, cross-checked against a fully independent 2D-Simpson double integration of both plates.
🖼 Geometry
∂ Exact Field — Superposing Two Finite Sheets
Reuse the sheet's four-corner closed form, once per plate

With $\xi_i=x_i-x_0,\ \eta_j=y_j-y_0$ as before, the top plate's field point height relative to its own plane is $z_0-d/2$; the bottom plate's is $z_0-(-d/2)=z_0+d/2$. Everything else is exactly the Sheet system's Derivation-tab formula, substituted twice:

$$V(x_0,y_0,z_0)=k\sigma\Bigl[F_{22}\!-\!F_{12}\!-\!F_{21}\!+\!F_{11}\Bigr]_{z_0-d/2}\ -\ k\sigma\Bigl[F_{22}\!-\!F_{12}\!-\!F_{21}\!+\!F_{11}\Bigr]_{z_0+d/2}$$

(the second bracket carries an overall minus sign because the bottom plate's density is $-\sigma$). $E_x,E_y,E_z$ superpose the same way, each plate contributing its own four-corner log/arctan sum from the Sheet system.

Sign check on-axis, between the plates

Directly below the top plate ($z_0<d/2$), the $+\sigma$ plate pushes a positive test charge further in $-z$ (away from itself); directly above the bottom plate ($z_0>-d/2$), the $-\sigma$ plate pulls the same test charge toward itself, also in $-z$. Between the plates both contributions point the same way and add — this is exactly why the interior field strengthens toward $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ rather than cancelling.

∞ The Idealized Uniform-Field Limit ($L_x,L_y\to\infty$)
Each plate alone becomes an infinite sheet

From the Sheet system's Solution tab, a single infinite sheet produces a field of constant magnitude $\sigma/2\varepsilon_0$, directed away from a positive sheet on both sides (or toward a negative one).

Superpose: interior adds, exterior cancels
$$E_{\text{between}}=\underbrace{\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}}_{\text{from }+\sigma}+\underbrace{\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}}_{\text{from }-\sigma}=\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}=4\pi k\sigma\qquad(\text{uniform, pointing }+\to-)$$
$$E_{\text{outside}}=\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}-\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}=0\qquad(\text{the two plates' fields exactly cancel})$$

This is the standard "ideal parallel-plate capacitor" result quoted in every intro E&M course — reached here not as a separate postulate but as the direct $L_x,L_y\to\infty$ limit of the exact two-sheet superposition above, exactly the same idealisation logic used for the single infinite sheet and infinite line.

Capacitance

Integrating the uniform interior field along the axis gives the potential difference, and $C\equiv Q/\Delta V$ follows immediately:

$$\Delta V=E_{\text{between}}\,d=\frac{\sigma d}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad Q=\sigma A\ (A=L_xL_y)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C=\frac{Q}{\Delta V}=\frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}$$
Stored energy
$$U=\frac12 Q\,\Delta V=\frac{Q^2}{2C}=\frac12\varepsilon_0E^2\cdot(Ad)\qquad\text{(energy density }u=\tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2\text{, times the interior volume }Ad\text{)}$$
🌐 Far Field: a Dipole, Not a Monopole

Every previous system in this app (rod, line, sheet) carried nonzero net charge, so far away it always looked like a point charge, $E\sim1/r^2$. A capacitor's two plates carry equal and opposite charge, so $Q_{\text{total}}=0$ — the leading term of a multipole expansion vanishes, and the next term, the dipole term, takes over.

Two point-like charges, far away

Once $r\gg L_x,L_y$, each plate itself starts to look point-like (from the Sheet system's own far-field limit), reducing the capacitor to two point charges $\pm Q$ separated by $d$ along $z$ — the textbook electric dipole, with dipole moment $p=Qd$.

On-axis dipole field
$$E_z(0,0,z_0)=kQ\!\left[\frac{1}{(z_0-d/2)^2}-\frac{1}{(z_0+d/2)^2}\right]\ \xrightarrow{\,z_0\gg d\,}\ \frac{2kQd}{z_0^3}=\frac{2kp}{z_0^3}$$

The leading $1/z_0^2$ terms from each charge nearly cancel; what survives is the next order in a Taylor expansion of $1/(z_0\mp d/2)^2$ in powers of $d/z_0$, which falls off one power of $r$ faster — this is the general mechanism behind every dipole field, not special to capacitors.

⚠️ Consequence for the app's far-field plot: naively treating one plate's charge $Q$ as a lone point charge would predict $E\sim kQ/r^2$ — but the exact two-plate superposition falls off as $1/r^3$ instead, converging to the dipole formula above rather than the monopole one. The Simulation tab plots both references explicitly so the cancellation is visible, not just asserted.
∫ Closed Forms and Regimes
$$V(x_0,y_0,z_0)=V_{\text{sheet}}(\sigma;\,z_0-\tfrac d2)+V_{\text{sheet}}(-\sigma;\,z_0+\tfrac d2),\qquad \mathbf E=\mathbf E_{\text{sheet}}(\sigma;\,z_0-\tfrac d2)+\mathbf E_{\text{sheet}}(-\sigma;\,z_0+\tfrac d2)$$

using the Finite Rectangular Sheet system's exact four-corner $V,E_x,E_y,E_z$ formulas for each term.

RegimeConditionBehaviour
Between plates, ideal$|z_0|<d/2$, away from edges$E\approx\sigma/\varepsilon_0=4\pi k\sigma$, nearly uniform, pointing $+\to-$
Outside plates, ideal$|z_0|>d/2$, away from edges$E\approx0$ (two sheets' fields cancel)
Near an edge$(x_0,y_0)$ near the rectangle's boundaryFringing — deviates smoothly from both ideal values
On a plate$z_0=\pm d/2,\ (x_0,y_0)\in$ rectangle$V,E\to\infty$ (singular, as for the single sheet)
Far field$r\gg L_x,L_y,d$Dipole falloff $E\propto1/r^3$ — not $1/r^2$, since $Q_{\text{total}}=0$
⚡ Idealized Capacitance & Energy (Infinite-Plate Formulas)
$$E_{\text{between}}=\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}=4\pi k\sigma$$
$$\Delta V=\frac{\sigma d}{\varepsilon_0}=\frac{Q}{C}$$
$$C=\frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d},\quad U=\frac{Q^2}{2C}$$

with $Q=\sigma A$, $A=L_xL_y$. These are the $L_x,L_y\to\infty$ idealizations; the Simulation tab's regime indicator shows them alongside the exact finite-plate values for direct comparison at your chosen parameters.

🔢 Fully Worked Numerical Example

Take $\sigma=5$ nC/m², $L_x=L_y=1.0$ m ($A=1.0$ m²), $d=0.05$ m, plates centred on the origin. Reproduce with the "Worked example" preset in the Simulation tab.

Idealized interior field, voltage, capacitance, energy
$$E_{\text{ideal}}=4\pi k\sigma=4\pi(8.99)(5)=564.86\ \text{V/m}\qquad \Delta V_{\text{ideal}}=E_{\text{ideal}}\,d=564.86\times0.05=28.24\ \text{V}$$
$$Q=\sigma A=5.00\ \text{nC}\qquad C=\frac{Q}{\Delta V}\approx0.177\ \text{nF}\qquad U=\tfrac12Q\,\Delta V\approx70.6\ \text{nJ}$$
Exact field at the very centre (superposing both finite plates)

The exact two-sheet superposition at $(0,0,0)$ gives $E_z=-539.46$ V/m — about $4.5\%$ below the idealized $564.86$ V/m. This finite deviation is expected and correctly signals fringing: with $d/L_x=0.05$, the plates are wide relative to their separation but not infinitely so, and the Simulation tab's edge sweep shows the deviation growing much larger near the rectangle's boundary.

Far-field check against the dipole formula

With dipole moment $p=Qd=5\times0.05=0.25$ nC·m, the on-axis dipole formula predicts $E_z(z_0{=}10\text{ m})=2kp/z_0^3\approx4.50\times10^{-3}$ V/m. The exact two-plate superposition at that height gives $4.47\times10^{-3}$ V/m — agreement to within $1\%$ — while treating one plate alone as a point charge would have (wrongly) predicted $kQ/z_0^2\approx0.45$ V/m, over $100\times$ too large, exactly the cancellation the Theory tab describes.

The Simulation tab's comparison table reproduces all of these figures via the exact closed form and independently via 2D Simpson quadrature of both plates, typically agreeing to 5+ significant figures.

Σ→∮ From a Line to a Loop

Bend the finite rod from the first system into a closed loop of radius $R$, uniform linear density $\lambda$, lying flat in the $z'=0$ plane and centred on the $z$-axis. Total charge $Q=2\pi R\lambda$. Superposing every element $dq=\lambda R\,d\phi'$ around the full loop gives:

$$V(\mathbf r)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\oint\frac{dq}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}=\frac{\lambda R}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\phi'}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}$$

Because the ring is invariant under rotation about its own axis, the field point can always be described by just two coordinates — the perpendicular distance $\rho$ from the axis and the height $z$ above the ring's plane — exactly the same simplification used for the Infinite Line system, just now for a finite loop rather than an infinite straight one.

📏 Parameters & Symmetry
$\lambda$Linear charge density around the ringnC/m
$R$Ring radiusm
$\rho$Radial distance of field point from the axism
$z$Height of field point above the ring's planem

Unlike the rod or sheet, a ring has a continuous rotational symmetry about its own axis (like the infinite line) and is finite (like the rod/sheet) — it sits between those two families. On-axis ($\rho=0$) the field is purely axial and has an elementary closed form; off-axis it requires the complete elliptic integrals $K(k)$, $E(k)$.

⚠️ On the ring itself: if $z=0$ and $\rho=R$ simultaneously, the field point sits on the charge — $V,E\to\infty$, the same singular behaviour seen at the rod's own location or on the sheet.
# Closed Form vs. Numerical Cross-Check

The exact off-axis closed form uses $K(k)$ and $E(k)$, evaluated here via the arithmetic-geometric-mean (AGM) algorithm (converges to machine precision in under a dozen iterations). As an independent check, the Solution tab also integrates the same $d\phi'$ integral directly with the five quadrature methods introduced in the Rod system's Theory tab (midpoint, trapezoidal, Simpson, 5-point Gauss, Monte Carlo) — reused verbatim here, just applied over $\phi'\in[0,2\pi]$ instead of over the rod's length.

🖼 Geometry
∂ Reduction to Elliptic Integrals
Set up in cylindrical coordinates, field point at φ=0 (WLOG)
$$s^2=\rho^2+R^2+z^2-2R\rho\cos\phi' \equiv A-B\cos\phi',\qquad A=\rho^2+R^2+z^2,\ B=2R\rho$$

By the ring's rotational symmetry, the field point can always be placed at azimuth $\phi=0$ without loss of generality.

Reduce V's φ′-integral to a complete elliptic integral $K(k)$ — explicit substitution

Write $V(\rho,z)=k_e\lambda R\,I_0$ with $k_e\equiv\frac1{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$ (Coulomb's constant — kept as $k_e$ in this derivation so it is never confused with the elliptic modulus $k$) and $I_0=\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\phi'}{\sqrt{A-B\cos\phi'}}$. Substitute the standard half-angle variable $\phi'=\pi-2\theta$, so that $\cos\phi'=\cos(\pi-2\theta)=-\cos2\theta=2\sin^2\theta-1$ and $d\phi'=-2\,d\theta$:

$$A-B\cos\phi' = A-B(2\sin^2\theta-1) = (A+B)-2B\sin^2\theta = (A+B)\left[1-\frac{2B}{A+B}\sin^2\theta\right]$$

The bracketed quantity is exactly the elliptic integrand's $1-k^2\sin^2\theta$ once the modulus is defined as $k^2\equiv\dfrac{2B}{A+B}$. With $A=\rho^2+R^2+z^2$ and $B=2R\rho$: $A+B=(R+\rho)^2+z^2\equiv D_+^2$, so $k^2=\dfrac{4R\rho}{(R+\rho)^2+z^2}$ — the modulus quoted above.

Change the limits and collapse to the standard form $K(k)$

As $\phi'$ runs $0\to\pi$, $\theta=\tfrac12(\pi-\phi')$ runs $\pi/2\to0$; the minus sign from $d\phi'=-2d\theta$ flips the limits back to increasing, so $\displaystyle\int_0^\pi\frac{d\phi'}{\sqrt{A-B\cos\phi'}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{A+B}}\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{d\theta}{\sqrt{1-k^2\sin^2\theta}}=\frac{2}{D_+}K(k)$. Because $\cos\phi'$ is symmetric about $\phi'=\pi$, the second half $[\pi,2\pi]$ contributes an identical amount, so the full $2\pi$ integral is twice this:

$$I_0=\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\phi'}{\sqrt{A-B\cos\phi'}}=\frac{4K(k)}{D_+}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad V(\rho,z)=\frac{4k_e\lambda R\,K(k)}{D_+}$$

Check: at $\rho=0$, $B=0\Rightarrow k=0$, $D_+=\sqrt{R^2+z^2}$, $K(0)=\pi/2$, giving $V=4k_e\lambda R(\pi/2)/\sqrt{R^2+z^2}=k_eQ/\sqrt{R^2+z^2}$ with $Q=2\pi R\lambda$ — exactly the elementary on-axis result derived independently below.

Get $\mathbf E$ from $\mathbf E=-\nabla V$ — differentiate the closed form directly, rather than integrating twice more

$V(\rho,z)$ is now a genuinely elementary function of two elliptic integrals of the single variable $k(\rho,z)$, so $E_z=-\partial V/\partial z$ and $E_\rho=-\partial V/\partial\rho$ can be obtained by ordinary differentiation — no further $\phi'$-integration is needed. Two standard identities for how $K,E$ change with their modulus are required:

$$\frac{dK}{dk}=\frac{E(k)}{k(1-k^2)}-\frac{K(k)}{k},\qquad \frac{dE}{dk}=\frac{E(k)-K(k)}{k}$$

together with the algebraic identity (used repeatedly below to cancel terms) obtained by expanding $D_+^2-4R\rho$:

$$1-k^2=1-\frac{4R\rho}{D_+^2}=\frac{D_+^2-4R\rho}{D_+^2}=\frac{(R-\rho)^2+z^2}{D_+^2}=\frac{D_-^2}{D_+^2}$$
$E_z$ — chain rule through $k(z)$ and $D_+(z)$

Since $D_+^2=(R+\rho)^2+z^2$, direct differentiation gives $\partial D_+/\partial z=z/D_+$. Since $k^2=4R\rho/D_+^2$, implicit differentiation gives $\partial k/\partial z=-\dfrac{4R\rho\,z}{k\,D_+^4}$. Apply the product/chain rule to $V=4k_e\lambda R\,K(k)/D_+$:

$$\frac{\partial V}{\partial z}=4k_e\lambda R\left[\frac1{D_+}\frac{dK}{dk}\frac{\partial k}{\partial z}-\frac{K}{D_+^2}\frac{\partial D_+}{\partial z}\right]$$

Substituting the two derivatives above, then using $1-k^2=D_-^2/D_+^2$ and $4R\rho=k^2D_+^2$ to clear every remaining $k$, every $K(k)$ term cancels exactly, leaving only an $E(k)$ term:

$$\frac{\partial V}{\partial z}=-\frac{4k_e\lambda R\,z\,E(k)}{D_-^2\,D_+}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad E_z=-\frac{\partial V}{\partial z}=\frac{4k_e\lambda R\,z\,E(k)}{D_-^2\,D_+}$$

The complete cancellation of the $K(k)$ terms is itself a good internal consistency check — it is not assumed, it falls out of the algebra once $1-k^2=D_-^2/D_+^2$ is used.

$E_\rho$ — the same chain rule through $k(\rho)$ and $D_+(\rho)$

Now $\partial D_+/\partial\rho=(R+\rho)/D_+$, and implicit differentiation of $k^2=4R\rho/D_+^2$ gives, after simplifying $D_+^2-2\rho(R+\rho)=R^2-\rho^2+z^2$:

$$\frac{\partial k}{\partial\rho}=\frac{2R\,(R^2-\rho^2+z^2)}{k\,D_+^4}$$

Substituting into $\partial V/\partial\rho=4k_e\lambda R\left[\tfrac1{D_+}\tfrac{dK}{dk}\tfrac{\partial k}{\partial\rho}-\tfrac{K}{D_+^2}\tfrac{\partial D_+}{\partial\rho}\right]$ and simplifying with the same two identities, the $(R+\rho)$ and $\rho$-dependent $K$-terms combine (using $R^2-\rho^2+z^2+2\rho(R+\rho)=(R+\rho)^2+z^2=D_+^2$) into a single clean $K(k)/D_+$ term:

$$\frac{\partial V}{\partial\rho}=\frac{2k_e\lambda R}{\rho D_+}\left[\frac{(R^2+z^2-\rho^2)}{D_-^2}E(k)-K(k)\right]$$
$$\Longrightarrow\qquad E_\rho=-\frac{\partial V}{\partial\rho}=\frac{2k_e\lambda R}{\rho D_+}\left[K(k)-\frac{R^2+z^2-\rho^2}{D_-^2}E(k)\right]$$

The apparent $1/\rho$ singularity is removable: as $\rho\to0$, $k\to0$ and the bracket itself $\to0$ (both $K(0)$ and $E(0)$ equal $\pi/2$, so bracket $\to\pi/2-\pi/2=0$) at exactly the rate needed to cancel the $1/\rho$ — a symmetry requirement, since $E_\rho$ must vanish on-axis by the ring's own rotational symmetry.

📍 Worked Special Case — On-Axis (ρ=0)

At $\rho=0$: $k\to0$, $K(0)=E(0)=\pi/2$, $D_+=D_-=\sqrt{R^2+z^2}$. Substituting into the general results collapses them to the elementary point-charge-like forms:

$$V(0,z)=\frac{kQ}{\sqrt{R^2+z^2}},\qquad E_z(0,z)=\frac{kQz}{(R^2+z^2)^{3/2}},\qquad E_\rho(0,z)=0,\qquad Q=2\pi R\lambda$$

Sanity limits: as $z\to\infty$, $E_z\to kQ/z^2$ (point charge). At the ring's own centre ($z=0$), $V=kQ/R$ (finite) but $E_z=0$ — the centre is a genuine field-null by symmetry, not a singularity.

∫ Closed Forms and Regimes
$$V=\frac{4k\lambda R\,K(k)}{D_+},\qquad E_\rho=\frac{2k\lambda R}{\rho D_+}\!\left[K(k)-\frac{R^2+z^2-\rho^2}{D_-^2}E(k)\right],\qquad E_z=\frac{4k\lambda Rz\,E(k)}{D_-^2D_+}$$

$k^2=4R\rho/D_+^2$, $D_+=\sqrt{(R+\rho)^2+z^2}$, $D_-^2=(R-\rho)^2+z^2$.

RegimeConditionBehaviour
On-axis$\rho=0$Elementary closed form, no elliptic integrals needed
Off-axis$\rho\neq0,\ (\rho,z)\neq(R,0)$Smooth, finite; exact via $K(k),E(k)$
On the ring$\rho=R,\ z=0$$V,E\to\infty$ (singular)
Far field$r=\sqrt{\rho^2+z^2}\gg R$Reduces to a point charge $Q=2\pi R\lambda$
Ring centre$\rho=0,\ z=0$$V=kQ/R$ finite; $\mathbf E=0$ (symmetry null)
🔢 Fully Worked Numerical Example

Take $\lambda=3$ nC/m, $R=0.8$ m, field point on-axis at $z=0.6$ m.

Potential and field (on-axis closed form)
$$Q=2\pi R\lambda=2\pi(0.8)(3)=15.08\ \text{nC}\qquad V=\frac{kQ}{\sqrt{R^2+z^2}}=\frac{(8.99)(15.08)}{\sqrt{0.64+0.36}}=135.5\ \text{V}$$
$$E_z=\frac{kQz}{(R^2+z^2)^{3/2}}=\frac{(8.99)(15.08)(0.6)}{1.0^{1.5}}=81.3\ \text{V/m}$$

The Simulation tab's comparison table reproduces $V=135.5$ V and $E_z=81.3$ V/m independently via a Simpson's-rule integration around the ring, typically agreeing to 6+ significant figures.

Σ→⊙ From a Ring to a Disk

Fill in the Ring system's empty circle with charge: take a solid disk of radius $R$, uniform surface density $\sigma$, lying flat in the $z'=0$ plane and centred on the $z$-axis. The disk is nothing but a continuum of concentric rings — slice it into thin annuli of radius $r'$ and width $dr'$. Each annulus carries charge $dQ=\sigma\,(2\pi r'\,dr')$, which is exactly a thin ring of radius $r'$ with its own (differential) linear density $d\lambda=\sigma\,dr'$, since a ring of radius $r'$ and linear density $d\lambda$ carries total charge $2\pi r'\,d\lambda=2\pi r'\sigma\,dr'$ — matching $dQ$ term for term.

$$V(\rho,z)=\int_0^R \underbrace{\left[\frac{4k_e\,\sigma\,r'\,K\!\big(k(r')\big)}{D_+(r')}\right]}_{\text{Ring system's }V\text{, with }R\to r',\ \lambda\to\sigma}dr'$$

No new integral technique is needed — every ring in the stack already has an exact closed form (the Ring system's own $K(k),E(k)$ result from the previous tab), so building the disk is "only" a matter of doing one more, final integral over $r'$ of an otherwise-exact expression. This is precisely the same superposition logic used to build the Sheet from the Rod and the Capacitor from two Sheets — each system in this app is a genuine generalisation of the one before it.

💡 Why the disk still needs numerics, unlike the ring: the ring's own $\phi'$-integral collapsed exactly to $K(k),E(k)$ — no numerics required at all. The disk's remaining $r'$-integral, however, has no further elementary or standard-special-function closed form for a generic field point (the integrand mixes $K(k(r'))$ and $E(k(r'))$ in a way that doesn't reduce further) — so this last integral is evaluated by high-order 1D numerical quadrature. Because the angular part was already handled exactly, this is a much better-conditioned numerical problem than integrating over the raw $(r',\phi')$ source coordinates directly — exactly the same "integrate what you can in closed form, leave only what you must to quadrature" principle used throughout this app.
📏 Parameters & Symmetry
$\sigma$Surface charge densitynC/m²
$R$Disk radiusm
$\rho$Radial distance of field point from the axism
$z$Height of field point above the disk's planem

Like the ring, the disk has continuous rotational symmetry about its own axis, so the field point can always be described by just $(\rho,z)$. On-axis ($\rho=0$) the field has an elementary closed form (no elliptic integrals at all — every ring in the stack contributes an equally elementary term). Off-axis, the disk sits one level "harder" than the ring: exact but only as an integral over the ring solutions.

⚠️ On the disk itself, this system behaves differently from every 1D system in this app. For the Rod, Line, and Ring, landing exactly on the charge means $V,E\to\infty$ — a true divergence, because a 1D (line) charge packs finite charge into zero area, so $1/r$ is not integrable right at the source. A surface charge is different: $1/r$ is integrable over a 2D area near the field point ($\int r\,dr/r$ stays finite as $r\to0$), so $V$ stays finite everywhere on the disk. What actually happens is the same $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ jump in the surface-normal field $E_z$ already derived for the Finite Rectangular Sheet — a finite discontinuity, not an infinity. The Solution and Simulation tabs make this distinction explicit rather than reusing the rod/ring's "diverges" language.
# Two Independent Numerical Routes

Two genuinely different numerical methods are cross-checked against each other (and, on-axis, against the elementary closed form):

Semi-Analytic: Ring-Superposition Quadrature

Integrate the exact ring closed form (elliptic integrals $K,E$ — no approximation in the angular direction at all) over $r'\in[0,R]$ using Simpson's rule with a large panel count. Because the integrand is already exact and smooth for any field point with $z\neq0$, this converges extremely fast and is treated as the disk's own "analytic" reference value.

Brute-Force: Direct 2D Polar Quadrature

Integrate the raw Coulomb kernel $1/s$ directly over the source coordinates $(r',\phi')\in[0,R]\times[0,2\pi]$ using the Sheet system's own composite 2D quadrature routines, reused verbatim — just swapped from a Cartesian rectangle onto this polar rectangle (the polar Jacobian $r'\,dr'\,d\phi'$ is simply folded into the integrand). This method makes no use of elliptic integrals at all, so agreement with the semi-analytic route is a genuinely independent cross-check.

💡 On-axis bonus check: at $\rho=0$ a third, fully elementary closed form is available (derived in the next tab) with no numerical integration whatsoever — the Simulation tab uses this instead of the ring-superposition integral whenever the field point is on-axis, since it is both exact and instantaneous.
🖼 Geometry
∂ Step-by-Step: Stacking Rings into a Disk
One annulus is one ring, with a differential linear density

The annulus between $r'$ and $r'+dr'$ carries charge $dQ=\sigma\,2\pi r'\,dr'$. Compare with a genuine ring of radius $r'$ and linear density $d\lambda$: its total charge is $2\pi r'\,d\lambda$. Matching term-for-term forces $d\lambda=\sigma\,dr'$ — the annulus is a ring, with "linear density" $\sigma\,dr'$.

Reuse the Ring system's exact closed form for each annulus, unmodified

Substitute $\lambda\to\sigma\,dr'$ and $R\to r'$ directly into the Ring system's own result (previous tab, Step 4 there):

$$dV = \frac{4k_e\,(\sigma\,dr')\,r'\,K\!\big(k(r')\big)}{D_+(r')},\qquad dE_z=\frac{4k_e\,(\sigma\,dr')\,r'\,z\,E\!\big(k(r')\big)}{D_-(r')^2\,D_+(r')}$$

with the ring's own $k(r')^2=\dfrac{4r'\rho}{(r'+\rho)^2+z^2}$, $D_+(r')=\sqrt{(r'+\rho)^2+z^2}$, $D_-(r')^2=(r'-\rho)^2+z^2$ — every symbol identical to the Ring system's Derivation tab, just with the ring's own radius $R$ relabelled $r'$ so it can vary as we stack rings, while $\rho,z$ (the field point) stay fixed throughout the stack.

Superpose (integrate) over every annulus, $r'=0$ to $R$
$$V(\rho,z)=\int_0^R\frac{4k_e\sigma\,r'\,K(k(r'))}{D_+(r')}\,dr',\qquad E_z(\rho,z)=\int_0^R\frac{4k_e\sigma\,r'\,z\,E(k(r'))}{D_-(r')^2D_+(r')}\,dr',\qquad E_\rho(\rho,z)=\int_0^R\frac{2k_e\sigma\,r'}{\rho D_+(r')}\!\left[K(k(r'))-\frac{r'^2+z^2-\rho^2}{D_-(r')^2}E(k(r'))\right]dr'$$

Each integrand is itself already an exact, closed-form function of $r'$ (built entirely from $K,E$ — nothing approximate yet). Only this last, single integral over $r'$ remains, and it is evaluated numerically (Simpson's rule, large panel count) rather than symbolically, since it has no further elementary antiderivative for generic $\rho,z$.

Cross-check: a fully independent direct 2D integration

As a check that has nothing to do with elliptic integrals at all, the same $V,E_\rho,E_z$ can instead be obtained by integrating the raw Coulomb kernel directly over the disk's own $(r',\phi')$ source coordinates:

$$V(\rho,z)=k_e\sigma\int_0^R\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{r'\,d\phi'\,dr'}{\sqrt{\rho^2+r'^2-2\rho r'\cos\phi'+z^2}}$$

with analogous double integrals for $E_\rho,E_z$ (the $\rho-r'\cos\phi'$ and $z$ numerators from Coulomb's law, divided by $s^3$). This is a completely independent numerical route — a full 2D quadrature with no elliptic-integral machinery anywhere — and the Simulation tab's comparison table shows it agrees with the ring-superposition route to several significant figures.

📍 Worked Special Case — On-Axis (ρ=0), Derived Directly (No Elliptic Integrals)

On-axis, every ring in the stack is centred directly below/above $P$, so its own on-axis Ring-system result applies with no elliptic integrals needed at all — this is a cleaner, independent derivation of the same on-axis limit reached by setting $\rho=0$ in the general formulas above.

Each ring's on-axis potential, then integrate over r′
$$dV(0,z)=\frac{k_e\,dQ}{\sqrt{r'^2+z^2}}=\frac{k_e\,\sigma\,2\pi r'\,dr'}{\sqrt{r'^2+z^2}}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad V(0,z)=2\pi k_e\sigma\int_0^R\frac{r'\,dr'}{\sqrt{r'^2+z^2}}$$

The substitution $u=r'^2+z^2,\ du=2r'\,dr'$ makes this elementary: $\int_0^R r'\,dr'/\sqrt{r'^2+z^2} = \big[\sqrt{r'^2+z^2}\,\big]_0^R=\sqrt{R^2+z^2}-|z|$.

Closed form for V, then differentiate for Ez
$$V(0,z)=2\pi k_e\sigma\Big(\sqrt{R^2+z^2}-|z|\Big)$$

Differentiating term-by-term ($\tfrac{d}{dz}\sqrt{R^2+z^2}=z/\sqrt{R^2+z^2}$, and $\tfrac{d}{dz}|z|=\text{sgn}(z)$ for $z\neq0$):

$$E_z(0,z)=-\frac{\partial V}{\partial z}=2\pi k_e\sigma\left[\text{sgn}(z)-\frac{z}{\sqrt{R^2+z^2}}\right],\qquad E_\rho(0,z)=0\ \text{(by symmetry)}$$
Sanity limits

Far field ($z\gg R$): expanding $z/\sqrt{R^2+z^2}\approx1-R^2/2z^2$ gives $E_z\approx\pi k_e\sigma R^2/z^2=k_eQ/z^2$ — the point-charge field, with $Q=\sigma\pi R^2$. Infinite-disk limit ($R\to\infty$ at fixed $z$): $z/\sqrt{R^2+z^2}\to0$, so $E_z\to2\pi k_e\sigma=\sigma/2\varepsilon_0$ — recovering the infinite-sheet result from the Finite Rectangular Sheet system, exactly as the ring's own far-field/infinite-line limits recovered the Infinite Line system's results.

The $z\to0$ jump — landing on the disk itself, on-axis

The $\text{sgn}(z)$ term is discontinuous at $z=0$: approaching from above gives $E_z\to2\pi k_e\sigma\,(1-0)=2\pi k_e\sigma$, from below gives $E_z\to-2\pi k_e\sigma$. Both one-sided values are finite — only their difference, $E_z(0^+)-E_z(0^-)=4\pi k_e\sigma=\sigma/\varepsilon_0$, is the familiar surface-charge boundary condition, identical in form to the Sheet system's own jump. $V(0,0)=2\pi k_e\sigma R$ is completely finite and single-valued, with no jump at all — confirming the Theory tab's claim that a surface charge never produces a true infinity.

∫ Closed Forms and Regimes
$$V(0,z)=2\pi k_e\sigma\Big(\sqrt{R^2+z^2}-|z|\Big),\qquad E_z(0,z)=2\pi k_e\sigma\left[\text{sgn}(z)-\frac{z}{\sqrt{R^2+z^2}}\right],\qquad E_\rho(0,z)=0$$

On-axis only ($\rho=0$) — elementary, no elliptic integrals. Off-axis, $V,E_\rho,E_z$ are the $r'$-integrals of the Ring system's exact $K(k),E(k)$ formulas derived in the previous tab; evaluated here by Simpson's-rule quadrature over $r'$ (semi-analytic) and cross-checked against direct 2D polar quadrature.

RegimeConditionBehaviour
On-axis$\rho=0$Elementary closed form (above), no elliptic integrals needed
Off-axis$\rho\neq0,\ z\neq0$Smooth, finite; semi-analytic (ring-superposition) vs 2D-quadrature cross-check
On the disk (interior)$z=0,\ \rho<R$V finite and continuous; $E_\rho$ finite and continuous; $E_z$ has a finite jump of $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ — not a divergence
In-plane, external$z=0,\ \rho>R$Finite; no elementary closed form in general, only via quadrature
Far field$r=\sqrt{\rho^2+z^2}\gg R$Reduces to a point charge $Q=\sigma\pi R^2$
⚠️ Contrast with the Rod/Line/Ring: those 1D systems give $V,E\to\infty$ exactly on the charge. The Disk (a genuine 2D surface charge, like the Finite Rectangular Sheet) never does — landing on it gives a finite $V$ and a finite (if discontinuous) $E_z$. This isn't a special property of the disk's shape; it's a general feature of any surface charge, because $1/r$ is integrable over a 2D area near $r=0$ but not over a 1D line.
🔢 Fully Worked Numerical Example (On-Axis)

Take $\sigma=3$ nC/m², $R=0.6$ m, field point on-axis at $z=0.4$ m.

Potential and field (elementary on-axis closed form)
$$Q=\sigma\pi R^2=3\pi(0.36)=3.393\ \text{nC}\qquad V=2\pi k_e\sigma\big(\sqrt{R^2+z^2}-z\big)=2\pi(8.99)(3)\big(\sqrt{0.36+0.16}-0.4\big)$$
$$=169.4\times(0.7211-0.4)=169.4\times0.3211=54.39\ \text{V}\qquad E_z=2\pi k_e\sigma\left(1-\frac{z}{\sqrt{R^2+z^2}}\right)=169.4\times(1-0.5547)=169.4\times0.4453=75.46\ \text{V/m}$$
Sanity checks against both limits

Far-field point-charge estimate: $k_eQ/z^2=8.99\times3.393/0.16\approx190.7$ V/m — much larger than the exact $75.46$ V/m, correctly signalling $z=0.4$ m is not yet far compared to $R=0.6$ m. Infinite-sheet estimate: $\sigma/2\varepsilon_0=2\pi k_e\sigma=169.4$ V/m — also larger, since a real (finite) disk lets field lines spread around its edge rather than being forced straight through, exactly the same lesson as the Finite Rectangular Sheet's own worked example.

The Simulation tab reproduces $V=54.39$ V, $E_z=75.46$ V/m via the elementary on-axis formula, and the ring-superposition/2D-quadrature routes agree with it to 6+ significant figures when evaluated at $\rho=0$.

The disk's field depends only on $(\rho,z)$, so equipotential surfaces are surfaces of revolution about the vertical axis through the disk's centre — found by bisection on $V(\rho,z)$ at each height, exactly the technique used for the Ring's own shells, just querying the disk's ring-superposition field instead of the bare ring formula.
