Σ→∮∮ From a Disk's Edge to a Closed Surface

Curl the Ring system's loop into a full closed surface: a hollow spherical shell of radius $R$, uniform surface charge density $\sigma$, centred at the origin. Where the Ring was a 1D loop (one degree of freedom, the azimuth $\phi'$) and the Disk was a 2D filled circle (radius $r'$ and azimuth $\phi'$), the shell is a genuine closed 2D surface parametrised by a polar angle $\theta'$ and azimuth $\phi'$ — the surface of a sphere. Chop it into patches $dA=R^2\sin\theta'\,d\theta'\,d\phi'$, each carrying $dq=\sigma\,dA$, and superpose exactly as every other system in this app:

$$V(\mathbf r)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\oiint\frac{\sigma\,R^2\sin\theta'\,d\theta'\,d\phi'}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}$$

The extra dimension brings a pleasant surprise: unlike the Ring and Disk systems (which needed complete elliptic integrals $K(k),E(k)$, or a numerical stack of them), the sphere's full solid-angle integral collapses to a completely elementary closed form — no special functions at all. This is a consequence of spherical symmetry being the strongest symmetry available in three dimensions: the azimuthal integral over $\phi'$ is trivial (a factor of $2\pi$, exactly as for the Ring and Disk), and the remaining $\theta'$ integral turns out to have an elementary antiderivative, worked out in full in the Derivation tab.

📏 Parameters & the Strongest Symmetry in This App
$\sigma_i$Surface charge density of shell $i$nC/m²
$R_i$Radius of shell $i$m
$r$Distance of the field point from the common centrem

A sphere is invariant under rotation about any axis through its centre — not just one axis, as for the Ring or Infinite Line. The consequence is the strongest possible simplification: the field point's position matters only through its distance $r$ from the centre. Direction is irrelevant by symmetry, so every quantity in this system is a function of $r$ alone — there is no analogue of the Ring/Disk/Sheet's separate "off-axis" regime, because there is no axis to be off of.

💡 Multiple shells, one common centre. This system allows several concentric shells, each with its own radius $R_i$ and density $\sigma_i$. Because $V$ and $\mathbf E$ superpose linearly — the same principle used for every system in this app, all the way back to the Rod's own Theory tab — the total field of $N$ shells is simply the sum of $N$ independent single-shell results, each evaluated at the same $r$. No new integral is required to add a shell.
⚠️ On a shell itself: landing exactly on a shell's own radius ($r=R_i$) is the spherical analogue of landing on the Sheet or Disk — a genuine 2D surface charge. As on those systems, $V$ stays finite (in fact continuous) right at $r=R_i$; only the radial field $E_r$ has a finite jump there, of size $\sigma_i/\varepsilon_0$ — the same general surface-charge boundary condition derived on the Sheet system's Solution tab. Nothing in this system actually diverges to infinity, in contrast to the Rod, Line, and Ring.
⬡ The Shell Theorem — a Preview

The full derivation is in the next tab, but the headline result is worth stating up front, since it is what makes multi-shell configurations worth exploring at all. For a single uniform shell of radius $R$ and total charge $Q=4\pi R^2\sigma$:

$$E_r(r)=0\ \ (r<R),\qquad\qquad E_r(r)=\frac{kQ}{r^2}\ \ (r>R)$$

A field point inside a shell feels no field at all from that shell, no matter how close it gets to the inner surface; a field point outside feels exactly the field of a point charge $Q$ concentrated at the centre — not an approximation, but an exact statement true at every exterior $r$, arbitrarily close to the shell. Stack several concentric shells and superpose: the field at any $r$ depends only on the shells enclosed within $r$ — every shell further out contributes exactly zero, however large its own charge. This is Newton's shell theorem (first derived for gravity; identical mathematics applies to Coulomb's law), and the Simulation tab lets you build multi-shell configurations and watch this rule play out directly in the $V(r)$ and $E(r)$ sweeps.

# Closed Form vs. Numerical Cross-Check

The exact closed form (derived next) is elementary — no series expansions, no special functions. As an independent check, the Solution tab also integrates the same $d\theta'$ integral directly using the generic 1D quadrature methods already introduced in the Rod system's Theory tab (midpoint, trapezoidal, Simpson, 5-point Gauss, Monte Carlo), reused verbatim here over $\theta'\in[0,\pi]$ — exactly the same code-reuse pattern already used for the Ring system's own $\phi'$-integral.

🖼 Geometry

By spherical symmetry, the field point $P$ can always be placed on the polar ($\theta'=0$) axis without loss of generality — the shell looks identical from any direction, so only $P$'s distance $r$ from the centre $O$ matters. The ring shown is one "ring of latitude": all points on it are equidistant from $P$.

∂ Derivation — Rings of Latitude (Elementary, No Elliptic Integrals)
Law of cosines for the separation distance

Place $P$ on the polar axis at distance $r$ from the centre $O$. A source point on the shell at polar angle $\theta'$ is a distance $R$ from $O$; the angle between $OP$ and the source point's own radius vector is exactly $\theta'$. The triangle $O$–(source point)–$P$ gives, by the law of cosines:

$$s^2=R^2+r^2-2Rr\cos\theta'$$

Notice $s$ depends on $\theta'$ but not on $\phi'$ — every point on a given "ring of latitude" (fixed $\theta'$, all $\phi'$) is exactly the same distance from $P$. This is the entire reason the sphere's integral is easier than the disk's: the disk's source points at fixed $r'$ are not all equidistant from an off-axis field point, but the shell's source points at fixed $\theta'$ are all equidistant from $P$, for any $r$.

Integrate over φ′ first — trivial, by the equidistance just noted

Since $s$ doesn't depend on $\phi'$, the $\phi'$-integral of $dq/s$ around one ring of latitude just multiplies by $2\pi$. The charge on the ring of latitude between $\theta'$ and $\theta'+d\theta'$ is $dq=\sigma\,(2\pi R\sin\theta')(R\,d\theta')=2\pi\sigma R^2\sin\theta'\,d\theta'$ (circumference $\times$ width), giving:

$$V(r)=k\!\int_0^\pi\frac{2\pi\sigma R^2\sin\theta'\,d\theta'}{\sqrt{R^2+r^2-2Rr\cos\theta'}}=2\pi k\sigma R^2\int_0^\pi\frac{\sin\theta'\,d\theta'}{\sqrt{R^2+r^2-2Rr\cos\theta'}}$$
Substitute u=cosθ′ — the integral becomes elementary

Let $u=\cos\theta'$, so $du=-\sin\theta'\,d\theta'$. As $\theta'$ runs $0\to\pi$, $u$ runs $1\to-1$; the sign flip from $du$ exactly cancels the reversal of limits:

$$V(r)=2\pi k\sigma R^2\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{du}{\sqrt{R^2+r^2-2Rru}}=2\pi k\sigma R^2\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{du}{\sqrt{A-Bu}},\qquad A=R^2+r^2,\ B=2Rr$$

This is now a completely elementary integral — the same $\int du/\sqrt{A-Bu}$ form as the very first line integral of the Charged Rod system, not an elliptic integral at all. The antiderivative is $-\dfrac{2}{B}\sqrt{A-Bu}$.

Evaluate at the limits — the key simplification, |R−r|
$$\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{du}{\sqrt{A-Bu}}=\left[-\frac{2}{B}\sqrt{A-Bu}\right]_{-1}^{1}=\frac{2}{B}\Bigl(\sqrt{A+B}-\sqrt{A-B}\Bigr)$$

Now substitute back $A=R^2+r^2,\ B=2Rr$: $A+B=(R+r)^2$ and $A-B=(R-r)^2$ are both perfect squares, so both square roots are elementary:

$$\sqrt{A+B}=\sqrt{(R+r)^2}=R+r\ \ (\text{always positive}),\qquad \sqrt{A-B}=\sqrt{(R-r)^2}=|R-r|$$

The absolute value is unavoidable — and it is exactly what will produce two different physical regimes in the next step, precisely as $|R-r|$ appeared for related reasons in the Ring system's derivation.

Assemble the closed form for V(r)
$$V(r)=2\pi k\sigma R^2\cdot\frac{2}{2Rr}\Bigl[(R+r)-|R-r|\Bigr]=\frac{2\pi k\sigma R}{r}\Bigl[(R+r)-|R-r|\Bigr]$$
Split into the two physical regimes

Exterior, $r>R$: then $|R-r|=r-R$, so $(R+r)-(r-R)=2R$:

$$V(r)=\frac{2\pi k\sigma R}{r}\cdot2R=\frac{4\pi k\sigma R^2}{r}=\frac{kQ}{r},\qquad Q=4\pi R^2\sigma$$

Interior, $r<R$: then $|R-r|=R-r$, so $(R+r)-(R-r)=2r$:

$$V(r)=\frac{2\pi k\sigma R}{r}\cdot2r=4\pi k\sigma R=\frac{kQ}{R}\qquad(\text{constant — independent of }r\text{!})$$

The interior potential is completely flat: moving the field point anywhere inside the shell changes $V$ not at all. This is not a coincidence of the algebra — it is the direct statement that no work is done moving a test charge around inside a shell, which is only possible if $\mathbf E=0$ there (Step 7 confirms this by direct differentiation).

Field E_r = −dV/dr — differentiate each branch
$$E_r(r)=-\frac{dV}{dr}=\begin{cases}\ \ 0 & r<R\quad(\text{derivative of a constant})\\[4pt] \ \ \dfrac{kQ}{r^2} & r>R\quad(\text{derivative of }kQ/r)\end{cases}$$

Both branches follow from ordinary single-variable differentiation of Step 6's results — no further integration is needed, exactly the same "get $\mathbf E$ from $-\nabla V$ once $V$ is in closed form" shortcut used for the Ring system.

⚖ Independent Cross-Check — Gauss's Law

Gauss's law reaches the same result in a fraction of the algebra, precisely mirroring the Infinite Line system's own Gauss-law cross-check.

Symmetry fixes the direction and functional form of E

Spherical symmetry means $\mathbf E$ can only point radially, $\mathbf E=E(r)\hat{\mathbf r}$, with magnitude depending only on $r$ — any other direction, or any dependence on angle, would have to look different after some rotation of the (perfectly symmetric) charge distribution, which is a contradiction.

Choose a concentric Gaussian sphere of radius r
$$\oint\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf A=E(r)\cdot4\pi r^2$$

since $\mathbf E$ is both constant in magnitude and everywhere parallel to $d\mathbf A$ over the whole Gaussian sphere — the same "symmetry does the work" logic used for the Infinite Line's cylindrical Gaussian surface.

Enclosed charge and Gauss's law
$$Q_{\text{enc}}=\begin{cases}0 & r<R\ \ (\text{Gaussian sphere entirely inside — encloses no shell charge})\\ Q=4\pi R^2\sigma & r>R\ \ (\text{Gaussian sphere encloses the whole shell})\end{cases}$$
$$E(r)\cdot4\pi r^2=\frac{Q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad E(r)=0\ (r<R),\qquad E(r)=\frac{kQ}{r^2}\ (r>R)$$
✔ Identical to Step 7's result from direct integration — Gauss's law is not a separate postulate here, it is the same Coulomb-law physics reached with far less algebra once the symmetry is high enough to exploit, exactly the lesson of the Infinite Line system's own comparison.
📍 Worked Special Case — the Boundary, r=R

Both branches of $V(r)$ agree at $r=R$: the exterior formula gives $kQ/R$, and the interior formula gives $kQ/R$ identically — $V$ is continuous across the shell, as it must be for any surface charge (verified generally on the Sheet system's Solution tab).

The E_r jump, computed both ways
$$E_r(R^+)-E_r(R^-)=\frac{kQ}{R^2}-0=\frac{k(4\pi R^2\sigma)}{R^2}=4\pi k\sigma=\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$$

Exactly the general surface-charge boundary condition $E_\perp(0^+)-E_\perp(0^-)=\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ derived on the Sheet system's Solution tab, now confirmed for a curved (rather than flat) surface — a good check that the boundary condition is truly local and doesn't care about the surface's shape, only about $\sigma$ at that point.

Limiting cases

Point-charge limit ($R\to0$ at fixed $Q$): the exterior formula $kQ/r$ holds for all $r>0$, recovering an ordinary point charge — a shell shrunk to zero radius is indistinguishable from a point charge from outside, exactly as expected. Far field ($r\gg R$): trivial, since the exterior formula is already exact at every $r>R$, not merely an asymptote — a genuinely different (and stronger) statement than the corresponding far-field limits on the Rod, Sheet, and Disk systems, which only approach the point-charge form as $r\to\infty$.

⊕ Multiple Shells — Superposition and the Shell Theorem
Superpose N concentric shells

With shells of radius $R_1<R_2<\dots<R_N$ and densities $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_N$ (charges $Q_i=4\pi R_i^2\sigma_i$), linearity gives the total field at any $r$ as a plain sum of each shell's own Step-6/7 result, evaluated at that same $r$:

$$V(r)=\sum_{i=1}^N V_i(r),\qquad E_r(r)=\sum_{i=1}^N E_{r,i}(r)$$
Only enclosed shells contribute to E(r) — the shell theorem

For a given $r$, split the sum into shells with $R_i<r$ (call this set "enclosed") and shells with $R_i>r$ ("exterior to $P$"). By Step 7, every enclosed shell contributes $E_{r,i}=kQ_i/r^2$ (it looks point-like from $P$'s vantage point), while every shell exterior to $P$ contributes exactly $E_{r,i}=0$ (because $P$ is inside that shell). So:

$$E_r(r)=\frac{k}{r^2}\!\!\sum_{i:\,R_i<r}\!\!Q_i=\frac{k\,Q_{\text{enc}}(r)}{r^2}$$

the field at radius $r$ depends only on the total charge enclosed within radius $r$ — every shell farther out is, as far as the field at $P$ is concerned, simply not there. This holds no matter how large or small the outer shells' own charges are.

V(r) is a genuinely step-wise-smooth function; E(r) is a step function

Because each shell's own $V_i(r)$ is continuous (Step 6) and each $E_{r,i}(r)$ is a step function (0 inside, $kQ_i/r^2$ outside), the sums $V(r)$ and $E_r(r)$ inherit these properties: $V(r)$ is continuous everywhere (with a slope-kink at each $R_i$), while $E_r(r)$ jumps by $\sigma_i/\varepsilon_0$ at each shell radius $R_i$ and is otherwise a smooth $1/r^2$-type curve between shells. The Simulation tab's $V(r)$/$E(r)$ sweep plots this directly, with each shell radius marked.

💡 Building intuition — a spherical capacitor. Two concentric shells with equal and opposite charge ($Q_2=-Q_1$, $R_1<R_2$) is the spherical analogue of the Parallel Plate Capacitor system: zero field for $r<R_1$ (nothing enclosed), an exact $kQ_1/r^2$ field between the shells (only the inner shell enclosed), and exactly zero field for $r>R_2$ (the enclosed charge $Q_1+Q_2=0$) — a textbook "spherical capacitor" and, taken further out, the spherical case of a shielded/Faraday-cage configuration. Try this configuration directly with the "Spherical capacitor" preset in the Simulation tab.
∫ Closed Forms and Regimes (Single Shell)
$$V(r)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{kQ}{R} & r\le R\\[6pt]\dfrac{kQ}{r} & r\ge R\end{cases}\qquad\qquad E_r(r)=\begin{cases}0 & r<R\\[4pt]\dfrac{kQ}{r^2} & r>R\end{cases}\qquad Q=4\pi R^2\sigma$$
RegimeConditionBehaviour
Interior$r<R$$V$ constant $=kQ/R$; $E_r=0$ identically
On the shell$r=R$$V$ finite and continuous ($=kQ/R$); $E_r$ has a finite jump of $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$
Exterior$r>R$Exactly a point charge $Q$ at every exterior $r$ — not just an asymptote
R→0 limitfixed $Q$Reduces to an ordinary point charge for all $r>0$
⚠️ Contrast with the Rod/Line/Ring: those 1D systems give $V,E\to\infty$ exactly on the charge. Like the Sheet and Disk (genuine 2D surface charges), the shell never does — $V$ stays finite and continuous everywhere, including at $r=R$; only $E_r$ has a finite jump there.
🔢 Fully Worked Numerical Examples — Single, Double, and Triple Shell

All three cases below use $k=8.99\ \text{V·m/nC}$, the same value used throughout this app, and every field value is cross-checked against the boundary condition $E_r(R_i^+)-E_r(R_i^-)=\sigma_i/\varepsilon_0=4\pi k\sigma_i$ derived on the Derivation tab — a good way to catch an arithmetic slip, since that jump must match $4\pi k\sigma_i$ at every shell, regardless of how many other shells are present.

1 · Single Shell

$\sigma=4$ nC/m², $R=0.5$ m. Evaluate at $r=0.3$ m (interior) and $r=1.2$ m (exterior).

Total charge
$$Q=4\pi R^2\sigma=4\pi(0.5)^2(4)=4\pi(0.25)(4)=12.57\ \text{nC}$$
Interior point, $r=0.3$ m $<R$
$$V(0.3)=\frac{kQ}{R}=\frac{(8.99)(12.57)}{0.5}=\frac{113.0}{0.5}=225.9\ \text{V},\qquad E_r(0.3)=0$$

$V$ takes the same value $225.9$ V at every interior radius — it does not depend on $r$ at all, only on $R$ — while $E_r$ vanishes identically no matter how close $r$ gets to $R$.

Exterior point, $r=1.2$ m $>R$
$$V(1.2)=\frac{kQ}{r}=\frac{113.0}{1.2}=94.2\ \text{V}\qquad E_r(1.2)=\frac{kQ}{r^2}=\frac{113.0}{1.44}=78.5\ \text{V/m}$$
Boundary check at $r=R=0.5$ m
$$E_r(R^+)=\frac{kQ}{R^2}=\frac{113.0}{0.25}=452.0\ \text{V/m},\qquad E_r(R^-)=0\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \Delta E_r=452.0\ \text{V/m}$$

Compare with the predicted jump $\sigma/\varepsilon_0=4\pi k\sigma=4\pi(8.99)(4)=451.9$ V/m — matches to within rounding. $V$ itself is continuous: both the interior formula (at $r\to R^-$) and the exterior formula (at $r\to R^+$) give $kQ/R=225.9$ V.

2 · Two Shells — Spherical Capacitor

$\sigma_1=+6$ nC/m² at $R_1=0.4$ m; $\sigma_2$ chosen so that $Q_2=-Q_1$, at $R_2=0.9$ m.

Charges
$$Q_1=4\pi R_1^2\sigma_1=4\pi(0.16)(6)=12.06\ \text{nC}\qquad Q_2=-Q_1=-12.06\ \text{nC}\quad\Rightarrow\quad \sigma_2=\frac{Q_2}{4\pi R_2^2}=\frac{-12.06}{4\pi(0.81)}=-1.185\ \text{nC/m}^2$$
Interior to both shells, $r=0.2$ m $<R_1$
$$V(0.2)=k\!\left(\frac{Q_1}{R_1}+\frac{Q_2}{R_2}\right)=8.99\!\left(\frac{12.06}{0.4}-\frac{12.06}{0.9}\right)=8.99(30.15-13.40)=8.99(16.75)=150.6\ \text{V},\qquad E_r(0.2)=0$$

Nothing is enclosed at this radius, so — exactly as for the single shell — $E_r=0$ while $V$ still sits at a nonzero, $r$-independent plateau set by both shells' own surface potentials.

Between the shells, $r=0.6$ m ($R_1<r<R_2$)
$$E_r(0.6)=\frac{kQ_1}{r^2}=\frac{(8.99)(12.06)}{0.36}=\frac{108.4}{0.36}=301.1\ \text{V/m}$$
$$V(0.6)=k\!\left(\frac{Q_1}{r}+\frac{Q_2}{R_2}\right)=8.99\!\left(\frac{12.06}{0.6}-13.40\right)=8.99(20.10-13.40)=8.99(6.70)=60.2\ \text{V}$$

Only the inner shell is enclosed here, so $E_r$ behaves exactly as if the outer shell didn't exist — a direct instance of the shell theorem.

Outside both shells, $r=1.5$ m $>R_2$
$$E_r(1.5)=\frac{k(Q_1+Q_2)}{r^2}=\frac{k(0)}{1.5^2}=0\ \text{V/m}\qquad\qquad V(1.5)=\frac{k(Q_1+Q_2)}{r}=\frac{k(0)}{1.5}=0\ \text{V}$$

Because the enclosed charge $Q_1+Q_2=0$, both $E_r$ and $V$ vanish everywhere outside — not merely negligible, but exactly zero at every exterior $r$. This is the textbook electrostatic-shielding result: from outside, a spherical capacitor with $Q_2=-Q_1$ is indistinguishable from no charge at all.

Boundary checks at $R_1=0.4$ m and $R_2=0.9$ m
$$\Delta E_r(R_1)=\frac{kQ_1}{R_1^2}-0=\frac{108.4}{0.16}=677.5\ \text{V/m}\quad\text{vs.}\quad \sigma_1/\varepsilon_0=4\pi(8.99)(6)=677.9\ \text{V/m}\ \checkmark$$
$$\Delta E_r(R_2)=0-\frac{kQ_1}{R_2^2}=0-\frac{108.4}{0.81}=-133.8\ \text{V/m}\quad\text{vs.}\quad \sigma_2/\varepsilon_0=4\pi(8.99)(-1.185)=-133.9\ \text{V/m}\ \checkmark$$

Both jumps match $4\pi k\sigma_i$ to within rounding, and $V$ is continuous at both boundaries (evaluating the formula on either side of $R_1$ or $R_2$ gives the same number in each case — $150.6$ V and $0$ V respectively). The Simulation tab's "Spherical capacitor" preset reproduces this exact configuration and its $V(r)$/$E(r)$ sweeps directly.

3 · Three Shells — Shielding Configuration

$\sigma_1=+5$ nC/m² at $R_1=0.5$ m; $\sigma_2=-4$ nC/m² at $R_2=1.0$ m; $\sigma_3=+2$ nC/m² at $R_3=1.8$ m — the same values as the Simulation tab's "Three-shell shielding" preset.

Charges and running totals
$$Q_1=4\pi(0.25)(5)=15.71\ \text{nC}\qquad Q_2=4\pi(1.0)(-4)=-50.27\ \text{nC}\qquad Q_3=4\pi(3.24)(2)=81.43\ \text{nC}$$
$$Q_1+Q_2=-34.56\ \text{nC}\qquad Q_1+Q_2+Q_3=Q_{\text{tot}}=46.87\ \text{nC}$$
Interior to all three, $r=0.3$ m $<R_1$
$$V(0.3)=k\!\left(\frac{Q_1}{R_1}+\frac{Q_2}{R_2}+\frac{Q_3}{R_3}\right)=8.99(31.42-50.27+45.24)=8.99(26.39)=237.3\ \text{V},\qquad E_r(0.3)=0$$
Between shells 1 and 2, $r=0.7$ m ($R_1<r<R_2$)
$$E_r(0.7)=\frac{kQ_1}{r^2}=\frac{(8.99)(15.71)}{0.49}=\frac{141.2}{0.49}=288.2\ \text{V/m}$$
$$V(0.7)=k\!\left(\frac{Q_1}{r}+\frac{Q_2}{R_2}+\frac{Q_3}{R_3}\right)=8.99(22.44-50.27+45.24)=8.99(17.41)=156.5\ \text{V}$$

Only shell 1 is enclosed, so $E_r$ depends only on $Q_1$ — shells 2 and 3 contribute nothing to the field here, only to $V$ (through their own, still-interior, constant terms).

Between shells 2 and 3, $r=1.3$ m ($R_2<r<R_3$)
$$E_r(1.3)=\frac{k(Q_1+Q_2)}{r^2}=\frac{(8.99)(-34.56)}{1.69}=\frac{-310.7}{1.69}=-183.9\ \text{V/m}$$
$$V(1.3)=k\!\left(\frac{Q_1+Q_2}{r}+\frac{Q_3}{R_3}\right)=8.99(-26.58+45.24)=8.99(18.66)=167.7\ \text{V}$$

$E_r$ is now negative — the net enclosed charge $Q_1+Q_2=-34.56$ nC is negative, so the field points inward here, toward the centre, exactly as the shell theorem predicts once you track the running enclosed charge rather than any single shell's own sign.

Outside all three, $r=2.5$ m $>R_3$
$$E_r(2.5)=\frac{kQ_{\text{tot}}}{r^2}=\frac{(8.99)(46.87)}{6.25}=\frac{421.4}{6.25}=67.4\ \text{V/m}\qquad V(2.5)=\frac{kQ_{\text{tot}}}{r}=\frac{421.4}{2.5}=168.6\ \text{V}$$

With all three shells enclosed, the configuration looks exactly like a single point charge $Q_{\text{tot}}=46.87$ nC sitting at the centre — the same exact-at-every-exterior-$r$ statement proved on the Derivation tab for one shell, now applied to the sum.

Boundary checks at all three radii
$$\Delta E_r(R_1)=\frac{kQ_1}{R_1^2}-0=\frac{141.2}{0.25}=564.6\ \text{V/m}\quad\text{vs.}\quad 4\pi(8.99)(5)=564.9\ \text{V/m}\ \checkmark$$
$$\Delta E_r(R_2)=\frac{k(Q_1+Q_2)}{R_2^2}-\frac{kQ_1}{R_2^2}=-310.7-141.2=-451.8\ \text{V/m}\quad\text{vs.}\quad 4\pi(8.99)(-4)=-451.9\ \text{V/m}\ \checkmark$$
$$\Delta E_r(R_3)=\frac{kQ_{\text{tot}}}{R_3^2}-\frac{k(Q_1+Q_2)}{R_3^2}=130.1-(-95.9)=226.0\ \text{V/m}\quad\text{vs.}\quad 4\pi(8.99)(2)=226.0\ \text{V/m}\ \checkmark$$

Every jump matches $4\pi k\sigma_i$ at its own shell, independent of how many other shells are present or what charge they carry — exactly the "boundary conditions are local" principle stated on the Derivation tab. $V(r)$ itself is continuous through all three boundaries: evaluating the formula from either side of each radius gives the same number — $V(R_1)=237.3$ V, $V(R_2)=k[(Q_1+Q_2)/R_2+Q_3/R_3]=8.99(-34.56+45.24)=96.0$ V, and $V(R_3)=kQ_{\text{tot}}/R_3=421.4/1.8=234.1$ V — matching whichever side's formula you evaluate it from. The Simulation tab's "Three-shell shielding" preset reproduces this exact configuration, with $r_0=1.3$ m matching Step 13 above.

In every case above, the Simulation tab's comparison table reproduces these figures independently via Simpson's-rule integration over the polar angle $\theta'$ (summed over however many shells are present), typically agreeing with the closed form to 6+ significant figures away from any $r=R_i$.

◈ Interactive 3D Field Visualization

Because the field depends only on $r$, every equipotential surface — for a single shell, for any combination of shells, for any point at all — is exactly a sphere centred at the origin. No bisection or root-finding is needed here, unlike every other curved-surface 3D scene in this app (Sheet, Plate, Ring, Disk): the condition "$V=$ const" literally is "$r=$ const". ∮∮→∭ From a Hollow Shell to a Solid Ball

Every system so far in this app has put charge on a curve (Rod, Ring) or a surface (Sheet, Disk, Shell). This system fills in the Shell system's empty interior: a solid ball of radius $R$ carrying a genuine volume charge density $\rho(r')$ — charge per unit volume (C/m³), possibly varying with distance from the centre but never with angle. Chop the ball into thin concentric shells of radius $r'$ and thickness $dr'$. Each shell carries $dq=\rho(r')\,4\pi r'^2\,dr'$ — precisely the Shell system's own charge element, with the shell's uniform surface density there now replaced by the differential $\sigma_{\text{eff}}=\rho(r')\,dr'$. Superposing every shell in the stack, exactly as the Disk system superposed rings to build a filled circle:

$$V(\mathbf r)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_0^R\!\left[\frac{4\pi r'^2\,\rho(r')\,dr'}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}\right]$$

No new geometry needs to be worked out — every shell in the stack already has an exact closed form (the Shell system's own $V(r),E_r(r)$ result from the previous tab). Building the solid sphere is "only" a matter of carrying out one further integral, over the shell radius $r'$, of an expression that is itself already exact.

💡 Why the uniform case is special. For $\rho(r')=\rho_0$ constant, this last integral has an elementary antiderivative (Derivation tab) — no quadrature is needed anywhere. For a graded density (denser toward the core, toward the surface, or with a diffuse Woods–Saxon-style edge, as used for nuclear charge distributions), the integral has no simple closed form in general and is evaluated numerically — but the angular part was already handled exactly by reusing the Shell system's result, so this is a well-conditioned 1D problem, not a raw 3D one.
📏 Parameters & the Master Formula
$\rho(r')$Volume charge density profilenC/m³
$R$Sphere radiusm
$r$Distance of the field point from the centrem

Spherical symmetry is exactly as strong here as for the hollow Shell: the field point's direction is irrelevant, and every quantity depends on $r$ alone. Gauss's law (Derivation tab) gives the single formula that governs every profile in this system, uniform or not:

$$E_r(r)=\frac{k\,Q_{\text{enc}}(r)}{r^2},\qquad Q_{\text{enc}}(r)=4\pi\!\int_0^{\min(r,R)}\!\rho(r')\,r'^2\,dr'$$

This is the volume-charge generalisation of the Shell system's own shell theorem: the field at $r$ depends only on the charge enclosed within $r$, and — because $\rho$ is now spread continuously rather than concentrated on a single radius — $Q_{\text{enc}}(r)$ grows smoothly with $r$ instead of jumping at discrete shell radii.

💡 Selectable density profiles. The Simulation and 3D Scene tabs let $\rho(r')$ be: uniform ($\rho_0$, elementary closed form); linear ($\rho_0[1+\alpha(1-r'/R)]$, denser toward the core for $\alpha>0$); power-law ($\rho_0(r'/R)^n$, concentrated toward the surface for $n>0$); and Woods–Saxon ($\rho_0/[1+e^{(r'-R)/a}]$, a smoothly diffuse edge of width $a$ — the standard empirical form for nuclear charge distributions, exactly the profile used elsewhere in this project's Woods–Saxon work).
⚠️ No true singularity anywhere. Like the Disk and Shell (both surface charges) — but for an even stronger reason — a volume charge never diverges. $\rho$ itself stays finite at every point, so $V$ and $\mathbf E$ are smooth and finite throughout the ball, including at $r=0$ and at $r=R$. There is no analogue anywhere in this system of the Rod/Line/Ring's on-the-charge divergence, nor even of the Sheet/Disk/Shell's finite $E$-jump — a volume density produces no discontinuity in $E_r$ at all (Solution tab).
# Two Independent Numerical Routes

Exactly the same cross-check philosophy as the Disk system, one dimension further in:

Semi-Analytic: Shell-Superposition Quadrature

Integrate the exact Shell-system closed form over $r'\in[0,R]$ with Simpson's rule at high panel count. For uniform $\rho$ this reduces to the elementary formula below; for graded profiles it converges rapidly since the angular integral was already done exactly.

Brute-Force: Direct 3D Monte Carlo

Integrate the raw Coulomb kernel $\rho(r')/s$ directly over the ball's own $(r',\theta',\phi')$ source coordinates by random sampling, with the volume element $r'^2\sin\theta'$ folded in explicitly as a Jacobian weight — no shell machinery, no elliptic integrals, nothing borrowed from the closed form. Genuinely independent, at the cost of the usual $O(1/\sqrt N)$ Monte Carlo convergence.

🖼 Geometry
∂ Derivation — Stacking Shells (No New Angular Integral)
One thin shell is one Shell-system charge, with a differential density

The shell between $r'$ and $r'+dr'$ carries $dq=\rho(r')\,4\pi r'^2\,dr'$. Compare with a genuine shell of radius $r'$ and surface density $d\sigma$: its total charge is $4\pi r'^2\,d\sigma$. Matching term-for-term forces $d\sigma=\rho(r')\,dr'$ — exactly the Disk system's own "annulus is a ring" argument, one dimension up.

Reuse the Shell system's exact result for each shell, unmodified

Substitute $\sigma\to\rho(r')\,dr'$ and $R\to r'$ directly into the Shell system's own two-branch result (previous tab):

$$dV(r)=\begin{cases} k\,dq/r' & r<r'\ \ (\text{shell exterior to }P)\\ k\,dq/r & r>r'\ \ (\text{shell enclosed})\end{cases}\qquad dE_r(r)=\begin{cases}0 & r<r'\\ k\,dq/r^2 & r>r'\end{cases}$$

with $dq=4\pi\rho(r')r'^2\,dr'$ — the same case split that produced the shell theorem, now applied to an infinitesimally thin shell at every radius in the stack.

Superpose (integrate) over every shell, r′=0 to R
$$V(r)=\frac{k}{r}\int_0^{r}4\pi\rho(r')r'^2\,dr' \;+\; k\!\int_{r}^{R}4\pi\rho(r')r'\,dr',\qquad E_r(r)=\frac{k}{r^2}\int_0^{r}4\pi\rho(r')r'^2\,dr'$$

(For $r\ge R$ the first integral runs to $R$ and the second is empty, collapsing both to the familiar exterior point-charge forms.) The $E_r$ integral is exactly $kQ_{\text{enc}}(r)/r^2$ from the Theory tab's master formula — Gauss's law, reached here by direct superposition rather than posited separately (Step 5 re-derives it independently).

Specialise to uniform ρ — both integrals become elementary

With $\rho(r')=\rho_0$ constant, $\int_0^r r'^2dr'=r^3/3$ and $\int_r^R r'dr'=(R^2-r^2)/2$:

$$V(r)=\frac{4\pi k\rho_0}{r}\cdot\frac{r^3}{3}+4\pi k\rho_0\cdot\frac{R^2-r^2}{2}=\frac{4\pi k\rho_0 r^2}{3}+2\pi k\rho_0(R^2-r^2)=2\pi k\rho_0\!\left(R^2-\frac{r^2}{3}\right)$$

With $Q=\tfrac43\pi R^3\rho_0$ (so $\rho_0=3Q/4\pi R^3$ and $2\pi k\rho_0=3kQ/2R^3$):

$$V(r)=\frac{kQ}{2R}\left(3-\frac{r^2}{R^2}\right)\quad(r\le R),\qquad\qquad E_r(r)=\frac{kQ\,r}{R^3}\quad(r<R)$$

Differentiating $V(r)$ directly, $E_r=-dV/dr=-\big(-kQ\cdot 2r/(2R^3)\big)=kQr/R^3$ — matching the Gauss's-law result of Step 5 term for term, exactly the $\mathbf E=-\nabla V$ cross-check used throughout this app.

Independent cross-check: Gauss's law, uniform ρ

A concentric Gaussian sphere of radius $r<R$ encloses a fraction $(r/R)^3$ of the total volume (volume scales as $r^3$ at fixed density), so $Q_{\text{enc}}(r)=Q(r/R)^3$. Gauss's law $E_r\cdot4\pi r^2=Q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0$ gives $E_r=kQ(r/R)^3/r^2=kQr/R^3$ — identical to Step 4, reached with far less algebra, mirroring every other Gauss-law cross-check in this app (Infinite Line, Hollow Shell).

Boundary check at r=R — E is continuous (unlike the Shell system)

Interior formula at $r\to R^-$: $E_r\to kQ/R^2$. Exterior formula at $r\to R^+$: $E_r=kQ/R^2$ identically. No jump. This is the key physical distinction from the hollow Shell system: that system's charge sits entirely at one radius, producing a true surface density and hence a finite $E_r$ jump of $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ there. A volume charge has no surface density anywhere — $\rho(R^-)$ can differ from the (zero) exterior density, but that is a jump in $\rho$, not in $\mathbf E$, and Gauss's law only ties a field discontinuity to a surface (delta-function) charge, which this system never has.

General (non-uniform) profile — the master formula stands

Nothing in Steps 1–3 assumed $\rho$ was constant — $Q_{\text{enc}}(r)=4\pi\int_0^{\min(r,R)}\rho(r')r'^2dr'$ and $E_r(r)=kQ_{\text{enc}}(r)/r^2$ hold for any spherically symmetric $\rho(r')$, graded or not. Only the closed-form evaluation of that integral was special to the uniform case; for graded profiles (linear, power-law, Woods–Saxon) the same integral is evaluated numerically on the Simulation tab, with the uniform case's exact result available throughout as a built-in sanity check (set the profile to "Uniform" and compare against Step 4's formula directly).

∫ Closed-Form Solutions for Graded Density Profiles

Step 7 noted that the general master formula holds for any $\rho(r')$, with only the uniform case singled out for an elementary antiderivative. That was more pessimistic than necessary: the power-law and linear profiles both integrate in closed form too — only the Woods–Saxon profile's exponential denominator genuinely resists an elementary antiderivative and is left to numerical quadrature (Simulation tab). Both derivations below follow the identical two-piece pattern as Step 4 (uniform case): integrate $Q_{\text{enc}}(r)$ for the inner ($r'<r$) shells, then add the outer ($r'>r$) shells' constant-potential contribution.

Power-Law Profile: $\rho(r')=\rho_0(r'/R)^n$

Enclosed charge — a single power-rule integral
$$Q_{\text{enc}}(r)=4\pi\!\int_0^r\!\rho_0\left(\frac{r'}{R}\right)^{\!n}\!r'^2\,dr'=\frac{4\pi\rho_0}{R^n}\int_0^r r'^{\,n+2}\,dr'=\frac{4\pi\rho_0}{R^n}\cdot\frac{r^{\,n+3}}{n+3}$$

Setting $r=R$ gives the total charge $Q=\dfrac{4\pi\rho_0 R^3}{n+3}$ — reducing to the familiar $Q=\tfrac43\pi R^3\rho_0$ at $n=0$, since a uniform ball is the $n=0$ member of this family.

Field, from Gauss's law / the master formula directly
$$E_r(r)=\frac{k\,Q_{\text{enc}}(r)}{r^2}=\frac{4\pi k\rho_0}{(n+3)R^n}\,r^{\,n+1}=\frac{kQ}{R^2}\left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^{\!n+1}\qquad(r\le R)$$

At $n=0$ this is $kQr/R^3$ — exactly Step 4's uniform result. Larger $n$ pushes charge toward the surface, so $E_r$ stays small through most of the interior and rises sharply only near $r=R$.

Potential — inner + outer pieces, then simplify

Inner piece $\frac{k}{r}Q_{\text{enc}}(r)$ and outer piece $4\pi k\!\int_r^R\rho_0(r'/R)^n r'\,dr'=\dfrac{4\pi k\rho_0}{(n+2)R^n}\big[R^{n+2}-r^{n+2}\big]$ add and simplify (using $Q=4\pi\rho_0R^3/(n+3)$) to a single closed polynomial in $x\equiv r/R$:

$$V(r)=\frac{kQ}{R(n+2)}\Big[(n+3)-x^{\,n+2}\Big],\qquad x=\frac{r}{R}\qquad(r\le R)$$

Sanity check: at $n=0$, $V(r)=\dfrac{kQ}{2R}\big[3-x^2\big]$ — identical to Step 4's uniform formula. Exterior ($r\ge R$) is unchanged from every other profile: $V=kQ/r$, $E_r=kQ/r^2$, since $Q_{\text{enc}}(r)=Q$ there regardless of how charge is distributed inside $R$.

Linear Profile: $\rho(r')=\rho_0\big[1+\alpha(1-r'/R)\big]$

Write as A − Br′ and integrate term by term

Expand $\rho(r')=\underbrace{\rho_0(1+\alpha)}_{A}-\underbrace{\dfrac{\rho_0\alpha}{R}}_{B}\,r'$ — a plain linear function of $r'$, so every integral below is elementary:

$$Q_{\text{enc}}(r)=4\pi\!\int_0^r(A-Br')r'^2\,dr'=4\pi\left[\frac{A r^3}{3}-\frac{Br^4}{4}\right]$$
Total charge
$$Q=4\pi R^3\!\left[\frac{A}{3}-\frac{BR}{4}\right]=\frac{\pi\rho_0R^3(4+\alpha)}{3}$$

(using $BR=\rho_0\alpha$). At $\alpha=0$ this is $\tfrac43\pi R^3\rho_0$ — the uniform case again, confirming $\alpha$ is a pure "shape" parameter layered on top of the same total-mass bookkeeping.

Field
$$E_r(r)=\frac{k\,Q_{\text{enc}}(r)}{r^2}=4\pi k\!\left[\frac{Ar}{3}-\frac{Br^2}{4}\right]=\frac{4\pi k\rho_0(1+\alpha)}{3}\,r\;-\;\frac{\pi k\rho_0\alpha}{R}\,r^2\qquad(r\le R)$$

At $\alpha=0$: $E_r=\tfrac{4\pi}{3}k\rho_0 r=kQr/R^3$ — Step 4's result. For $\alpha>0$ (denser core), the linear-in-$r$ term dominates near the centre exactly as it must, since a denser core means more enclosed charge at small $r$.

Potential — same inner+outer pattern, collected into a cubic in x=r/R

Adding $\frac{k}{r}Q_{\text{enc}}(r)$ to the outer shells' contribution $4\pi k\!\int_r^R(Ar'-Br'^2)\,dr'$ and collecting powers of $x=r/R$:

$$V(r)=2\pi k\rho_0R^2\!\left(1+\frac{\alpha}{3}\right)\;-\;\frac{2\pi k\rho_0R^2}{3}(1+\alpha)\,x^2\;+\;\frac{\pi k\rho_0R^2\alpha}{3}\,x^3\qquad(r\le R)$$

Sanity check: at $\alpha=0$ every $\alpha$-term vanishes, leaving $V(r)=2\pi k\rho_0R^2(1-x^2/3)=2\pi k\rho_0(R^2-r^2/3)$ — exactly Step 4's uniform result. The cubic $x^3$ term is the genuinely new feature: unlike the uniform and power-law cases (whose $V(r)$ is a pure even function of $x$ inside the ball, at least for integer-adjacent $n$), a linearly graded density breaks that symmetry and needs one more power of $x$ to describe.

💡 Why these two integrate but Woods–Saxon doesn't. Both profiles above are finite polynomials (or power functions) in $r'$, so $\int \rho(r')\,r'^k\,dr'$ is always another power function — elementary by construction. The Woods–Saxon profile $\rho_0/[1+e^{(r'-R)/a}]$ has no such structure: $\int r'^2/[1+e^{(r'-R)/a}]\,dr'$ is not expressible in elementary functions (it's related to the polylogarithm), so that profile is deliberately left to Simpson's-rule quadrature on the Simulation tab rather than forced into a closed form that doesn't exist.
📍 Worked Special Case — the Centre, r=0

At the exact centre, $Q_{\text{enc}}(0)=0$ for any profile with finite $\rho(0)$, so $E_r(0)=0$ identically — a genuine field-null by symmetry (every direction is equally "outward," so the vector sum must vanish), not a coincidence of the uniform formula. $V(0)$ is finite and, for uniform $\rho$, equals $V(0)=\tfrac32\,kQ/R$ — the single largest potential anywhere in the whole configuration, since every other point is farther from some of the charge.

∫ Closed Forms — Uniform ρ
$$V(r)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{kQ}{2R}\!\left(3-\dfrac{r^2}{R^2}\right) & r\le R\\[8pt]\dfrac{kQ}{r} & r\ge R\end{cases}\qquad\quad E_r(r)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{kQ\,r}{R^3} & r\le R\\[8pt]\dfrac{kQ}{r^2} & r\ge R\end{cases}\qquad Q=\tfrac43\pi R^3\rho_0$$
RegimeConditionBehaviour
Centre$r=0$$V$ maximal ($=\tfrac32 kQ/R$); $E_r=0$ (symmetry null)
Interior$0<r<R$$E_r$ rises linearly with $r$ — unlike the hollow Shell, which gives zero everywhere inside
Boundary$r=R$Both $V$ and $E_r$ are continuous — no jump, unlike a surface charge
Exterior$r>R$Exactly a point charge $Q$ at every exterior $r$ — not just an asymptote
R→0 limitfixed $Q$Reduces to an ordinary point charge for all $r>0$
⚠️ Contrast across every system in this app: a 1D line charge (Rod/Line/Ring) diverges on the charge; a 2D surface charge (Sheet/Disk/Shell) stays finite in $V$ but jumps in the normal $E$; this 3D volume charge is finite and continuous in both $V$ and $E_r$ everywhere, including on its own boundary $r=R$. Each step up in the source's dimensionality removes one more type of discontinuity.
∫ General Profile — the Master Formula
$$Q_{\text{enc}}(r)=4\pi\!\int_0^{\min(r,R)}\!\!\rho(r')\,r'^2\,dr',\qquad E_r(r)=\frac{k\,Q_{\text{enc}}(r)}{r^2},\qquad V(r)=\frac{k\,Q_{\text{enc}}(r)}{r}+4\pi k\!\int_{\min(r,R)}^{R}\!\!\rho(r')\,r'\,dr'$$

Valid for any spherically symmetric $\rho(r')$; the second integral in $V(r)$ is empty (and $Q_{\text{enc}}=Q_{\text{tot}}$) once $r\ge R$, correctly collapsing to $V=kQ_{\text{tot}}/r$. Evaluated by Simpson's rule on the Simulation tab for the linear, power-law, and Woods–Saxon profiles; the uniform closed form above serves as a built-in exact check.

Denser Core (linear, α>0)

$Q_{\text{enc}}(r)$ grows faster than $r^3$ near the centre, so $E_r(r)$ rises more steeply than the uniform case's straight line for small $r$, then flattens as it approaches $R$ (where density is lowest).

Diffuse Edge (Woods–Saxon)

Density stays nearly flat out to $r\approx R$, then falls smoothly over a width $\sim a$ rather than stopping sharply — the standard empirical fit to real nuclear charge distributions. $E_r(r)$ correspondingly peaks near $r\approx R$ and rolls over smoothly rather than meeting the exterior $1/r^2$ curve at a sharp corner.

🔢 Fully Worked Numerical Example (Uniform Sphere)

Take $\rho_0=3$ nC/m³, $R=0.8$ m. Evaluate at $r=0.4$ m (interior) and $r=1.5$ m (exterior), and check continuity at $r=R$.

Total charge
$$Q=\tfrac43\pi R^3\rho_0=\tfrac43\pi(0.512)(3)=6.434\ \text{nC}$$
Interior point, r=0.4 m
$$E_r(0.4)=\frac{kQr}{R^3}=\frac{(8.99)(6.434)(0.4)}{0.512}=45.24\ \text{V/m}\qquad V(0.4)=\frac{kQ}{2R}\!\left(3-\frac{r^2}{R^2}\right)=\frac{(8.99)(6.434)}{1.6}(3-0.25)=32.60\ \text{V}$$
Exterior point, r=1.5 m
$$E_r(1.5)=\frac{kQ}{r^2}=\frac{57.84}{2.25}=25.71\ \text{V/m}\qquad V(1.5)=\frac{kQ}{r}=\frac{57.84}{1.5}=38.56\ \text{V}$$
Continuity check at r=R=0.8 m
$$E_r(R^-)=\frac{kQ}{R^2}=\frac{57.84}{0.64}=90.38\ \text{V/m}=E_r(R^+)\qquad V(R^-)=\frac{kQ}{2R}(3-1)=\frac{kQ}{R}=72.30\ \text{V}=V(R^+)$$

Both branches agree exactly at $r=R$, with no jump in $E_r$ — confirming Step 6 of the Derivation tab. The Simulation tab's comparison table reproduces every one of these figures independently via shell-superposition Simpson quadrature and via 3D Monte Carlo, typically agreeing with the closed form to 4+ significant figures.

Σ→∮dx′ From a Ring to a Tube

Take the Ring system's loop of radius $R$ and slide copies of it along the $x$-axis from $x_1$ to $x_2$, giving each one the same radius but an infinitesimal share $d\sigma=\sigma\,dx'$ of a uniform surface density $\sigma$ (C/m²) — exactly the same "annulus is a ring" logic used to build the Disk, just stacked along the axis instead of stacked in radius. The result is a finite hollow cylindrical shell: a genuine 2D surface (like the Sheet, Disk, and hollow Sphere), curved in one direction and straight in the other.

$$V(x_0,\rho_0)=\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\underbrace{\left[\frac{4k\,\sigma\,R\,K\!\big(k(x')\big)}{D_+(x')}\right]}_{\text{Ring system's }V,\ \lambda\to\sigma\,dx',\ z\to x_0-x'}dx'$$

No new geometry needs to be solved from scratch — every ring in the stack already has the Ring system's own exact closed form in $K(k),E(k)$; building the cylinder is "only" a matter of one further integral over $x'$, of an expression that is itself already exact. This mirrors the Disk (stack of rings in $r'$) and the solid Sphere (stack of shells in $r'$) precisely, just with the stacking variable now along the cylinder's own axis.

📏 Parameters & the On-Axis Shortcut
$\sigma$Surface charge densitynC/m²
$R$Cylinder (shell) radiusm
$L$Cylinder length, $x_1=c_x-L/2,\ x_2=c_x+L/2$m
$x_0,\rho_0$Field point: axial position, radial distance from the axism

Like the Rod and Infinite Line, this system is symmetric under rotation about its own axis, so the field point needs only two numbers: $x_0$ (position along the axis) and $\rho_0=\sqrt{y_0^2+z_0^2}$ (radial distance from it). A remarkable simplification happens exactly on the axis ($\rho_0=0$): a point sitting on a ring's own axis is geometrically identical to a point on the Rod system's own $y_0$-offset field point, with $y_0\to R$ fixed. That means the cylinder's on-axis $V$ and $E_x$ are obtained by calling the Rod system's own closed form with an effective density $\lambda_{\text{eff}}=2\pi R\sigma$ and $y_0=R$ — no elliptic integrals, no new derivation, and no numerical integration at all.

⚠️ On the shell itself — finite jump, not a divergence. Like the Sheet, Disk, and hollow Sphere (all genuine surface charges), landing exactly on the cylinder's own surface ($\rho_0=R$, $x_0\in[x_1,x_2]$) leaves $V$ finite; only the radial (surface-normal) field $E_\rho$ has a finite jump of $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ there — the same general boundary condition derived on the Sheet system's Solution tab, now confirmed for a curved surface with straight-line generators rather than a flat plane or a sphere.
# Two Independent Numerical Routes

Semi-Analytic: Ring-Superposition Quadrature

Integrate the exact Ring closed form over $x'\in[x_1,x_2]$ with Simpson's rule at high panel count — every sample is already exact in the angular direction, so this converges quickly for any off-axis field point.

Brute-Force: Direct 2D Surface Quadrature

Integrate the raw Coulomb kernel directly over the shell's own surface coordinates $(x',\phi')\in[x_1,x_2]\times[0,2\pi]$, reusing the Sheet system's generic 2D-quadrature routines verbatim — the surface-area Jacobian here is just the constant $R$ (no $r'$ factor, since the radius is fixed), making this an even simpler rectangle-domain integral than the Disk's own polar one. No elliptic-integral machinery anywhere, so agreement with the ring-superposition route is a genuinely independent check.

💡 Infinite-cylinder limit. As $L\to\infty$, the field outside the shell ($\rho_0>R$) approaches the Infinite Line system's own result with an effective line density $\lambda_{\text{eff}}=2\pi R\sigma$: $E_\rho\to 2k\lambda_{\text{eff}}/\rho_0$. Inside the shell ($\rho_0<R$), the field approaches zero everywhere — the cylindrical analogue of the hollow Sphere's own shell theorem, though (unlike the sphere) this is only exact in the strict $L\to\infty$ limit, since a finite cylinder's ends always leak a little field into its own interior near the openings.
🖼 Geometry
∂ Stacking Rings Along the Axis
One thin band is one ring, with a differential density

The band between $x'$ and $x'+dx'$ carries charge $dQ=\sigma\,(2\pi R\,dx')$ — exactly a ring of radius $R$ and linear density $d\lambda=\sigma\,dx'$, since $2\pi R\,d\lambda=2\pi R\sigma\,dx'$ matches $dQ$ term for term (the same matching argument used to build the Disk from rings and the solid Sphere from shells).

Reuse the Ring system's exact closed form for each band, unmodified

Substitute $\lambda\to\sigma\,dx'$ into the Ring system's own result, with the ring's "$z$" (height above its own plane) now equal to the axial separation $x_0-x'$, and the ring's "$\rho$" equal to the cylinder's own $\rho_0$ (unchanged, since every ring in the stack shares the same axis and radius):

$$dV=\frac{4k\,\sigma\,R\,K(k)}{D_+}\,dx',\qquad dE_x=\frac{4k\,\sigma\,R\,(x_0-x')\,E(k)}{D_-^2D_+}\,dx',\qquad dE_\rho=\frac{2k\,\sigma\,R}{\rho_0 D_+}\!\left[K(k)-\frac{R^2+(x_0-x')^2-\rho_0^2}{D_-^2}E(k)\right]dx'$$

with $k^2(x')=\dfrac{4R\rho_0}{(R+\rho_0)^2+(x_0-x')^2}$, $D_+=\sqrt{(R+\rho_0)^2+(x_0-x')^2}$, $D_-^2=(R-\rho_0)^2+(x_0-x')^2$ — every symbol identical to the Ring system's own Derivation tab, just with the ring's own $z$ relabelled $x_0-x'$ so it can vary as $x'$ sweeps across the stack.

Superpose (integrate) over the whole shell, $x'=x_1$ to $x_2$
$$V(x_0,\rho_0)=\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\!\frac{4k\sigma R\,K(k)}{D_+}\,dx',\quad E_x=\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\!\frac{4k\sigma R(x_0-x')E(k)}{D_-^2D_+}\,dx',\quad E_\rho=\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\!\frac{2k\sigma R}{\rho_0D_+}\!\left[K-\frac{R^2+(x_0-x')^2-\rho_0^2}{D_-^2}E\right]dx'$$

Each integrand is already exact in the angular direction (built entirely from $K,E$); only this last integral over $x'$ is evaluated numerically (Simpson's rule), since it has no further elementary antiderivative for generic $\rho_0\neq0$ — the same "integrate what you can exactly, leave only what you must to quadrature" principle used for the Disk and the Sphere.

📍 Worked Special Case — On-Axis ($\rho_0=0$), No Elliptic Integrals At All

At $\rho_0=0$, every ring in the stack is seen edge-on from directly above its own centre, and the Ring system's own on-axis result applies to each band without any elliptic integrals:

$$dV(x_0,0)=\frac{k\,dQ}{\sqrt{R^2+(x_0-x')^2}}=\frac{k\,\sigma\,2\pi R\,dx'}{\sqrt{R^2+(x_0-x')^2}}$$

Compare this term-by-term with the Charged Rod system's own potential integrand, $dV_{\text{rod}}=k\lambda\,dx'/\sqrt{(x_0-x')^2+y_0^2}$: the two are identical in $x'$-dependence once $\lambda\to\lambda_{\text{eff}}\equiv2\pi R\sigma$ and $y_0\to R$. The rod's own perpendicular-offset geometry and the cylinder's own ring-stack geometry produce the exact same integral — a genuine coincidence of the mathematics, not merely an analogy — so the Rod system's already-derived closed form can be reused verbatim:

$$V(x_0,0)=k\lambda_{\text{eff}}\,\ln\!\left[\frac{(x_2-x_0)+\sqrt{(x_2-x_0)^2+R^2}}{(x_1-x_0)+\sqrt{(x_1-x_0)^2+R^2}}\right],\qquad E_x(x_0,0)=k\lambda_{\text{eff}}\!\left[\frac1{r_2}-\frac1{r_1}\right],\qquad \lambda_{\text{eff}}=2\pi R\sigma$$

with $r_1=\sqrt{(x_0-x_1)^2+R^2},\ r_2=\sqrt{(x_0-x_2)^2+R^2}$ — the Rod system's own $r_1,r_2$, evaluated at $y_0=R$. Because $V(x_0,0)$ as a function of $x_0$ is literally the rod's own function (not just numerically close to it), $E_x=-\partial V/\partial x_0$ inherits the rod's own $E_x$ formula automatically — no separate differentiation is needed. $E_\rho(x_0,0)=0$ identically, by the same on-axis symmetry argument used for the Ring and Disk systems.

💡 Sanity check against the far-field limit. As $x_0$ moves far from the shell ($|x_0-c_x|\gg L,R$), $\lambda_{\text{eff}}L=2\pi R\sigma L=Q$ (the shell's total charge), and the rod-reused formula above reduces to the familiar $V\approx kQ/r$ point-charge limit — exactly as the Rod system's own far-field limit does, since the reused formula is the rod's own.
∞ Infinite-Cylinder Limit — Reduction to the Infinite Line

Let $L\to\infty$ at fixed $R,\sigma$, with the field point held at fixed $\rho_0>R$ (outside the shell). By the same translational-symmetry argument used for the Rod system's own $L\to\infty$ reduction to the Infinite Line, the axial position $x_0$ stops mattering and only $\rho_0$ survives:

$$E_\rho(\rho_0)\ \xrightarrow{\,L\to\infty\,}\ \frac{2k\lambda_{\text{eff}}}{\rho_0}=\frac{2k(2\pi R\sigma)}{\rho_0}=\frac{\sigma R}{\varepsilon_0\rho_0}\qquad(\rho_0>R)$$

— exactly the Infinite Line system's own closed form, with $\lambda\to2\pi R\sigma$. For $\rho_0<R$ (inside the shell), $E_\rho\to0$ in the same limit: the cylindrical shell, made infinitely long, produces no field anywhere inside it — the cylindrical cousin of the hollow Sphere's shell theorem, though here it is a large-$L$ asymptote rather than an exact statement at every finite $L$ (a finite cylinder's open ends always let a little field leak inward near them, visible in the Simulation tab's sweep plots as $L$ is increased toward this limit).

σ(x′) Varying Density Along the Axis

Every closed form above assumed uniform σ. Nothing in Steps 1–3 required that: replace σ dx′ by σ(x′) dx′ in the ring-superposition integrals and they stay exactly correct for any axial profile σ(x′) — the angular part (built from K,E per ring) is untouched.

General on-axis integral

On-axis (ρ₀=0), every ring is seen edge-on exactly as in the uniform case, so the problem again collapses to the Rod system's own integral, only now with a position-dependent effective linear density:

$$V(x_0,0)=k\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\frac{\lambda_{\text{eff}}(x')\,dx'}{\sqrt{(x_0-x')^2+R^2}},\qquad \lambda_{\text{eff}}(x')=2\pi R\,\sigma(x')$$

For a general σ(x′) this has no elementary antiderivative and is evaluated numerically (Simpson's rule), exactly the Rod Theory tab's non-uniform-λ machinery reused verbatim with y₀→R.

A solvable case — linear profile

Take $\sigma(x')=\sigma_0\!\left[1+\beta\,\dfrac{x'-c_x}{L/2}\right]$, $c_x=(x_1+x_2)/2$ — denser toward one end for $\beta\neq0$. Then $\lambda_{\text{eff}}(x')=a+b(x'-c_x)$ is linear in $x'$, with $a=2\pi R\sigma_0$, $b=4\pi R\sigma_0\beta/L$, and the integral splits into a constant piece (the uniform result already derived) plus a linear piece with its own elementary antiderivative:

$$\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\frac{x'\,dx'}{\sqrt{(x_0-x')^2+R^2}}=\Big[r_2-r_1\Big]+x_0\,\Lambda,\qquad \Lambda=\ln\!\left[\frac{(x_2-x_0)+r_2}{(x_1-x_0)+r_1}\right]$$

(the same antiderivative trick used for the rectangular sheet's $F(\xi,\eta,z_0)$Q: $\int u\,du/\sqrt{u^2+R^2}=\sqrt{u^2+R^2}$, $\int du/\sqrt{u^2+R^2}=\ln(u+\sqrt{u^2+R^2})$, combined via $x'=u+x_0$.) Subtracting $c_x\Lambda$ and assembling:

$$V(x_0,0)=k\lambda_{\text{eff}}(x_0)\,\Lambda\;+\;k\,b\,(r_2-r_1)$$

with $\lambda_{\text{eff}}(x_0)=a+b(x_0-c_x)$ — the local effective density right at the field point's own axial position, plus a correction term from the density gradient. Setting $\beta=0$ ($b=0$) collapses this exactly to the uniform on-axis formula above, confirming the result.

⚠️ Off-axis with varying density: the same substitution $\sigma\to\sigma(x')$ applies to the general ring-superposition integrals for $E_\rho,E_x$, but off-axis these mix $K(k(x')),E(k(x'))$ with a non-constant weight and have no elementary closed form even for the linear profile — evaluated by Simpson's rule over $x'$, exactly as the uniform off-axis case already is.
∫ Closed Form (On-Axis) and Regimes
$$V(x_0,0)=k\lambda_{\text{eff}}\ln\!\left[\frac{(x_2-x_0)+r_2}{(x_1-x_0)+r_1}\right],\quad E_x(x_0,0)=k\lambda_{\text{eff}}\!\left[\frac1{r_2}-\frac1{r_1}\right],\quad E_\rho(x_0,0)=0,\quad \lambda_{\text{eff}}=2\pi R\sigma$$

with $r_1=\sqrt{(x_0-x_1)^2+R^2},\ r_2=\sqrt{(x_0-x_2)^2+R^2}$ — the Rod system's own formula, reused verbatim at $y_0=R$. Off-axis ($\rho_0\neq0$), $V,E_x,E_\rho$ are the $x'$-integrals of the Ring system's exact $K(k),E(k)$ formulas, evaluated by Simpson's-rule quadrature (semi-analytic) and cross-checked against a direct 2D surface quadrature over $(x',\phi')$.

RegimeConditionBehaviour
On-axis$\rho_0=0$Elementary — exact reuse of the Rod system's own closed form
Off-axis, exterior$\rho_0>R$Smooth, finite; semi-analytic (ring-superposition) vs direct 2D quadrature
Interior$\rho_0<R,\ x_0\in[x_1,x_2]$Smooth, finite; generally nonzero for finite $L$ (only $\to0$ as $L\to\infty$)
On the shell$\rho_0=R,\ x_0\in[x_1,x_2]$V finite; $E_\rho$ has a finite jump of $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ — not a divergence
Far field$r\gg L,R$Reduces to a point charge $Q=2\pi R\sigma L$
⚠️ Contrast with the Rod/Line/Ring: those 1D systems diverge exactly on the charge. Like the Sheet, Disk, and hollow Sphere (all genuine surface charges), the cylindrical shell never does — $V$ stays finite and continuous everywhere, including at $\rho_0=R$; only the radial field has a finite jump there.
🔢 Fully Worked Numerical Example (On-Axis)

Take $\sigma=3$ nC/m², $R=0.4$ m, $L=2$ m, shell centred at the origin ($x_1=-1,\ x_2=1$), field point on-axis at $x_0=1.8$ m.

Effective line density and total charge
$$\lambda_{\text{eff}}=2\pi R\sigma=2\pi(0.4)(3)=7.540\ \text{nC/m}\qquad Q=\lambda_{\text{eff}}L=15.08\ \text{nC}$$
Potential and field (reusing the Rod system's own closed form)
$$r_1=\sqrt{(1.8-(-1))^2+0.4^2}=2.836,\qquad r_2=\sqrt{(1.8-1)^2+0.4^2}=0.894$$
$$V=k\lambda_{\text{eff}}\ln\!\left[\frac{(1-1.8)+0.894}{(-1-1.8)+2.836}\right]=(8.99)(7.540)\ln\!\left[\frac{0.094}{0.036}\right]=67.79\times0.960=65.08\ \text{V}$$
$$E_x=k\lambda_{\text{eff}}\left[\frac1{0.894}-\frac1{2.836}\right]=67.79\,(1.119-0.353)=67.79\times0.766=51.9\ \text{V/m}$$

The Simulation tab's comparison table reproduces $V=65.08$ V, $E_x=51.9$ V/m independently via ring-superposition Simpson's-rule integration and direct 2D surface quadrature, typically agreeing to 5+ significant figures.

Σ→∭ From a Disk to a Solid Cylinder

Take the Charged Disk system's filled circle of radius $R$ and slide copies of it along the $x$-axis from $x_1$ to $x_2$, giving each one an infinitesimal share $\rho(x')\,dx'$ of a volume charge density $\rho$ (C/m³). Chop the cylinder into thin disks of thickness $dx'$: the disk between $x'$ and $x'+dx'$ carries charge $dq=\rho(x')\,\pi R^2\,dx'$ — exactly a Disk-system disk of radius $R$ with surface density $d\sigma=\rho(x')\,dx'$, since $\pi R^2\,d\sigma=\pi R^2\rho(x')\,dx'$ matches term for term. Superposing every disk in the stack:

$$V(x_0,\rho_0)=\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\Big[V_{\text{disk}}\big(\sigma\!=\!\rho(x')\,dx',\,R,\,\rho_0,\,x_0-x'\big)\Big]$$

No new source geometry needs solving: every disk in the stack already has the Disk system's own exact result (elementary on-axis; ring-superposition off-axis). Building the solid cylinder is "only" one further integral over $x'$, of an expression that is itself already exact in the radial direction.

💡 Why on-axis is fully elementary here. The Disk system's own on-axis formula, $V_{\text{disk}}(0,d)=2\pi k\sigma(\sqrt{R^2+d^2}-|d|)$, is already elementary (no elliptic integrals — unlike its own off-axis case). Stacking elementary functions along $x'$ and integrating still gives an elementary function, so the solid cylinder's on-axis $V,E_x$ have full closed forms even though the Hollow Cylinder and Disk systems both needed numerics or elliptic integrals off-axis.
📏 Parameters
$\rho_0$Volume charge density (uniform case)nC/m³
$R$Cylinder radiusm
$L$Cylinder length, $x_1=c_x-L/2,\ x_2=c_x+L/2$m
$x_0,\rho_0$Field point: axial position, radial distance from axism

Like the Rod and Hollow Cylinder, rotational symmetry about the axis means the field point needs only two numbers, $(x_0,\rho_0)$. On-axis ($\rho_0=0$) every disk contributes its own elementary on-axis field; off-axis, each disk needs the Disk system's ring-superposition (Simpson over its own radius), so the full off-axis field is a nested quadrature — one integral inherited from the Disk, one new integral over $x'$.

⚠️ No true divergence anywhere — genuinely stronger than the Hollow Cylinder. The hollow (surface-charge) cylinder has a finite $E_\rho$ jump at $\rho_0=R$. A volume charge has no surface density at all, so — exactly as for the solid Sphere versus the hollow Shell — $V$ and $\mathbf E$ are smooth and finite throughout the solid cylinder, including on its own lateral surface $\rho_0=R$ and at its flat end faces $x_0=x_1,x_2$.
🖼 Geometry

The field point $P$ sits at axial position $x_0$ and radial distance $\rho_0$ from the cylinder's axis. Every source point inside the cylinder is labelled by $(x',r',\phi')$ — its own axial position, its radial distance from the axis, and its azimuth — with $x'\in[x_1,x_2]$ and $r'\in[0,R]$. On-axis ($\rho_0=0$), symmetry collapses this to a single relevant separation $u=x_0-x'$, independent of $r'$ and $\phi'$ entirely (Step 1 below explains why). Off-axis, the full three-coordinate integral is needed, which is why that case is left to quadrature.

∂ On-Axis Derivation — Full Step-by-Step
Why a single disk's own on-axis result can be reused directly

Fix the field point on-axis, $\rho_0=0$. For a single thin disk sitting at $x'$, every point within that disk is characterized only by its radial distance $r'\le R$ from the axis — the disk's own azimuthal symmetry means all points at the same $r'$ are equidistant from $P$ (this is exactly the same symmetry fact used in the Charged Disk system's own on-axis derivation). So the disk's own on-axis potential, already derived there, applies unchanged:

$$dV_{\text{disk}}(u)=2\pi k\,(d\sigma)\Big(\sqrt{R^2+u^2}-|u|\Big),\qquad d\sigma=\rho(x')\,dx',\quad u=x_0-x'$$
Define the kernel h(u) and set up the stacking integral

Write $h(u)\equiv\sqrt{R^2+u^2}-|u|$ for the disk's own on-axis potential shape (up to the constant $2\pi k\,d\sigma$). Superposing every disk in the stack from $x_1$ to $x_2$:

$$V(x_0,0)=\int_{x_1}^{x_2}2\pi k\,\rho(x')\,h(x_0-x')\,dx'=2\pi k\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\rho(x')\Big[\sqrt{R^2+(x_0-x')^2}-|x_0-x'|\Big]dx'$$

For uniform $\rho(x')=\rho_0$, this factors outside the integral, leaving a pure geometry integral in $x'$ — exactly parallel to how $\lambda$ or $\sigma$ factored out in every earlier system's uniform case.

The antiderivative of h(u), piece by piece

Split $h(u)=\sqrt{R^2+u^2}-|u|$ into two terms and antidifferentiate each separately, since each has a standard elementary form:

$$\int\sqrt{R^2+u^2}\,du=\frac u2\sqrt{R^2+u^2}+\frac{R^2}2\,\text{asinh}\!\Big(\frac uR\Big)+C_1,\qquad \int|u|\,du=\frac{u|u|}2+C_2$$

The first is the standard "area under a hyperbola" antiderivative (verify by differentiating: $\frac{d}{du}\big[\frac u2\sqrt{R^2+u^2}\big]=\frac12\sqrt{R^2+u^2}+\frac{u^2}{2\sqrt{R^2+u^2}}$, and $\frac{d}{du}\big[\frac{R^2}2\text{asinh}(u/R)\big]=\frac{R^2}{2}\cdot\frac{1/R}{\sqrt{1+u^2/R^2}}=\frac{R}{2\sqrt{R^2+u^2}/R}=\frac R2\cdot\frac{R}{\sqrt{R^2+u^2}}$; adding these and simplifying reproduces $\sqrt{R^2+u^2}$ — a good exercise). The second follows since $\frac{d}{du}\big[\frac{u|u|}2\big]=|u|$ for every real $u$ (check both signs of $u$ separately: for $u>0$, $\frac{d}{du}\frac{u^2}2=u=|u|$; for $u<0$, $\frac{d}{du}\big(\!-\!\frac{u^2}2\big)=-u=|u|$).

Combining both pieces gives the disk-stack antiderivative $H(u)$:

$$H(u)=\frac u2\sqrt{R^2+u^2}+\frac{R^2}2\,\text{asinh}\!\Big(\frac uR\Big)-\frac{u|u|}2,\qquad H'(u)=h(u)$$
Evaluate the definite integral — substitute u=x0−x′ and flip the limits

With $u=x_0-x'$, $du=-dx'$: as $x'$ runs $x_1\to x_2$, $u$ runs $(x_0-x_1)\to(x_0-x_2)$, and the sign flip from $du$ reverses those limits back to the natural "upper minus lower" order:

$$\int_{x_1}^{x_2}h(x_0-x')\,dx'=\int_{x_0-x_1}^{x_0-x_2}h(u)\,(-du)=\int_{x_0-x_2}^{x_0-x_1}h(u)\,du=H(x_0-x_1)-H(x_0-x_2)$$
Closed form for V (uniform ρ)
$$V(x_0,0)=2\pi k\rho_0\Big[H(x_0-x_1)-H(x_0-x_2)\Big]$$

This is exact — no approximation has been made anywhere in Steps 1–5, only the elementary disk-stacking substitution.

Field, from Ex = −∂V/∂x0 — differentiate directly, no second integral needed

Since $V$ is already a closed-form function of $x_0$ (through the two arguments $x_0-x_1$ and $x_0-x_2$), differentiate term by term using the chain rule and $H'(u)=h(u)$:

$$\frac{\partial V}{\partial x_0}=2\pi k\rho_0\Big[H'(x_0-x_1)\cdot1-H'(x_0-x_2)\cdot1\Big]=2\pi k\rho_0\big[h(x_0-x_1)-h(x_0-x_2)\big]$$
$$E_x(x_0,0)=-\frac{\partial V}{\partial x_0}=2\pi k\rho_0\Big[h(x_0-x_2)-h(x_0-x_1)\Big]$$

Written out fully: $E_x=2\pi k\rho_0\Big[\big(\sqrt{R^2+(x_0-x_2)^2}-|x_0-x_2|\big)-\big(\sqrt{R^2+(x_0-x_1)^2}-|x_0-x_1|\big)\Big]$ — literally the difference of two Disk-system on-axis field contributions, one "virtual" disk sitting at each end of the cylinder. This is exactly what stacking a continuum of disks and integrating must reduce to: the interior disks' contributions telescope away in the derivative, leaving only the two boundary terms.

Independent check: direct differentiation of a single disk's own field, reused

An equivalent route confirms Step 6 without going through $H(u)$ at all. Differentiate inside the integral first (Leibniz's rule for a definite integral with fixed limits — valid here since $\rho(x')$ and the integrand are smooth):

$$E_x(x_0,0)=-\frac{\partial}{\partial x_0}\!\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\!2\pi k\rho_0\,h(x_0-x')\,dx'=-2\pi k\rho_0\!\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\!h'(x_0-x')\,dx'$$

Since $h'(u)=\dfrac{u}{\sqrt{R^2+u^2}}-\text{sgn}(u)$ (this is exactly $-E_z^{\text{disk}}/(2\pi k\,d\sigma)$ up to sign, i.e. the Disk system's own on-axis field kernel), the integral over $x'$ of this quantity — pulled through the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus one more time — again collapses to boundary terms only, reproducing Step 6 exactly. Two independent routes (stack-then-differentiate, and differentiate-then-integrate) agreeing is the same cross-check philosophy used throughout this app (Rod Step 6, Sheet Step 6, Ring Step 4).

Sanity limits

Thin-disk limit ($L\to0$ with $\rho_0L\to\sigma$ fixed): both boundary terms in $E_x$ merge into a single derivative of $h$, and $H(u)$'s own definition collapses back exactly to the Disk system's $V_{\text{disk}}$ — confirming the disk is the $L\to0$ limit of this system, just as the rod was the $\rho_0\to0$ (line) limit of other systems. Long-cylinder limit ($L\to\infty$ at fixed $\rho_0$, field point on-axis well inside): each $h(x_0-x_i)\to0$ as the corresponding end recedes to infinity (since $h(u)=\sqrt{R^2+u^2}-|u|\to0$ as $|u|\to\infty$ — a good exercise in binomial-expanding the square root), so $E_x\to0$ deep inside an infinitely long uniformly-charged cylinder — consistent with the translational-symmetry argument used for the Infinite Line and the infinite Hollow Cylinder limit (no preferred axial direction once end effects vanish, so $E_x$ must vanish by symmetry).

🧭 Off-Axis — Why No Elementary Closed Form Survives

Off-axis ($\rho_0\neq0$), Step 1's key simplification breaks down: points within a single disk at radius $r'$ are no longer all equidistant from $P$, since $P$ itself is displaced from the axis. The disk's own field then requires the Disk system's own off-axis machinery (ring-superposition in $K(k),E(k)$ or direct polar quadrature) — and that result must itself be integrated over $x'$ to stack the disks. The result is a genuinely nested double integral with no further elementary reduction, evaluated in this app as: an inner call to the Disk system's own exact `diskFieldAnalytic` at each $x'$ (itself either elementary on-axis or a ring-superposition Simpson sum), composed with an outer Simpson's-rule integral over $x'$ — reusing two already-validated numerical engines rather than deriving a third from scratch.

💡 Consistency check available to the reader: at $\rho_0\to0$, the nested off-axis quadrature must reproduce the elementary Step 5/6 closed forms above to within numerical roundoff — the Simulation tab's comparison table performs exactly this check at every field point, on-axis or not.
ρ(x′) Varying Density Along the Axis — Linear Profile, Closed Form

Let $\rho(x')=a+b(x'-c_x)$, $c_x=(x_1+x_2)/2$ — denser toward one end for $b\neq0$ (the cylindrical analogue of the Hollow Cylinder's own linear-$\sigma(x')$ card, and of the solid Sphere's linear radial profile). Nothing in Steps 1–2 required uniform $\rho$, so the same kernel $h(u)$ applies; only the weight changes.

A second antiderivative is needed for the linear term

Using $\int u\sqrt{R^2+u^2}\,du=\tfrac13(R^2+u^2)^{3/2}$ and $\int u|u|\,du=\tfrac13 u^2|u|$ (check: $\tfrac{d}{du}\big[\tfrac13u^2|u|\big]=\tfrac13\big(2u|u|+u^2\,\text{sgn}(u)\big)=u|u|$ ✓), define:

$$J(u)=\frac13(R^2+u^2)^{3/2}-\frac{u^2|u|}3,\qquad J'(u)=u\,h(u)$$
Substitute u=x0−x′ and integrate the linear-weight term

With $x'-c_x=(x_0-c_x)-u$, the $b$-piece of the integral becomes $\int (x_0-c_x-u)\,h(u)\,du$ evaluated between $u=x_0-x_2$ and $u=x_0-x_1$, giving $(x_0-c_x)\big[H(x_0-x_1)-H(x_0-x_2)\big]-\big[J(x_0-x_1)-J(x_0-x_2)\big]$.

Closed form for V — collect both pieces
$$V(x_0,0)=2\pi k\Big\{\big[a+b(x_0-c_x)\big]\big[H(x_0-x_1)-H(x_0-x_2)\big]-b\big[J(x_0-x_1)-J(x_0-x_2)\big]\Big\}$$

Note $a+b(x_0-c_x)=\rho(x_0)$ — the local density right at the field point's own axial position (when it lies inside the cylinder), plus a correction term from the gradient — exactly the same structure found for the Hollow Cylinder's own linear-$\sigma(x')$ result. Setting $b=0$ collapses this exactly to the uniform-$\rho$ formula above.

Field, by differentiating term by term
$$E_x(x_0,0)=-2\pi k\Big\{b\big[H(x_0-x_1)-H(x_0-x_2)\big]+\big[a+b(x_0-c_x)\big]\big[h(x_0-x_1)-h(x_0-x_2)\big]-b\big[(x_0-x_1)h(x_0-x_1)-(x_0-x_2)h(x_0-x_2)\big]\Big\}$$

Consistency check: setting $b=0$ collapses this to $E_x=2\pi ka\big[h(x_0-x_2)-h(x_0-x_1)\big]$ — exactly Step 4 of the uniform derivation above, confirming the two results agree at $b=0$.

⚠️ Off-axis, uniform or graded: the same substitution $\rho\to\rho(x')$ applies to the general (off-axis) disk-superposition integral, but off-axis each "disk" term already needs the Disk system's own ring-superposition quadrature — so a graded off-axis field is a genuinely nested (nonelementary) double quadrature, evaluated numerically on the Simulation tab exactly as the uniform off-axis case already is.
∫ Closed Forms (On-Axis) and Regimes
$$V(x_0,0)=2\pi k\rho_0\big[H(x_0-x_1)-H(x_0-x_2)\big],\qquad E_x(x_0,0)=2\pi k\rho_0\big[h(x_0-x_2)-h(x_0-x_1)\big]$$

with $h(u)=\sqrt{R^2+u^2}-|u|$, $H(u)=\tfrac u2\sqrt{R^2+u^2}+\tfrac{R^2}2\,\text{asinh}(u/R)-\tfrac{u|u|}2$. Off-axis, $V,E$ are obtained by Simpson's-rule quadrature over $x'$ of the Disk system's exact ring-superposition field.

RegimeConditionBehaviour
On-axis$\rho_0=0$Elementary — closed form above, no quadrature needed
Off-axis, interior$\rho_0<R,\ x_0\in[x_1,x_2]$Smooth, finite; nested quadrature (Disk's own + one more over x′)
On the lateral surface$\rho_0=R$Smooth, finite — no jump anywhere; this is a volume charge, not a surface charge
Far field$r\gg L,R$Reduces to a point charge $Q=\rho_0\pi R^2L$ (uniform case)

This solid cylinder never does — $V$ and every component of $\mathbf E$ stay smooth and finite everywhere, exactly as the solid Sphere improves on the hollow Shell.
🔢 Fully Worked Numerical Example (Uniform, On-Axis)

Take $\rho_0=3$ nC/m³, $R=0.5$ m, $L=2$ m, centred at the origin ($x_1=-1,\ x_2=1$), field point on-axis at $x_0=1.8$ m.

Kernel values
$$h(x_0-x_2)=h(0.8)=\sqrt{0.25+0.64}-0.8=0.943-0.8=0.143$$
$$h(x_0-x_1)=h(2.8)=\sqrt{0.25+7.84}-2.8=2.846-2.8=0.046$$
Field
$$E_x=2\pi(8.99)(3)\,[0.143-0.046]=169.4\times0.097=16.4\ \text{V/m}$$

The Simulation tab's comparison table reproduces this value via the closed form and independently via a nested Simpson quadrature over the disk stack (reusing the Disk system's own field), typically agreeing to 5+ significant figures.

⬮ From a Sphere to a Triaxial Ellipsoid

The Homogeneously Charged Sphere system's field point needed only the distance $r$ from the centre, because a sphere is invariant under rotation about any axis. Squash that sphere along two independent directions into a solid ellipsoid of semi-axes $a\ge b\ge c>0$, uniform volume density $\rho$, centred at the origin — the rotational symmetry is gone, and the field point now genuinely needs all three coordinates $(x,y,z)$.

The classical route (MacLaurin, later Chandrasekhar) replaces the sphere's simple radial coordinate with a single new parameter $\lambda$ — the confocal ellipsoidal parameter — defined as the largest root of

$$\frac{x^2}{a^2+\lambda}+\frac{y^2}{b^2+\lambda}+\frac{z^2}{c^2+\lambda}=1$$

For a point inside the ellipsoid this equation is already satisfied at $\lambda=0$ (the ellipsoid's own defining surface), so $\lambda\equiv0$ there. For a point outside, $\lambda$ is the unique positive root — geometrically, $\lambda$ labels which confocal ellipsoid (same foci, larger semi-axes $\sqrt{a^2+\lambda}$ etc.) the field point sits on.

💡 Why this works: confocal ellipsoids are exactly the level surfaces that make this problem separable — the same way spheres of constant $r$ were the natural surfaces for the point charge and shell systems. $\lambda$ plays the role $r$ played there.
📏 Parameters
$\rho$Volume charge density (uniform)nC/m³
$a,b,c$Semi-axes ($a\ge b\ge c$)m
$x,y,z$Field point, centred framem
⚠️ No true divergence anywhere — exactly like the solid Sphere, a volume charge never blows up. $V$ and $\mathbf E$ are smooth and finite everywhere, including on the ellipsoid's own surface; only setting $a=b=c$ recovers the Sphere system's results exactly, as a built-in consistency check.
# Two Independent Numerical Routes

The interior formula is a closed-form quadratic (no integration needed at all). The exterior formula needs one semi-infinite integral over $s\in[\lambda,\infty)$, evaluated here by a substitution $s=\lambda+\frac{w}{1-w}$ mapping to $w\in[0,1)$, then Simpson's rule — cross-checked against a fully independent brute-force 3D Monte-Carlo volume integral over the ellipsoid's own $(x',y',z')$ interior, with no confocal machinery at all (the same cross-check philosophy used for the Homogeneously Charged Sphere's graded profiles).

🖼 Geometry
∂ The Potential Integral and Field
MacLaurin's integral (stated; classical result)
$$V(x,y,z)=\pi k\rho\,abc\int_\lambda^\infty\!\left[1-\frac{x^2}{a^2+s}-\frac{y^2}{b^2+s}-\frac{z^2}{c^2+s}\right]\frac{ds}{\Delta(s)},\qquad \Delta(s)=\sqrt{(a^2+s)(b^2+s)(c^2+s)}$$

For interior points $\lambda=0$; for exterior points $\lambda$ is the positive root defined in the Theory tab. This is the ellipsoidal generalisation of the Sphere system's own shell-superposition integral — $\Delta(s)$ plays the role the sphere's $r'^2$ radial weighting played there.

Field — the boundary term vanishes for free

Differentiating under the integral sign, the term from $\partial\lambda/\partial x_i$ carries a factor equal to the bracket evaluated at $s=\lambda$ — which is exactly zero, by $\lambda$'s own defining equation. So only the explicit $x_i$-dependence inside the bracket needs differentiating:

$$E_x=2\pi k\rho\,abc\,x\!\int_\lambda^\infty\!\frac{ds}{(a^2+s)\Delta(s)},\quad E_y=2\pi k\rho\,abc\,y\!\int_\lambda^\infty\!\frac{ds}{(b^2+s)\Delta(s)},\quad E_z=2\pi k\rho\,abc\,z\!\int_\lambda^\infty\!\frac{ds}{(c^2+s)\Delta(s)}$$

Exactly the same "$\mathbf E=-\nabla V$ with the boundary term dropping out" shortcut used for the Ring and Shell systems' own derivations.

Interior closed form (λ=0, fully elementary once the three integrals are tabulated)
$$V_{\text{int}}=\pi k\rho\,abc\Big[A_0-x^2A_a-y^2A_b-z^2A_c\Big],\qquad A_0=\!\int_0^\infty\!\frac{ds}{\Delta(s)},\ \ A_i=\!\int_0^\infty\!\frac{ds}{(a_i^2+s)\Delta(s)}$$

$A_0,A_a,A_b,A_c$ depend only on the ellipsoid's shape, not on the field point — computed once per $(a,b,c)$ and reused for every interior evaluation.

Sphere limit — reduces exactly to the Sphere system

Setting $a=b=c=R$ gives $\Delta(s)=(R^2+s)^{3/2}$, $A_i=\tfrac23R^{-3}$, and the formulas above collapse term-for-term to $V(r)=\tfrac{kQ}{2R}\big(3-r^2/R^2\big)$, $E_r=kQr/R^3$ — the Homogeneously Charged Sphere system's own uniform-density result, with $Q=\tfrac43\pi abc\,\rho$.

∫ Closed Forms and Regimes
$$V=\pi k\rho\,abc\int_\lambda^\infty\!\Big[1-\tfrac{x^2}{a^2+s}-\tfrac{y^2}{b^2+s}-\tfrac{z^2}{c^2+s}\Big]\tfrac{ds}{\Delta(s)},\qquad E_i=2\pi k\rho\,abc\,x_i\!\int_\lambda^\infty\!\tfrac{ds}{(a_i^2+s)\Delta(s)}$$
RegimeConditionBehaviour
Interior$\lambda=0$Elementary quadratic in $x,y,z$ — no integration per field point
Boundaryon the ellipsoid$V,\mathbf E$ continuous — no jump, exactly like the solid Sphere
Exterior$\lambda>0$Semi-infinite integral from $\lambda$; smooth, finite
Far field$r\gg a$Reduces to a point charge $Q=\tfrac43\pi abc\,\rho$
Sphere limit$a=b=c$Exactly the Homogeneously Charged Sphere system's own results
