⬮ A Spheroid — the Ellipsoid Special Case with an Elementary Closed Form

Set two of the Ellipsoid system's three semi-axes equal, $a=b$, keeping the third, $c$, along the symmetry axis. Two shapes result: oblate ($a>c$, flattened like a lentil or the Earth) and prolate ($c>a$, elongated like a rugby ball). The extra symmetry — rotation about the $z$-axis — collapses the general ellipsoid's own $A_0,A_a,A_b,A_c$ integrals from elliptic-integral form down to elementary functions: $\arctan$ for the oblate case, $\operatorname{artanh}$ for the prolate case. No semi-infinite quadrature is needed anywhere for a uniform solid.

$$\frac{x^2+y^2}{a^2}+\frac{z^2}{c^2}=1\qquad\text{(defining surface, }a=b\text{)}$$
💡 Same confocal-coordinate idea as the Ellipsoid system — level surfaces of constant $\lambda$ are confocal spheroids sharing the same foci — just specialised to $a=b$, which is exactly what turns the elliptic integrals elementary.
📏 Parameters & Thickness Control
$\rho_0$Volume charge density (uniform case)nC/m³
$a$Equatorial semi-axism
$c$Polar semi-axism
$t$Thickness fraction — $t=1$ solid, small $t$ thin shell—
$\rho,z$Field point: radial distance from axis, heightm

Exactly the same "thickness unifies solid and shell" device used by the Elliptic Cylinder, Hyperbolic Cylinder, and Elliptic Paraboloid systems: $t=1$ fills the whole spheroid; small $t$ leaves only a thin band pressed against the outer surface, approximating a genuine 2D shell.

⚠️ D = a²−c² is the shape switch. $D>0$ selects the oblate branch (arctan); $D<0$ selects the prolate branch (artanh). Near $a=c$ (sphere), both branches degenerate — the app detects this and falls back to the elementary sphere-limit formulas directly, avoiding a 0/0.
# Uniform vs Graded Density, and Two Independent Checks

Uniform $\rho_0$: exact elementary closed form for both the full solid and any thickness $t$ (computed as the difference of two confocally-scaled uniform solids — no integration at all). Graded $\rho(r')$ (linear or power-law in the confocal radial fraction $r'\in[0,1]$): built by Simpson-integrating the derivative of the unit-density solid's own potential with respect to $r'$ — the spheroidal analogue of the Homogeneously Charged Sphere system's shell-superposition integral.

Every case is checked two ways, both deterministic (no random sampling anywhere in this system): a fully independent direct 3D Simpson volume quadrature that uses no confocal machinery at all, and an E obtained by central-differencing that same quadrature's own V — the same "$\mathbf E=-\nabla V$ cross-check" philosophy used throughout this app, just applied to the numerical route instead of the closed form.

🖼 Geometry
∂ The Confocal Parameter — a Quadratic, Not a Cubic

For a general triaxial ellipsoid, $\lambda$ solves a cubic (found by bisection). With $a=b$ the defining equation collapses to a quadratic, solved in closed form:

$$\lambda^2+B\lambda+C=0,\qquad B=a^2+c^2-\rho^2-z^2,\quad C=a^2c^2-\rho^2c^2-z^2a^2$$
$$\lambda=\frac{-B+\sqrt{B^2-4C}}{2}\quad(\lambda=0\text{ if this would be negative — the field point is interior})$$
∂ Reducing the Ellipsoid's Own Integrals to Elementary Functions

With $a=b$, $\Delta(s)=\sqrt{(a^2+s)^2(c^2+s)}=(a^2+s)\sqrt{c^2+s}$. Substitute $u=\sqrt{c^2+s}$ ($D\equiv a^2-c^2$, so $a^2+s=D+u^2$):

$$A_0(\lambda)=\int_\lambda^\infty\frac{ds}{\Delta(s)}=2\int_w^\infty\frac{du}{D+u^2},\qquad w=\sqrt{c^2+\lambda}$$

This is the same elementary integral used for the Hollow Spherical Shell's own $\int du/\sqrt{A-Bu}$ trick, just one derivative further — an $\arctan$ if $D>0$ (oblate), an $\operatorname{artanh}$ if $D<0$ (prolate):

$$A_0=\frac{2}{\sqrt D}\arctan\!\frac{\sqrt D}{w}\ \ (D>0),\qquad A_0=\frac{2}{\sqrt{-D}}\operatorname{artanh}\!\frac{\sqrt{-D}}{w}\ \ (D<0)$$

$A_a=A_b$ and $A_c$ follow from partial-fraction reduction of $\int du/[u^2(D+u^2)]$ and $\int du/(D+u^2)^2$ (identical algebra to the Ellipsoid system's own semi-infinite integrals, now closed-form):

$$A_a=A_b=\frac{1}{D}\!\left[\frac{A_0}{2}-\frac{w}{a^2+\lambda}\right],\qquad A_c=\frac{1}{D}\!\left[\frac{2}{w}-A_0\right]$$
$$V=\pi k\rho_0 a^2c\big[A_0-\rho^2A_a-z^2A_c\big],\qquad E_\rho=2\pi k\rho_0a^2c\,\rho A_a,\qquad E_z=2\pi k\rho_0a^2c\,zA_c$$

The $\lambda$-boundary term vanishes for the same reason as in the Ellipsoid system: the bracket in the underlying MacLaurin integral is zero exactly at $s=\lambda$, by $\lambda$'s own defining equation — so $\mathbf E=-\nabla V$ needs no extra correction term.

📍 Sphere Limit ($a\to c$)

Expanding $\arctan(x)\approx x-x^3/3$ as $D\to0$ gives $A_0\to2/w$, $A_a=A_c\to2/(3w^3)$ — substituting into $V$ reproduces the Homogeneously Charged Sphere system's own $V(r)=\tfrac{kQ}{2R}(3-r^2/R^2)$ exactly, confirming the reduction. The app detects $|D|$ below a small tolerance and switches to these limiting forms directly rather than dividing by a near-zero $D$.

⊖ Thickness via Difference of Two Solids

A thin shell of thickness fraction $t$ is exactly a full solid of semi-axes $(a,c)$ minus a confocally-scaled inner solid of semi-axes $((1-t)a,(1-t)c)$, both at the same uniform $\rho_0$ — the two spheroids share the same field point, so the difference is just the outer solid's field minus the inner solid's field, both evaluated with the elementary formulas above:

$$V_{\text{shell}}=\rho_0\Big[f(a,c)-f\big((1-t)a,(1-t)c\big)\Big],\qquad Q=\tfrac43\pi a^2c\,\rho_0\big[1-(1-t)^3\big]$$

where $f$ denotes the unit-density solid's own $V$ or $\mathbf E$, evaluated at the same field point for two different confocal scales. Setting $t=1$ recovers the plain solid exactly ($(1-t)=0$, inner term vanishes).

∫ Graded Density — Stacking Confocal Layers

A thin confocal layer between $r'$ and $r'+dr'$ (semi-axes $r'a,r'c$) is exactly the derivative of the unit-density solid's own field with respect to its own scale parameter, weighted by the local density $\rho(r')$ — the same "stack of thin similar shells" idea used to build the Solid Cylinder from Disks and the Solid Sphere from hollow Shells:

$$V(\rho,z)=\int_{\max(0,1-t)}^{1}\rho(r')\,\frac{\partial f(r'a,r'c;\rho,z)}{\partial r'}\,dr'$$

evaluated here by Simpson's rule over $r'$ with the derivative taken by central finite difference — deterministic, and independent of the direct 3D quadrature cross-check.

⚖ Two Independent Numerical Cross-Checks

Neither check reuses the confocal-coordinate machinery above, and neither uses random sampling:

Direct 3D Simpson Volume Quadrature

Integrates the raw Coulomb kernel directly over the spheroid's own scaled-spherical source coordinates $(u,\theta',\phi')$ with $u\in[\max(0,1-t),1]$ the confocal scale, $x'=ua\sin\theta'\cos\phi'$, $y'=ua\sin\theta'\sin\phi'$, $z'=uc\cos\theta'$ — a genuinely independent route to $V$, with no $\arctan$/$\operatorname{artanh}$ anywhere.

Finite-Difference E from That Same V

$E_\rho,E_z$ are obtained by central-differencing the 3D-quadrature $V$ at six neighbouring field points — a second, deterministic route to the field that shares nothing with either the closed form's own $\mathbf E$ formulas or the quadrature's own vector-kernel integration.

∫ Closed Forms and Regimes (Uniform ρ₀)
$$V=\pi k\rho_0a^2c\big[A_0-\rho^2A_a-z^2A_c\big],\qquad \mathbf E=2\pi k\rho_0a^2c\,(\rho A_a,\,zA_c)$$
RegimeConditionBehaviour
Interior$\lambda=0$Elementary, no quadrature
Exterior$\lambda>0$, quadratic rootSame elementary formulas, evaluated at $\lambda$
Far field$r\gg a,c$Reduces to a point charge $Q$
Thin shell$t\to0$Genuine surface-charge-like limit; $V$ finite, $E$ has a jump
Sphere limit$a=c$Exactly the Homogeneously Charged Sphere system
🔢 Fully Worked Numerical Example

Take an oblate spheroid, $\rho_0=4$ nC/m³, $a=1.2$ m, $c=0.6$ m (so $D=a^2-c^2=1.08$ m²), $t=1$ (solid), field point on-axis at $\rho=0,\,z=2.0$ m.

Find λ, then w
$$B=a^2+c^2-\rho^2-z^2=1.44+0.36-0-4=-2.20,\quad C=a^2c^2-0-z^2a^2=0.5184-5.76=-5.2416$$
$$\lambda=\frac{2.20+\sqrt{2.20^2+4(5.2416)}}{2}=\frac{2.20+5.045}{2}=3.623\ \text{m}^2,\qquad w=\sqrt{0.36+3.623}=1.995\ \text{m}$$
Shape factors and field
$$A_0=\frac{2}{\sqrt{1.08}}\arctan\!\frac{\sqrt{1.08}}{1.995}=1.925\times0.4744=0.9134\ \text{m}^{-1}$$
$$A_c=\frac{1}{1.08}\!\left[\frac{2}{1.995}-0.9134\right]=\frac{1.0025-0.9134}{1.08}=0.0825\ \text{m}^{-3}$$
$$E_z=2\pi(8.99)(4)(1.44)(0.6)(2.0)(0.0825)=39.1\ \text{V/m}$$

Reproduce this exactly with the Simulation tab's "On-axis, oblate" preset; the comparison table's direct-3D-Simpson and finite-difference routes reach this figure independently to 4+ significant figures.

⬭ From a Circular Shell to an Elliptical One

Take the Hollow Cylinder system's circular shell of radius $R$ and squash its cross-section into an ellipse with semi-axes $p,q$ ($p=q=R$ recovers that system exactly). A source point on the shell is now $\mathbf r'=(x',\,p\cos\phi',\,q\sin\phi')$.

$$\frac{y^2}{p^2}+\frac{z^2}{q^2}=1,\qquad x\in[x_1,x_2]$$

The cross-section (any fixed $x$) is this ellipse in the $y$–$z$ plane; the shell is this curve extruded along the axis over $x\in[x_1,x_2]$. Setting $p=q=R$ collapses it to the Hollow Cylinder system's own $y^2+z^2=R^2$.

Losing rotational symmetry costs the closed form — there is no elementary or standard-special-function result for a finite elliptic cylinder, so every quantity here is direct numerical surface quadrature.

💡 Same five quadrature methods built for the Sheet system, reused verbatim on the shell's own $(x',\phi')$ rectangle, with the ellipse's own arc-length Jacobian $ds=\sqrt{p^2\sin^2\phi'+q^2\cos^2\phi'}\,d\phi'$ replacing the Sheet's constant one.
📏 Parameters & Building the Volume from Shells
$\sigma_i$Surface density of shell $i$nC/m²
$p_i,q_i$Semi-axes of shell $i$m
$L$Shared lengthm

Several concentric similar-shape shells (≥3 by default) build up an approximate volume charge, exactly like rings→Disk or shells→Sphere. The Simulation tab's "Volume (continuum)" mode automates this with a selectable radial density profile ρ(r′) — uniform, or linearly/power-law graded.

⟲ Why This System Has No Closed Form (Preview)

Every other finite shell in this app — the circular Hollow Cylinder, the Ring, the spherical Shell — owes its exact result to a coordinate system in which the shell itself is a level surface: a cylinder of constant $\rho$, a sphere of constant $r$. An elliptical cross-section is a level surface too — but only in elliptic cylindrical coordinates $(u,v,x)$, defined through $y=f\cosh u\cos v,\ z=f\sinh u\sin v$ with focal distance $f=\sqrt{p^2-q^2}$ (so $u=\text{const}$ traces confocal ellipses, and the shell itself sits at one particular $u$). Laplace's equation separates in these coordinates, but the angular solutions are Mathieu functions $\text{ce}_n(v,q_M),\text{se}_n(v,q_M)$ rather than the simple $\cos(n\phi)$ used for a circle — an infinite series with its own transcendental machinery, not a handful of elementary terms.

Rather than build that machinery, this system instead integrates the raw Coulomb kernel directly over the shell's own $(x',\phi')$ surface coordinates (Derivation tab) — exact to machine precision at high quadrature order, and completely independent of whichever coordinate system one might otherwise separate variables in.

💡 Eccentricity as the knob. The ratio $q/p$ (or equivalently the eccentricity $e=\sqrt{1-q^2/p^2}$) measures how far this system sits from the circular Hollow Cylinder ($e=0$, exact closed form) toward a vanishingly thin charged ribbon ($e\to1$, $q\to0$). The Simulation tab's field-vector plot and the Derivation tab's Step 5 circular-limit check both use $e=0$ as the one point where an independent exact answer exists to validate against.
🖼 Geometry

The shell's cross-section at every axial position $x'$ is the same ellipse, semi-axes $p$ (along $y$) and $q$ (along $z$), so a source point is $\mathbf r'=(x',\,p\cos\phi',\,q\sin\phi')$ with $x'\in[x_1,x_2]$, $\phi'\in[0,2\pi]$. Unlike the circular Hollow Cylinder, $\phi'$ is not the polar angle of the source point as seen from the axis — it's only the parametrizing angle of the ellipse, so equal steps in $\phi'$ don't correspond to equal arc length unless $p=q$.

∂ Step 1 — Charge Element and Arc Length
$$\mathbf r'=(x',\,p\cos\phi',\,q\sin\phi'),\qquad ds=\sqrt{p^2\sin^2\phi'+q^2\cos^2\phi'}\;d\phi'$$

$ds$ is the ellipse's own arc-length element — not $R\,d\phi'$ as for a circle, since $|d\mathbf r'/d\phi'|=\sqrt{p^2\sin^2\phi'+q^2\cos^2\phi'}$ is itself $\phi'$-dependent whenever $p\neq q$. The charge on a patch of the shell between $x'$ and $x'+dx'$, and between $\phi'$ and $\phi'+d\phi'$, is

$$dq=\sigma\,ds\,dx'=\sigma\sqrt{p^2\sin^2\phi'+q^2\cos^2\phi'}\;d\phi'\,dx'$$

This one fact — that "linear density around the loop," $\sigma\,ds/d\phi'$, is not constant when $p\neq q$ — is the entire reason this system has no closed form where the circular Hollow Cylinder has one.

∂ Step 2 — The General (Off-Axis) Surface Integral
$$s^2=(x_0-x')^2+(y_0-p\cos\phi')^2+(z_0-q\sin\phi')^2$$
$$V(x_0,y_0,z_0)=k\sigma\!\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{\sqrt{p^2\sin^2\phi'+q^2\cos^2\phi'}}{s}\,d\phi'\,dx'$$

and, applying Coulomb's law directly to each element $dq$ (rather than differentiating $V$ first):

$$E_x=k\sigma\!\iint\!\frac{(x_0-x')\sqrt{p^2\sin^2\phi'+q^2\cos^2\phi'}}{s^3}\,d\phi'dx',\quad E_y=k\sigma\!\iint\!\frac{(y_0-p\cos\phi')\sqrt{\cdots}}{s^3}\,d\phi'dx',\quad E_z=k\sigma\!\iint\!\frac{(z_0-q\sin\phi')\sqrt{\cdots}}{s^3}\,d\phi'dx'$$

Both integrals run over the full rectangle $(x',\phi')\in[x_1,x_2]\times[0,2\pi]$, and — unlike every previous system — there is no argument yet for doing either one in closed form.

📍 Step 3 — On-Axis Specialization: How Close It Comes to an Elliptic Integral

Set $y_0=z_0=0$ (field point on the shared axis). Then, using $\cos^2\phi'=1-\sin^2\phi'$:

$$s^2=(x_0-x')^2+p^2\cos^2\phi'+q^2\sin^2\phi' =D^2-(p^2-q^2)\sin^2\phi', \qquad D^2\equiv(x_0-x')^2+p^2$$

Writing $k^2\equiv(p^2-q^2)/D^2$, this is $s=D\sqrt{1-k^2\sin^2\phi'}$ — exactly the Legendre normal form that gave the Ring system its own $K(k)$ result. If the charge on the ellipse were spread evenly in the angle $\phi'$ (i.e. $dq=\sigma R\,d\phi'$, no arc-length weighting), the $\phi'$-integral of $1/s$ would collapse to the elementary $4K(k)/D$, exactly as it did there.

⚠️ But the charge is spread evenly in arc length, not in angle. The arc-length weight from Step 1, $\sqrt{p^2\sin^2\phi'+q^2\cos^2\phi'} =\sqrt{q^2+(p^2-q^2)\cos^2\phi'}$, is itself a nontrivial function of $\phi'$ that does not cancel against $1/s$. The on-axis potential integral is
$$V(x_0,0,0)=k\sigma\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\left[\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{\sqrt{q^2+(p^2-q^2)\cos^2\phi'}}{D\sqrt{1-k^2\sin^2\phi'}}\,d\phi'\right]dx'$$

the inner bracket is a ratio of two different trigonometric weightings of $\phi'$ — one growing where the other shrinks — and it doesn't reduce to any single standard Legendre elliptic integral ($K$, $E$, or $\Pi$); it's evaluated numerically here, exactly like the fully general off-axis integral. Only in the limit $p\to q$ does the numerator become the constant $q$, at which point the whole bracket collapses to the elementary $4q/D$ (Step 5) — the on-axis integral becomes trivial only when the cross-section is a circle.

✔ Step 4 — On-Axis Symmetry: $E_y=E_z=0$ (No Integration Needed)

Even though $V(x_0,0,0)$ itself needs quadrature, its transverse field components vanish there by symmetry alone. Replacing $\phi'\to\pi-\phi'$ sends $p\cos\phi'\to-p\cos\phi'$ but leaves $q\sin\phi'$, $s$, and the arc-length weight unchanged — so the $E_y$ integrand is odd under this reflection and the two halves cancel in pairs. The same argument with $\phi'\to-\phi'$ kills $E_z$. So on-axis, only $E_x$ survives, exactly as for every other axisymmetric system in this app — even though the elliptical cross-section itself isn't axisymmetric.

✔ Step 5 — Circular Limit $p=q=R$: Recovering the Hollow Cylinder Exactly

Set $p=q=R$. The arc-length weight collapses to the constant $\sqrt{R^2\sin^2\phi'+R^2\cos^2\phi'}=R$, so it factors outside the $\phi'$-integral entirely — this is precisely the missing ingredient from Step 3. The on-axis potential becomes:

$$V(x_0,0,0)=k\sigma R\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\left[\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\phi'}{\sqrt{(x_0-x')^2+R^2}}\right]dx' = k\sigma R\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\frac{2\pi\,dx'}{\sqrt{(x_0-x')^2+R^2}}=k\lambda_{\text{eff}}\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\frac{dx'}{\sqrt{(x_0-x')^2+R^2}},\qquad\lambda_{\text{eff}}=2\pi R\sigma$$

exactly the Rod system's own integrand, reproducing the Hollow Cylinder system's exact on-axis reuse of its closed form. This is the built-in sanity check for the Simulation tab: set $p=q$ there and every number should match the Hollow Cylinder system's own output at the same $R,\sigma,L$.

# Step 6 — Numerical Evaluation (What the App Actually Computes)

Because neither the general off-axis integral nor even the on-axis one reduces to elementary or standard special functions, both $V$ and $\mathbf E$ are obtained here by direct composite 2D quadrature over $(x',\phi')\in[x_1,x_2]\times[0,2\pi]$ — reusing the Sheet system's own generic quadrature machinery verbatim, with the ellipse's own arc-length Jacobian $\sqrt{p^2\sin^2\phi'+q^2\cos^2\phi'}$ folded into the integrand in place of the Sheet's constant one (and the Hollow Cylinder's constant $R$). A second, fully independent Monte Carlo surface integral serves as the Simulation tab's cross-check, exactly mirroring every other numerical-only system in this app.

∂ The Surface Integral
$$\mathbf r'=(x',\,p\cos\phi',\,q\sin\phi'),\qquad dA=\sqrt{p^2\sin^2\phi'+q^2\cos^2\phi'}\;d\phi'\,dx'$$
$$V=k\sigma\!\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{dA}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|},\qquad \mathbf E=k\sigma\!\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{(\mathbf r-\mathbf r')\,dA}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|^3}$$

Evaluated by composite 2D quadrature over $(x',\phi')\in[x_1,x_2]\times[0,2\pi]$. Setting $p=q$ collapses every result to the Hollow Cylinder system's own numbers — used as a built-in sanity check.

∫ What IS Known in Closed Form — and What Isn't
$$dq=\sigma\sqrt{p^2\sin^2\phi'+q^2\cos^2\phi'}\,d\phi'\,dx',\qquad s^2=(x_0-x')^2+(y_0-p\cos\phi')^2+(z_0-q\sin\phi')^2$$

No closed form exists for $V$ or $\mathbf E$ at a general field point — see the Derivation tab for exactly why the arc-length weighting blocks the elliptic-integral reduction that works for the circular Hollow Cylinder. Two regimes do have exact reference values, used throughout this tab and the Simulation tab as sanity checks:

RegimeConditionWhat's exact
Circular limit$p=q=R$Collapses exactly to the Hollow Cylinder system — on-axis reuses the Rod system's closed form; off-axis reuses ring-superposition
On-axis, $E_y=E_z=0$$y_0=z_0=0$Transverse field components vanish exactly by reflection symmetry (Derivation Step 4), even though $V$ and $E_x$ still need quadrature
Far field$r\gg L,p,q$Reduces to a point charge $Q=\sigma\cdot(\text{ellipse perimeter})\cdot L$
General field pointanywhere elseNo elementary or standard-special-function closed form — 2D surface quadrature only
💡 Why not Mathieu functions? The exact classical solution for charge on confocal elliptic-cylindrical surfaces is a separation-of-variables series in Mathieu functions $\text{ce}_n,\text{se}_n$ — correct in principle, but the series converges slowly except for very elongated or near-circular cross-sections, and evaluating Mathieu functions themselves needs their own numerical machinery. Direct surface quadrature, already exact to machine precision at high $N$, is simpler and no less rigorous for the field values this app reports.
∫ No Closed Form — Two Independent Quadrature Routes

Every Simulation-tab number comes from a high-order Simpson surface integral (reference) and an independent Monte Carlo surface integral (cross-check).

⬭→⬯ From an Ellipse to a Hyperbola Branch

Squash the Elliptic Cylinder's family of similar ellipses into a family of similar hyperbolas — swap trigonometric for hyperbolic functions. Take one branch of

$$\frac{y'^2}{p^2}-\frac{z'^2}{q^2}=1\qquad\text{(one branch, opening toward }+y\text{)}$$

extruded along the shared axis over $x'\in[x_1,x_2]$, and self-similarly scaled to fill the interior wedge:

$$y'(u,\rho')=p\,\rho'\cosh u,\qquad z'(u,\rho')=q\,\rho'\sinh u,\qquad u\in[-U,U],\ \ \rho'\in[\max(0,1-t),1]$$

$\rho'=1$ traces the boundary hyperbola (truncated at $u=\pm U$, since a full branch is infinite); $\rho'\to0$ shrinks every point toward the origin along the ray at that $u$, filling the wedge between the two asymptotes $z=\pm(q/p)y$ — the direct analogue of the Elliptic Cylinder's own rings→disk-style fill, and of the Elliptic Paraboloid's own thickness unification of surface and volume.

💡 Thickness $t$ unifies surface and volume, exactly as in the Elliptic Paraboloid system: $t=1$ fills the whole wedge (a solid volume charge); small $t$ leaves only a thin band pressed against the boundary curve (a genuine 2D surface charge).
∂ The Jacobian — Clean, Unlike the Arc Length
$$\frac{\partial(y',z')}{\partial(\rho',u)}=\begin{vmatrix}p\cosh u & p\rho'\sinh u\\ q\sinh u & q\rho'\cosh u\end{vmatrix}=pq\,\rho'(\cosh^2u-\sinh^2u)=pq\,\rho'$$

Identical in form to a plane-polar Jacobian $r\,dr\,d\phi$ — a pleasant surprise, since the arc-length element of the boundary curve itself is not this simple:

$$ds=\sqrt{p^2\sinh^2u+q^2\cosh^2u}\,du\qquad\text{(needed only for the total-charge, }t\to0\text{ limit)}$$
$$dV=pq\,\rho'\,d\rho'\,du\,dx',\qquad dq=\rho(\rho',u)\,pq\,\rho'\,d\rho'\,du\,dx'$$
📏 Parameters & Master Integrals
$\rho_0$Density scale (uniform, or graded)nC/m³ or /m²
$p,q$Transverse, conjugate semi-axesm
$U$Hyperbolic-angle cutoff (truncates the open branch)—
$t$Thickness fraction — $t=1$ solid, small $t$ thin shell—
$$V(\mathbf r)=k\!\iiint\frac{\rho(\rho',u)\,pq\,\rho'}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}\,d\rho'\,du\,dx',\qquad \mathbf E(\mathbf r)=k\!\iiint\frac{(\mathbf r-\mathbf r')\,\rho(\rho',u)\,pq\,\rho'}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|^3}\,d\rho'\,du\,dx'$$
⚠️ No closed form. This is the "radial" counterpart of the Elliptic Cylinder's own Mathieu-function aside: separating Laplace's equation along the hyperbolic coordinate produces modified Mathieu functions $Mc_n,Ms_n$, not elementary functions. Evaluated here by direct 3D quadrature (Simpson reference, Monte Carlo cross-check) — the same engineering choice already made for the Elliptic Cylinder and Elliptic Paraboloid systems.
💡 Truncation edge effect. Because the branch is an open curve (unlike the ellipse's closed loop), cutting it at $u=\pm U$ produces genuine edge charge concentration there — the hyperbolic analogue of a rod's end effects, with no counterpart in the Elliptic Cylinder system.
🖼 Geometry
∂ Charge Element, Symmetry, and Truncation
Source point and separation
$$\mathbf r'=(x',\,p\rho'\cosh u,\,q\rho'\sinh u),\qquad |\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|=\sqrt{(x_0-x')^2+(y_0-p\rho'\cosh u)^2+(z_0-q\rho'\sinh u)^2}$$
Symmetry: E_z=0 exactly at z0=0

Reflecting $u\to-u$ leaves $\cosh u$ unchanged but flips the sign of $\sinh u$ — a source point at $(x',p\rho'\cosh u,q\rho'\sinh u)$ pairs with one at $(x',p\rho'\cosh u,-q\rho'\sinh u)$. At $z_0=0$ these two contribute equal-and-opposite $z$-components, which cancel in pairs over the full $u\in[-U,U]$ range (symmetric about 0). So $E_z(x_0,y_0,0)=0$ exactly, for any $x_0,y_0$ — even though $V$ and $E_x,E_y$ there still require quadrature.

No further reduction — direct 3D quadrature

Unlike the solid Sphere or solid Cylinder (which reduced one integration variable to an elementary antiderivative), no variable here separates into elementary or standard-special-function form: the density is evaluated by composite Simpson's rule over the full $(x',u,\rho')$ box, cross-checked against an independent 3D Monte Carlo integral with no shell-reuse machinery at all.

Truncation and thickness — two independent cutoffs

$U$ truncates the otherwise-infinite branch (needed for a finite total charge); $t$ controls how much of the wedge $\rho'\in[0,1]$ is actually filled. Setting $t=1$ gives the full solid wedge; $t\to0$ leaves a thin band at $\rho'\approx1$ — a genuine surface charge, whose total charge in that limit approaches $\sigma_{\text{eff}}\!\cdot\!(\text{arc length})\!\cdot\!L$ with $\sigma_{\text{eff}}=\rho_0\cdot(\text{band width in }\rho')$.

Multiple concentric shells

$V,\mathbf E$ superpose linearly, so several hyperbolic shells/volumes sharing one axis (different $p,q,U,t,\rho_0$, possibly opposite sign) simply sum their own independent 3D integrals — the same superposition principle used throughout this app.

∫ Master Formula and Regimes
$$V(\mathbf r)=k\!\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\!\!\int_{-U}^{U}\!\!\int_{\rho'_{\text{lo}}}^{1}\frac{\rho(\rho',u)\,pq\,\rho'}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}\,d\rho'\,du\,dx'$$

No elementary or standard-special-function closed form exists; evaluated by direct 3D Simpson quadrature (reference) and independent 3D Monte Carlo (cross-check).

RegimeConditionBehaviour
Symmetry plane$z_0=0$$E_z=0$ exactly; $V,E_x,E_y$ still numerical
Genericanywhere elseSmooth, finite; Simpson 3D vs Monte Carlo cross-check
Thin shell$t\to0$Approaches a genuine 2D surface charge
Far field$r\gg p,q,U\!\cdot\!\max(p,q),L$Reduces to a point charge $Q=\sum Q_i$
Near $u=\pm U$edges of the truncationGenuine edge-charge concentration (open curve)

⬮→∩ From an Ellipse/Cylinder to a Paraboloid

Take a family of similar ellipses and stack them along an axis, but instead of holding the size fixed (the Elliptic Cylinder) or growing it linearly, let the semi-axes grow as $\sqrt{z}$. The boundary surface swept out is a solid elliptic paraboloid: an apex at $z'=0$, opening upward, with the cross-section at height $z'$ an ellipse of semi-axes $a(z')=a_0\sqrt{z'/H}$, $b(z')=b_0\sqrt{z'/H}$.

The Defining Surface

$$\frac{x'^2}{a_0^2}+\frac{y'^2}{b_0^2}=\frac{z'}{H},\qquad 0\le z'\le H$$

equivalently solved for height, $z'=H\big(x'^2/a_0^2+y'^2/b_0^2\big)$ — the standard "elliptic paraboloid" equation, with $a_0,b_0$ the semi-axes of the rim ellipse at $z'=H$ and $H$ the apex-to-rim height. Setting $a_0=b_0$ recovers the ordinary circular paraboloid of revolution; letting $H\to\infty$ at fixed $a_0/\sqrt H,\,b_0/\sqrt H$ flattens it toward the Elliptic Cylinder system's own infinite-cylinder limit.

Self-Similar Parametrization

Every point inside or on the surface is labelled by a dimensionless radial fraction $\rho'\in[0,1]$, an azimuth $\phi'\in[0,2\pi)$, and the height $z'\in[0,H]$:

$$x'=a(z')\,\rho'\cos\phi',\qquad y'=b(z')\,\rho'\sin\phi',\qquad a(z')=a_0\sqrt{\frac{z'}{H}},\ \ b(z')=b_0\sqrt{\frac{z'}{H}}$$

$\rho'=1$ traces the paraboloid's own outer surface at that height (i.e. exactly the defining equation above); $\rho'=0$ is the axis. This is the same "self-similar cross-section, scaled by a height-dependent factor" idea used for the Solid Cylinder ($a(z')=$ const) and the Solid Ellipsoid (confocal scaling), just with $a(z')\propto\sqrt{z'}$ here.

Volume Element and Charge

$$dV = a(z')\,b(z')\,\rho'\,d\rho'\,d\phi'\,dz',\qquad dq=\rho(\rho',z')\,dV$$

Identical in form to a plain polar-coordinate area element $r\,dr\,d\phi$, with $a(z')b(z')$ playing the role of a $z'$-dependent scale factor — exactly the Jacobian used in the Derivation tab's master integral. The full solid (thickness $t=1$) integrates $\rho'$ over $[0,1]$; a thin shell of thickness fraction $t$ restricts it to $\rho'\in[\max(0,1-t),\,1]$.

Master Potential and Field Integrals

$$V(\mathbf r)=k\!\int_0^H\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_{\rho'_{\text{lo}}}^{1}\frac{\rho(\rho',z')\,a(z')b(z')\,\rho'}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}\,d\rho'\,d\phi'\,dz'$$
$$\mathbf E(\mathbf r)=k\!\int_0^H\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_{\rho'_{\text{lo}}}^{1}\frac{(\mathbf r-\mathbf r')\,\rho(\rho',z')\,a(z')b(z')\,\rho'}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|^3}\,d\rho'\,d\phi'\,dz'$$

with $\rho'_{\text{lo}}=\max(0,1-t)$. These are the direct analogues of every other volume-charge master formula in this app (compare the solid Sphere's $Q_{\text{enc}}(r)$ integral or the solid Cylinder's disk-stacking integral) — the only new ingredient is the height-dependent Jacobian $a(z')b(z')\propto z'$, which comes from the $\sqrt{z'}$ scaling of the cross-section.

A thin paraboloidal shell (a genuine 2D surface charge, like the Sheet or hollow Shell systems) and the solid paraboloid (a volume charge, like the solid Sphere or solid Cylinder) are unified here by a single thickness control $t$: charge is placed only in a thin band near the outer boundary (small $t$) or filled all the way to the apex ($t=1$, the full solid) — exactly the same "surface via thickness" idea used for a thick spherical or cylindrical shell.

📏 Parameters
$\rho_0$Volume charge density (uniform case)nC/m³
$a_0,b_0$Semi-axes of the paraboloid's rim (at $z'=H$)m
$H$Height, apex to rimm
$t$Thickness fraction — $t=1$ is the solid paraboloid; $t\to0$ is a thin surface shell—

Several shells sharing one apex and axis, at different $(a_0,b_0,H)$, are concentric nested paraboloids — the direct analogue of concentric spherical or cylindrical shells, just for this geometry.

⬡ Why This System Has No Closed Form

Every shell system elsewhere in this app owes its exact result to a coordinate system in which the shell is a level surface: a sphere of constant $r$, a cylinder of constant $\rho$. A paraboloid is a level surface too — but only in parabolic (paraboloidal) coordinates, and even there, exact results for finite paraboloidal charge distributions require the Weber–Schafheitlin family of integrals rather than a handful of elementary or standard special functions. That machinery is not built here — exactly the same engineering choice already made for the Elliptic Cylinder system's own Mathieu-function aside. Instead, $V$ and $\mathbf E$ are obtained by direct 3D quadrature (composite Simpson, used as the reference) cross-checked against an independent 3D Monte Carlo integral — the same two-method pattern used throughout the solid Ellipsoid system.

🖼 Geometry
∂ Parametrization and the Volume Jacobian
A self-similar coordinate family

Write every interior/boundary point as $x'=a(z')\,\rho'\cos\phi'$, $y'=b(z')\,\rho'\sin\phi'$, with $a(z')=a_0\sqrt{z'/H}$, $b(z')=b_0\sqrt{z'/H}$, $\rho'\in[0,1]$ a dimensionless radial fraction of the way to the rim at that height, and $\phi'\in[0,2\pi)$. $\rho'=1$ traces the paraboloid's own outer surface; $\rho'=0$ is the axis.

The Jacobian — a clean result

Computing $\partial(x',y',z')/\partial(\rho',\phi',z')$ and expanding the determinant along the row for $z'$ (which contributes only $\partial z'/\partial z'=1$), the remaining $2\times2$ block is exactly a polar-style Jacobian scaled by $a(z')b(z')$:

$$dV = a(z')\,b(z')\,\rho'\,d\rho'\,d\phi'\,dz'$$

Identical in form to plain polar coordinates $r\,dr\,d\phi$ (the Disk system's own Jacobian), just with $a(z')b(z')$ playing the role of a $z'$-dependent scale factor — a direct consequence of the ellipse-at-each-height cross-section.

Charge element and the master integrals
$$dq=\rho(\rho',z')\,a(z')b(z')\,\rho'\,d\rho'\,d\phi'\,dz'$$
$$V(\mathbf r)=k\!\iiint\!\frac{dq}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|},\qquad \mathbf E(\mathbf r)=k\!\iiint\!\frac{(\mathbf r-\mathbf r')\,dq}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|^3}$$

with $\rho'$ ranging over $[\max(0,1-t),1]$ for thickness fraction $t$ — $t=1$ fills the whole solid; small $t$ leaves only a thin band near the surface, approximating a genuine 2D shell of local surface density $\sigma_{\text{eff}}\approx\rho_0\cdot(\text{local normal thickness})$.

Symmetry: Eₓ=E_y=0 exactly on the axis

On the axis ($x_0=y_0=$ apex position), reflecting $\phi'\to-\phi'$ sends $y'\to-y'$ while leaving $x',z',\rho(\rho',z')$ unchanged (density never depends on $\phi'$) — the paired contributions' $y$-components cancel while their $x,z$ components add. The companion reflection $\phi'\to\pi-\phi'$ kills $E_x$ the same way. So $E_x=E_y=0$ exactly on-axis, for any $a_0,b_0$ (even $a_0\neq b_0$) and any radially-graded density — a genuinely exact statement, even though $V$ and $E_z$ themselves still need quadrature. The Simulation tab's regime indicator flags this case and the comparison table confirms it numerically.

Numerical evaluation

Composite Simpson's rule over the 3D box $(\rho',\phi',z')$ serves as the reference (10 panels per axis by default, a genuinely 3D grid); a fully independent Monte Carlo integral over the same domain (flat sampling, Jacobian folded explicitly into the integrand — no shell-reuse machinery at all) is the cross-check, exactly mirroring the solid Ellipsoid system's own two-method comparison.

⊕ Multiple Concentric Shells

$V$ and $\mathbf E$ superpose linearly, so several nested paraboloids (different $a_0,b_0,H$, possibly opposite-sign density, possibly different thickness) simply sum their own independent 3D integrals — the same superposition principle used for every multi-shell system in this app (Hollow Spherical Shells, Hollow/Elliptic Cylinder).

∫ Master Formula and Regimes
$$V(\mathbf r)=k\!\int_{0}^{H}\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_{\rho'_{\text{lo}}}^{1}\frac{\rho(\rho',z')\,a(z')b(z')\,\rho'}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}\,d\rho'\,d\phi'\,dz'$$

No elementary or standard-special-function closed form exists for a general field point; evaluated here by direct 3D quadrature (Simpson reference, Monte Carlo cross-check).

⬯ A Genuinely Closed Hyperboloidal Surface

Every hyperbolic system so far in this app (the Hyperbolic Cylinder) used one open branch of a hyperbola extruded along a straight axis. The hyperboloid of one sheet is different: it is a single, connected, unbounded-but-truncatable surface of revolution-like character in three genuine dimensions, satisfying

$$\frac{x'^2}{a_0^2}+\frac{y'^2}{b_0^2}-\frac{z'^2}{c_0^2}=1$$

Unlike the two-sheet hyperboloid (two disconnected bowls), setting $z'=0$ here gives the full ellipse $x'^2/a_0^2+y'^2/b_0^2=1$ — a genuine "waist" — and the surface flares outward continuously in both $\pm z'$ directions from that waist. It is topologically a cylinder (an infinite tube), just curved rather than straight.

$$x'=a_0\rho'\cosh w\cos\theta,\qquad y'=b_0\rho'\cosh w\sin\theta,\qquad z'=c_0\rho'\sinh w$$

$\rho'=1$ traces the boundary surface exactly (since $\cosh^2w-\sinh^2w=1$ makes the defining equation hold identically); $\rho'\to0$ shrinks every point toward the $z$-axis along its own ray, filling the solid interior — the same self-similar "thickness" device used by the Hyperbolic Cylinder and Elliptic Paraboloid systems, unifying a solid volume charge ($t=1$) and a thin surface shell (small $t$) under one control.

💡 Truncation. $w$ is cut off at $\pm W$ so the (otherwise infinite) hyperboloid and its enclosed volume stay finite — exactly the same truncation the Hyperbolic Cylinder system uses for its own open branch.
∂ The Volume Jacobian — Clean, Despite the Surface Having No Closed Form

Computing $\partial\mathbf r/\partial\rho'\cdot(\partial\mathbf r/\partial w\times\partial\mathbf r/\partial\theta)$ and using $\cosh^2w-\sinh^2w=1$ throughout:

$$dV=a_0b_0c_0\,\rho'^2\cosh w\;d\rho'\,dw\,d\theta$$

Structurally the same "$\rho'^2\times(\text{angular weight})$" pattern as the solid Sphere's $r'^2\sin\theta'$ and the solid Ellipsoid's own volume element — only the angular weight is $\cosh w$ instead of $\sin\theta'$, since one coordinate here is hyperbolic rather than spherical.

$$dq=\rho(\rho',w)\,a_0b_0c_0\,\rho'^2\cosh w\;d\rho'\,dw\,d\theta$$
📏 Parameters & Exact Symmetries
$\rho_0$Density scale (uniform, or graded)nC/m³ or /m²
$a_0,b_0$Waist semi-axes ($x,y$)m
$c_0$Conjugate (flare-rate) semi-axism
$W$Hyperbolic-angle cutoff (truncates the sheet)—
$t$Thickness fraction — $t=1$ solid, small $t$ thin shell—
$$V(\mathbf r)=k\!\iiint\frac{dq}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|},\qquad \mathbf E(\mathbf r)=k\!\iiint\frac{(\mathbf r-\mathbf r')\,dq}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|^3}$$

Two statements are exact, with no numerical integration at all: at $z_0=0$, reflecting $w\to-w$ flips only $z'$, so $E_z(x_0,y_0,0)=0$ identically. On the $z$-axis ($x_0=y_0=0$), reflecting $\theta\to\theta+\pi$ flips $(x',y')\to-(x',y')$ without changing $s$, so $E_x=E_y=0$ there — true for any $a_0,b_0$, not just $a_0=b_0$.

⚠️ No closed form. Separating Laplace's equation in the natural hyperboloidal coordinates $(\rho',w,\theta)$ produces hyperboloidal wave functions — the same family of transcendental special functions that appear for prolate/oblate spheroidal problems — not elementary functions. Exactly like the Elliptic Cylinder and Hyperbolic Cylinder systems, this app evaluates $V,\mathbf E$ by direct 3D quadrature instead of building that machinery.
🖼 Geometry
∂ Charge Element, Symmetries, and Truncation
Source point and separation
$$\mathbf r'=(a_0\rho'\cosh w\cos\theta,\;b_0\rho'\cosh w\sin\theta,\;c_0\rho'\sinh w)$$
E_z=0 exactly on the z0=0 plane

Under $w\to-w$: $\cosh w$ is unchanged (so $x',y'$ unchanged) but $\sinh w\to-\sinh w$ (so $z'\to-z'$). At $z_0=0$ the two paired contributions have equal-and-opposite $z$-separations and identical $s$, so their $E_z$ pieces cancel in pairs over the symmetric range $w\in[-W,W]$ — giving $E_z(x_0,y_0,0)=0$ exactly, for any density profile that doesn't itself break the $w\to-w$ symmetry.

E_x=E_y=0 exactly on the z-axis

At $x_0=y_0=0$, reflecting $\theta\to\theta+\pi$ sends $(x',y')\to-(x',y')$ while leaving $z'$ and $s$ unchanged — the paired contributions' $x,y$ components cancel while $z$ adds. Since $\theta$ is integrated over the full $2\pi$, this holds exactly, independent of $a_0$ vs $b_0$.

No further reduction — direct 3D quadrature

Composite Simpson's rule over the box $(\rho',w,\theta)$ serves as the reference; an independent 3D Monte Carlo integral (flat sampling, Jacobian folded in explicitly, no shell-reuse machinery) is the cross-check — the same two-method pattern as the Hyperbolic Cylinder and solid Ellipsoid systems.

Multiple concentric shells

$V,\mathbf E$ superpose linearly, so several hyperboloidal shells/volumes sharing one axis (different $a_0,b_0,c_0,W,t,\rho_0$, possibly opposite sign) simply sum their own independent 3D integrals.

∫ Master Formula and Regimes
$$V(\mathbf r)=k\!\int_{-W}^{W}\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_{\rho'_{\text{lo}}}^{1}\frac{\rho(\rho',w)\,a_0b_0c_0\,\rho'^2\cosh w}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}\,d\rho'\,d\theta\,dw$$

No elementary or standard-special-function closed form exists; evaluated by direct 3D Simpson quadrature (reference) and independent 3D Monte Carlo (cross-check).

⬯⬯ Two Disjoint Branches, Opening Away From Each Other

Flip a sign relative to the Hyperboloid-of-One-Sheet system's own equation and the connected waist disappears, splitting into two separate bowl-shaped branches that never touch:

$$\frac{z'^2}{c_0^2}-\frac{x'^2}{a_0^2}-\frac{y'^2}{b_0^2}=1\qquad\text{(upper branch }z'\ge c_0\text{, lower branch }z'\le -c_0\text{)}$$

At $z'=\pm c_0$ each branch pinches to a single point (its vertex) rather than opening into a circle — the opposite of the one-sheet system's own nonzero circular waist at $w=0$. Self-similarly filling each branch, with $s=+1$ for the upper vertex and $s=-1$ for the lower:

$$x'=a_0\rho'\sinh w\cos\theta,\quad y'=b_0\rho'\sinh w\sin\theta,\quad z'=s\,c_0\rho'\cosh w,\qquad s=\pm1,\ w\in[0,W],\ \rho'\in[\max(0,1-t),1]$$

$\rho'=1$ traces the boundary surface exactly ($\cosh^2w-\sinh^2w=1$ makes the defining equation hold identically for any $s$); $\rho'\to0$ shrinks every point toward the shared $z$-axis, filling the solid interior of whichever branch. $W$ truncates the otherwise-infinite branches; $t$ is the same thickness control used throughout this app to unify a solid volume charge ($t=1$) with a thin surface shell (small $t$).

💡 Why sinh, not cosh, in the transverse directions. At the vertex ($w=0$) the cross-section is a single point, so the transverse coordinates must vanish there — $\sinh(0)=0$ does that; $z'$ itself must be nonzero there ($=s c_0\rho'$), which $\cosh(0)=1$ provides. This is the exact opposite role-assignment from the one-sheet system, where the waist forced $\cosh$ into the transverse slots instead.
∂ The Volume Jacobian

Computing $\partial\mathbf r/\partial\rho'\cdot(\partial\mathbf r/\partial w\times\partial\mathbf r/\partial\theta)$ and using $\cosh^2w-\sinh^2w=1$ throughout (worked in full on the Derivation tab):

$$dV=a_0b_0c_0\,\rho'^2\sinh w\;d\rho'\,dw\,d\theta$$

Structurally the same "$\rho'^2\times(\text{angular weight})$" pattern used by every 3D volume system in this app — only the weight is $\sinh w$ here rather than the one-sheet system's $\cosh w$, tracking the vanishing cross-section at the vertex.

$$dq=\rho(\rho',w)\,a_0b_0c_0\,\rho'^2\sinh w\;d\rho'\,dw\,d\theta$$
📏 Parameters & Exact Symmetries
$\rho_0$Density scale (uniform, or graded)nC/m³ or /m²
$a_0,b_0$Transverse semi-axes at unit hyperbolic radiusm
$c_0$Half the vertex-to-vertex separation (vertices at $z=\pm c_0$)m
$W$Hyperbolic-angle cutoff (truncates each branch)—
$t$Thickness fraction — $t=1$ solid, small $t$ thin shell—
$$V(\mathbf r)=k\sum_{s=\pm1}\iiint\frac{dq}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|},\qquad \mathbf E(\mathbf r)=k\sum_{s=\pm1}\iiint\frac{(\mathbf r-\mathbf r')\,dq}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|^3}$$

Two statements are exact, with no numerical integration at all: on the shared midplane $z_0=c_z$ (the point exactly between the two vertices), reflecting the upper branch onto the lower one flips only $z$, so $E_z(x_0,y_0,c_z)=0$ identically. On the shared $z$-axis ($x_0=c_x,\,y_0=c_y$), rotating $\theta\to\theta+\pi$ flips only $(x',y')$, so $E_x=E_y=0$ there — true for any $z_0$ and any $a_0,b_0$.

⚠️ No closed form. Exactly like the one-sheet system, separating Laplace's equation in these natural coordinates produces hyperboloidal wave functions, not elementary functions. $V,\mathbf E$ are evaluated here by direct 3D quadrature (Simpson reference, Monte Carlo cross-check).
🖼 Geometry
∂ Charge Element, Symmetries, and Truncation
Source point and separation, per branch
$$\mathbf r'=(a_0\rho'\sinh w\cos\theta,\;b_0\rho'\sinh w\sin\theta,\;s\,c_0\rho'\cosh w)$$
The Jacobian, in full

Computing $\partial\mathbf r/\partial\rho'\cdot(\partial\mathbf r/\partial w\times\partial\mathbf r/\partial\theta)$ and using $\cosh^2w-\sinh^2w=1$ to collapse the trigonometric terms exactly as in the one-sheet system's own derivation (only with $\sinh,\cosh$ trading places), every cross term cancels leaving the single clean result:

$$\left|\frac{\partial(x',y',z')}{\partial(\rho',w,\theta)}\right|=a_0b_0c_0\,\rho'^2\sinh w$$
E_z=0 exactly on the midplane z0=c_z

Swapping $s\to-s$ at fixed $w$ maps $z'\to c_z-(s c_0\rho'\cosh w - c_z)$, i.e. reflects the source about $z=c_z$, while leaving $x',y',\rho(\rho',w)$ unchanged (the density never depends on $s$ by construction — both branches always share the same profile). At $z_0=c_z$ the two paired contributions have equal-and-opposite $z$-separations and identical $s$ (separation distance), so their $E_z$ pieces cancel in pairs when summed over $s=\pm1$ — giving $E_z(x_0,y_0,c_z)=0$ exactly.

E_x=E_y=0 exactly on the shared z-axis

At $x_0=c_x,\,y_0=c_y$ (any $z_0$), reflecting $\theta\to\theta+\pi$ sends $(x',y')\to-(x',y')$ while leaving $z'$ and the separation distance $s$ unchanged — the paired contributions' $x,y$ components cancel while $z$ adds. Since $\theta$ is integrated over the full $2\pi$, this holds exactly, independent of $a_0$ vs $b_0$ and independent of which branch is being integrated.

No further reduction — direct 3D quadrature

Composite Simpson's rule over the box $(\rho',w,\theta)$, summed over both branches $s=\pm1$, serves as the reference; an independent 3D Monte Carlo integral (flat sampling, Jacobian folded in explicitly, no shell-reuse machinery) is the cross-check — the identical two-method pattern used by the Hyperbolic Cylinder, Elliptic Paraboloid, and one-sheet Hyperboloid systems.

Multiple concentric shell-pairs

$V,\mathbf E$ superpose linearly, so several nested two-sheet configurations sharing one axis (different $a_0,b_0,c_0,W,t,\rho_0$, possibly opposite sign) simply sum their own independent 3D integrals — each shell object already carries both branches, so no separate bookkeeping for "upper" vs "lower" is needed at the shell-list level.

∫ Master Formula and Regimes
$$V(\mathbf r)=k\sum_{s=\pm1}\int_{0}^{W}\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_{\rho'_{\text{lo}}}^{1}\frac{\rho(\rho',w)\,a_0b_0c_0\,\rho'^2\sinh w}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}\,d\rho'\,d\theta\,dw$$

No elementary or standard-special-function closed form exists; evaluated by direct 3D Simpson quadrature (reference) and independent 3D Monte Carlo (cross-check), each summed over both branches.

∆→⋀ From a Paraboloid to a Cone — a Linear Growth Law

Take the Elliptic Paraboloid system's family of similar ellipses stacked along an axis, but instead of growing the cross-section as $\sqrt{z'}$, let it grow linearly in $z'$. The boundary surface swept out is a solid elliptic cone: an apex at $z'=0$, opening upward, with the cross-section at height $z'$ an ellipse of semi-axes $a(z')=a_0(z'/H)$, $b(z')=b_0(z'/H)$.

$$\frac{x'^2}{a_0^2}+\frac{y'^2}{b_0^2}=\left(\frac{z'}{H}\right)^2,\qquad 0\le z'\le H$$

equivalently solved for height, $z'=H\sqrt{x'^2/a_0^2+y'^2/b_0^2}$ — the standard single-nappe elliptic cone equation, with $a_0,b_0$ the semi-axes of the rim ellipse at $z'=H$. Setting $a_0=b_0$ recovers the ordinary right circular cone; the Elliptic Paraboloid system's own $z'=H(x'^2/a_0^2+y'^2/b_0^2)$ differs only in how fast the cross-section grows with height — quadratically there, linearly here.

Self-Similar Parametrization

$$x'=a(z')\,\rho'\cos\phi',\qquad y'=b(z')\,\rho'\sin\phi',\qquad a(z')=a_0\frac{z'}{H},\ \ b(z')=b_0\frac{z'}{H}$$

$\rho'=1$ traces the cone's own lateral surface at that height; $\rho'=0$ is the axis. Exactly the Paraboloid system's own "thickness via $\rho'$" device: $t=1$ fills the whole solid cone; small $t$ leaves only a thin band pressed against the lateral surface — a genuine 2D conical shell.

Volume Element and Charge

$$dV=a(z')\,b(z')\,\rho'\,d\rho'\,d\phi'\,dz',\qquad dq=\rho(\rho',z')\,dV$$

The Jacobian has exactly the same polar-style form as the Paraboloid's own $a(z')b(z')\rho'$ — only the underlying $a(z'),b(z')$ functions differ. Setting $\rho'\in[0,1]$, $\phi'\in[0,2\pi)$, integrating $a(z')b(z')\rho'$ over the whole solid at uniform density reproduces the textbook cone volume $V=\tfrac13\pi a_0b_0H$, confirming the parametrization.

📏 Parameters
$\rho_0$Volume charge density (uniform case)nC/m³
$a_0,b_0$Semi-axes of the cone's rim (at $z'=H$)m
$H$Height, apex to rimm
$t$Thickness fraction — $t=1$ solid cone, $t\to0$ thin conical shell—

Several shells sharing one apex and axis (different $a_0,b_0,H,t$) are concentric nested cones — the direct analogue of concentric paraboloids or spheres.

$$V(\mathbf r)=k\!\int_0^H\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_{\rho'_{\text{lo}}}^{1}\frac{\rho(\rho',z')\,a(z')b(z')\,\rho'}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}\,d\rho'\,d\phi'\,dz'$$
⬡ Why This System Has No Closed Form

The classical exact solutions for charge on a cone (e.g. a charged conducting cone) are built from Legendre/conical functions in the polar angle measured from the apex — a genuinely different special-function family from the Paraboloid's own numerics-only treatment, and not one this app builds machinery for. Instead, $V$ and $\mathbf E$ are obtained by direct 3D quadrature (composite Simpson, the reference) cross-checked against an independent 3D Monte Carlo integral — the same two-method pattern used throughout the Ellipsoid/Paraboloid/Hyperboloid systems.

🖼 Geometry
∂ Parametrization and the Volume Jacobian
A self-similar coordinate family

Write every interior/boundary point as $x'=a(z')\rho'\cos\phi'$, $y'=b(z')\rho'\sin\phi'$, with $a(z')=a_0(z'/H)$, $b(z')=b_0(z'/H)$ — the semi-axes now scale linearly with height, in contrast to the Paraboloid system's $\sqrt{z'/H}$. $\rho'\in[0,1]$ is the dimensionless fraction of the way to the lateral surface at that height.

The Jacobian — identical algebra to the Paraboloid, different a(z),b(z)

Computing $\partial(x',y',z')/\partial(\rho',\phi',z')$: the row for $z'$ contributes only $\partial z'/\partial z'=1$, leaving the same $2\times2$ polar-style block as the Paraboloid's own derivation:

$$dV=a(z')\,b(z')\,\rho'\,d\rho'\,d\phi'\,dz'$$

Only $a(z'),b(z')$ differ from the Paraboloid system; the Jacobian's own functional form does not.

Charge element and the master integrals
$$dq=\rho(\rho',z')\,a(z')b(z')\,\rho'\,d\rho'\,d\phi'\,dz'$$
$$V(\mathbf r)=k\!\iiint\!\frac{dq}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|},\qquad \mathbf E(\mathbf r)=k\!\iiint\!\frac{(\mathbf r-\mathbf r')\,dq}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|^3}$$

with $\rho'$ ranging over $[\max(0,1-t),1]$ — $t=1$ fills the whole solid cone; small $t$ leaves a thin band near the lateral surface, approximating a genuine 2D conical shell of local surface density $\sigma_{\text{eff}}\approx\rho_0\cdot(\text{local normal thickness})$.

Symmetry: E_x=E_y=0 exactly on the axis

On the axis ($x_0=y_0=$ apex position), reflecting $\phi'\to-\phi'$ sends $y'\to-y'$ while leaving $x',z',\rho(\rho',z')$ unchanged (density never depends on $\phi'$) — paired contributions' $y$-components cancel while $x,z$ add. The companion reflection $\phi'\to\pi-\phi'$ kills $E_x$ the same way. So $E_x=E_y=0$ exactly on-axis, for any $a_0,b_0$ and any radially- or height-graded density — identical to the Paraboloid system's own axial symmetry argument, since neither derivation depended on how $a(z'),b(z')$ scale with $z'$.

Total charge, uniform ρ — a built-in geometry check
$$Q=\rho_0\!\int_0^H\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^1 a(z')b(z')\rho'\,d\rho'\,d\phi'\,dz'=\rho_0\,a_0b_0\!\int_0^H\!\left(\frac{z'}{H}\right)^{\!2}dz'\cdot\pi=\frac{\pi a_0b_0H}{3}\,\rho_0$$

using $\int_0^1\rho'd\rho'=\tfrac12$ and $\int_0^H(z'/H)^2dz'=H/3$. This reproduces the textbook cone volume $V=\tfrac13\pi a_0b_0H$ exactly, confirming the parametrization — the Simulation tab's own numeric charge integral is checked against this closed form whenever the profile is uniform and $t=1$.

Numerical evaluation

Composite Simpson's rule over the 3D box $(\rho',\phi',z')$ serves as the reference; a fully independent Monte Carlo integral over the same domain (flat sampling, Jacobian folded explicitly into the integrand) is the cross-check — exactly mirroring the Paraboloid system's own two-method comparison.

⊕ Multiple Concentric Shells

$V$ and $\mathbf E$ superpose linearly, so several nested cones (different $a_0,b_0,H$, possibly opposite-sign density, possibly different thickness) simply sum their own independent 3D integrals — the same superposition principle used for every multi-shell system in this app.

∫ Master Formula and Regimes
$$V(\mathbf r)=k\!\int_{0}^{H}\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_{\rho'_{\text{lo}}}^{1}\frac{\rho(\rho',z')\,a(z')b(z')\,\rho'}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}\,d\rho'\,d\phi'\,dz',\qquad a(z')=a_0\frac{z'}{H},\ b(z')=b_0\frac{z'}{H}$$

No elementary or standard-special-function closed form exists for a general field point; evaluated by direct 3D quadrature (Simpson reference, Monte Carlo cross-check).

RegimeConditionBehaviour
On-axis$x_0=y_0=$ apex$E_x=E_y=0$ exactly (symmetry); $V,E_z$ still numerical
Off-axisgenericSmooth, finite; Simpson 3D vs Monte Carlo cross-check
Thin shell$t\to0$Approaches a genuine 2D conical surface charge
Far field$r\gg a_0,b_0,H$Reduces to a point charge $Q=\sum Q_i$
Apexat the apex itself$V$ finite; the surface itself pinches to a point there — no singularity for a volume charge
🔢 Fully Worked Numerical Example

Take $\rho_0=4$ nC/m³, $a_0=1.0$ m, $b_0=0.7$ m, $H=2.5$ m, $t=1$ (solid), field point on-axis at $z_0=2.5$ m above the apex.

Total charge (closed form check)
$$Q=\frac{\pi a_0b_0H}{3}\rho_0=\frac{\pi(1.0)(0.7)(2.5)}{3}(4)=7.33\ \text{nC}$$
Field, cross-checked two ways

Because the field point is on-axis, $E_x=E_y=0$ exactly (Derivation tab, Step 4) — the Simulation tab's comparison table confirms this: both the Simpson-3D reference and the Monte Carlo cross-check return these components at the level of their own numerical noise, while $V,E_z$ agree with each other to a few percent (Monte Carlo's own $O(1/\sqrt N)$ convergence rate).

⊙→◯ From a Ring to a Torus

Take the Ring system's own loop of radius $R$ and thicken it into a solid tube: sweep a small disk of radius $a$ (the "tube" or "minor" radius) around a large circle of radius $R_0$ (the "major" radius) lying in the $z'=0$ plane. Every point inside or on the tube is labelled by three coordinates:

$$x'=(R_0+r'\cos\psi)\cos\phi,\qquad y'=(R_0+r'\cos\psi)\sin\phi,\qquad z'=r'\sin\psi$$

with $r'\in[0,a]$ the distance from the tube's own centreline, $\psi\in[0,2\pi)$ the poloidal angle (around the tube's own small circle), and $\phi\in[0,2\pi)$ the toroidal angle (around the big circle) — exactly the Ring system's own azimuthal angle, generalised.

The key simplification. Unlike the Elliptic Cylinder or Elliptic Cone (whose cross-sections break rotational symmetry), a torus is invariant under rotation about the $z$-axis for any $\phi$. That means the field point can always be placed at azimuth $\phi=0$ without loss of generality — exactly as for the Ring, Disk, and hollow/solid Sphere systems — and $\mathbf E$ has no azimuthal component anywhere: $E_\phi\equiv0$.

∂ The Volume Element and the Filament-Ring Trick
$$dV = r'(R_0+r'\cos\psi)\,dr'\,d\psi\,d\phi,\qquad dq=\rho(r',\psi)\,dV$$

Fix $r'$ and $\psi$ and sweep $\phi$ over the full $2\pi$: every such point traces exactly a Ring-system ring of radius $R_{\text{ring}}=R_0+r'\cos\psi$, sitting in the plane $z'=r'\sin\psi$. The charge on that filament, per unit $dr'\,d\psi$, works out (Derivation tab) to the clean differential linear density $\lambda_{\text{eff}}=\rho(r',\psi)\,r'$ — the factor $(R_0+r'\cos\psi)$ cancels against the ring's own circumference. So the whole 3D torus is built by stacking a 2-parameter family of exact Ring-system rings, and the Ring system's own closed form (elliptic integrals $K(k),E(k)$, computed via AGM) does the toroidal ($\phi$) integral for free.

$$V(\rho_0,z_0)=\int_{r'_{\text{lo}}}^{a}\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\Big[V_{\text{ring}}\big(\lambda\!=\!\rho(r',\psi)r',\ R=R_0+r'\cos\psi,\ \rho_0,\ z_0-r'\sin\psi\big)\Big]\,d\psi\,dr'$$

with $\mathbf E$ built the same way from the Ring system's own $E_\rho,E_z$. Only this last, genuinely 2D integral over $(r',\psi)$ is evaluated numerically (Simpson's rule) — a much better-conditioned problem than a raw 3D quadrature, since the angular ($\phi$) direction is already exact.

📏 Parameters & Thickness
$\rho_0$Volume charge density (uniform case)nC/m³
$R_0$Major radius (hole centre to tube centre)m
$a$Minor (tube) radiusm
$t$Thickness fraction — $t=1$ solid torus, small $t$ a thin surface shell—

Exactly the same "thickness unifies solid and shell" device used by the Hyperbolic Cylinder and Elliptic Paraboloid systems: $r'$ ranges over $[\max(0,1-t)\,a,\ a]$. $t=1$ fills the whole tube; small $t$ leaves only a thin band pressed against the torus's own surface — a genuine 2D surface charge.

⚠️ Surface vs. volume, same as elsewhere in this app. The full solid torus ($t=1$) has $V,\mathbf E$ smooth and finite everywhere, including inside the tube. The thin-shell limit ($t\to0$) is a genuine surface charge: $V$ stays finite, but the surface-normal component of $\mathbf E$ has a finite jump of $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ across the tube's own boundary — the same boundary condition derived on the Sheet system's Solution tab, now for a curved, doubly-periodic surface.
⟲ Exact Symmetries

$E_\phi=0$ everywhere, for any density profile — a direct consequence of the torus's continuous rotational symmetry about $z$, not an approximation. If the density is also symmetric under $\psi\to-\psi$ (true for uniform density, any purely $r'$-graded profile, or any $\cos\psi$-type poloidal grading), then on the equatorial plane $z_0=0$: $E_z(\rho_0,0)=0$ exactly, by the same reflection argument used throughout this app (Sheet Step 4, Elliptic Paraboloid Step 4).

🖼 Geometry
∂ The Filament-Ring Reduction
Charge on one filament

The patch between $r',r'+dr'$ and $\psi,\psi+d\psi$, swept over the full $\phi\in[0,2\pi)$, carries $dQ=\rho(r',\psi)\,r'(R_0+r'\cos\psi)\,dr'\,d\psi\,\int_0^{2\pi}d\phi = 2\pi\rho\,r'(R_0+r'\cos\psi)\,dr'\,d\psi$.

Match against a genuine Ring-system ring

A ring of radius $R_{\text{ring}}=R_0+r'\cos\psi$ and linear density $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ carries total charge $2\pi R_{\text{ring}}\lambda_{\text{eff}}$. Setting this equal to $dQ$ above and solving:

$$2\pi(R_0+r'\cos\psi)\,\lambda_{\text{eff}} = 2\pi\rho\,r'(R_0+r'\cos\psi)\,dr'\,d\psi\ \Longrightarrow\ \lambda_{\text{eff}}=\rho(r',\psi)\,r'\,dr'\,d\psi$$

The factor $(R_0+r'\cos\psi)$ cancels exactly — the same kind of cancellation used to build the Disk from Rings and the solid Sphere from hollow Shells.

Reuse the Ring system's own exact closed form, unmodified
$$dV=\frac{4k\,\lambda_{\text{eff}}\,R_{\text{ring}}\,K(k)}{D_+},\qquad dE_\rho=\frac{2k\lambda_{\text{eff}}R_{\text{ring}}}{\rho_0D_+}\!\left[K-\frac{R_{\text{ring}}^2+(z_0-z')^2-\rho_0^2}{D_-^2}E\right],\qquad dE_z=\frac{4k\lambda_{\text{eff}}R_{\text{ring}}(z_0-z')E}{D_-^2D_+}$$

with $z'=r'\sin\psi$, and $k,D_+,D_-$ built from $(R_{\text{ring}},\rho_0,z_0-z')$ exactly as in the Ring system's own Derivation tab.

Integrate over the remaining two variables

Superposing every filament, $r'\in[r'_{\text{lo}},a]$, $\psi\in[0,2\pi)$, gives the master formulas quoted on the Theory tab — a genuinely 2D integral, evaluated by composite Simpson's rule (two nested sums), reusing ringFieldAnalytic() at every sample point.

📍 Thin-Ring Limit — Reduces Exactly to the Ring System

Let $a\to0$ with $t=1$ (so $r'$ collapses to $0$) while holding the total charge $Q=\rho_0\cdot(2\pi R_0)(\pi a^2)$ fixed. Every filament ring then sits at $R_{\text{ring}}\to R_0$, $z'\to0$, and the double integral collapses to a single evaluation of the Ring system's own formula with $\lambda=Q/(2\pi R_0)$ — exactly the Ring system's own $V,E_\rho,E_z$. This is the built-in sanity check available on the Simulation tab: shrink $a$ far below $R_0$ and the torus's own numbers should match a direct call to the Ring system at the same $R_0,\rho_0,z_0$.

⚖ No Closed Form for a General Field Point

Even though the toroidal ($\phi$) direction is handled exactly, the remaining $(r',\psi)$ integral has no further elementary or single standard-special-function reduction for a general off-axis $(\rho_0,z_0)$ — the exact classical solution lives in toroidal coordinates and is built from Legendre functions of half-integer degree (toroidal harmonics), a heavier machinery this app does not build. Instead, both quantities reported on the Simulation tab come from the same deterministic route: the 2D Simpson double integral above supplies $V,E_\rho,E_z$ directly (its own analytic-in-$\phi$ vector kernel), and a second, independent number for $E_\rho,E_z$ is obtained by central-differencing that same integral's own $V$ — no random sampling anywhere, exactly the finite-difference cross-check already used by the Hyperboloid-of-Two-Sheets system.

∫ Master Formula and Regimes
$$V(\rho_0,z_0)=\int_{r'_{\text{lo}}}^{a}\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\!V_{\text{ring}}\big(\rho(r',\psi)r',\,R_0+r'\cos\psi,\,\rho_0,\,z_0-r'\sin\psi\big)\,d\psi\,dr',\qquad r'_{\text{lo}}=\max(0,1-t)\,a$$

No elementary closed form for a general field point; evaluated by 2D Simpson quadrature (reusing the Ring system's own exact closed form at every sample), cross-checked by central-differencing that same integral.

RegimeConditionBehaviour
Everywhereany $(\rho_0,z_0)$$E_\phi=0$ exactly (axisymmetry)
Equatorial plane$z_0=0$, $\psi$-symmetric profile$E_z=0$ exactly; $V,E_\rho$ still numerical
Thin ring limit$a\ll R_0$Reduces exactly to the Ring system's own result
